cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are alternating voltage (ac voltage) and alternating current (ac current)?
cards.back: The electric mains supply in our homes and offices is a voltage that varies like a sine function with time. Such a voltage is called alternating voltage (ac voltage) and the current driven by it in a circuit is called the alternating current (ac current).
cards.quote: The electric mains supply in our homes and offices is a voltage that varies like a sine function with time. Such a voltage is called alternating voltage (ac voltage) and the current driven by it in a circuit is called the alternating current (ac current).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is ac voltage preferred over dc voltage?
cards.back: The main reason for preferring use of ac voltage over dc voltage is that ac voltages can be easily and efficiently converted from one voltage to the other by means of transformers.
cards.quote: The main reason for preferring use of ac voltage over dc voltage is that ac voltages can be easily and efficiently converted from one voltage to the other by means of transformers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a pure resistor, the voltage and current are ____.
cards.back: In a pure resistor, the voltage and current are in phase.
cards.quote: In a pure resistor, the voltage and current are in phase.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a resistor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For resistors, Ohm's law works equally well for which kind of voltages?
cards.back: Ohm's law, which for resistors, works equally well for both ac and dc voltages.
cards.quote: Ohm's law, which for resistors, works equally well for both ac and dc voltages.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a resistor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the average value of an alternating current over one complete cycle?
cards.back: Thus, the sum of the instantaneous current values over one complete cycle is zero, and the average current is zero.
cards.quote: Thus, the sum of the instantaneous current values over one complete cycle is zero, and the average current is zero.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a resistor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the rms current of an alternating current?
cards.back: In fact, the I or rms current is the equivalent dc current that would produce the same average power loss as the alternating current.
cards.quote: In fact, the I or rms current is the equivalent dc current that would produce the same average power loss as the alternating current.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a resistor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the ampere defined for an alternating current?
cards.back: Joule heating is such a property, and there is one ampere of rms value of alternating current in a circuit if the current produces the same average heating effect as one ampere of dc current would produce under the same conditions.
cards.quote: Joule heating is such a property, and there is one ampere of rms value of alternating current in a circuit if the current produces the same average heating effect as one ampere of dc current would produce under the same conditions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a value is given for ac voltage or current, it is ordinarily the ____.
cards.back: When a value is given for ac voltage or current, it is ordinarily the rms value.
cards.quote: When a value is given for ac voltage or current, it is ordinarily the rms value.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The power rating of an element used in ac circuits refers to its ____.
cards.back: The power rating of an element used in ac circuits refers to its average power rating.
cards.quote: The power rating of an element used in ac circuits refers to its average power rating.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are phasors?
cards.back: The phase relationship between current and voltage in an ac circuit can be shown conveniently by representing voltage and current by rotating vectors called phasors.
cards.quote: The phase relationship between current and voltage in an ac circuit can be shown conveniently by representing voltage and current by rotating vectors called phasors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The magnitude of a phasor represents the ____ of the quantity (voltage or current) represented by the phasor.
cards.back: The magnitude of a phasor represents the amplitude or peak value of the quantity (voltage or current) represented by the phasor.
cards.quote: The magnitude of a phasor represents the amplitude or peak value of the quantity (voltage or current) represented by the phasor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a resistor in an ac circuit, what is the phase angle between voltage and current?
cards.back: phasors V and I for the case of a resistor are in the same direction. This is so for all times. This means that the phase angle between the voltage and the current is zero.
cards.quote: phasors V and I for the case of a resistor are in the same direction. This is so for all times. This means that the phase angle between the voltage and the current is zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Are ac voltage and current, represented by phasors, vectors or scalars?
cards.back: Though voltage and current in ac circuit are represented by phasors – rotating vectors, they are not vectors themselves. They are scalar quantities.
cards.quote: Though voltage and current in ac circuit are represented by phasors – rotating vectors, they are not vectors themselves. They are scalar quantities.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does inductive reactance do in a purely inductive ac circuit?
cards.back: The inductive reactance limits the current in a purely inductive circuit in the same way as the resistance limits the current in a purely resistive circuit.
cards.quote: The inductive reactance limits the current in a purely inductive circuit in the same way as the resistance limits the current in a purely resistive circuit.

source.section: AC voltage applied to an inductor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The inductive reactance is ____ to the inductance and to the frequency of the current.
cards.back: The inductive reactance is directly proportional to the inductance and to the frequency of the current.
cards.quote: The inductive reactance is directly proportional to the inductance and to the frequency of the current.

source.section: AC voltage applied to an inductor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Inductive reactance: how does its dimension compare with resistance, and what is its SI unit?
cards.back: The dimension of inductive reactance is the same as that of resistance and its SI unit is ohm
cards.quote: The dimension of inductive reactance is the same as that of resistance and its SI unit is ohm

source.section: AC voltage applied to an inductor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a dc circuit, what happens to the current once a capacitor is fully charged?
cards.back: When the capacitor is fully charged, the current in the circuit falls to zero.
cards.quote: When the capacitor is fully charged, the current in the circuit falls to zero.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a capacitor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does capacitive reactance do, and how does it depend on frequency and capacitance?
cards.back: The capacitive reactance limits the amplitude of the current in a purely capacitive circuit in the same way as the resistance limits the current in a purely resistive circuit. But it is inversely proportional to the frequency and the capacitance.
cards.quote: The capacitive reactance limits the amplitude of the current in a purely capacitive circuit in the same way as the resistance limits the current in a purely resistive circuit. But it is inversely proportional to the frequency and the capacitance.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a capacitor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: As in the case of inductor, the average power supplied to a capacitor over one complete cycle is ____.
cards.back: As in the case of inductor, the average power supplied to a capacitor over one complete cycle is zero.
cards.quote: As in the case of inductor, the average power supplied to a capacitor over one complete cycle is zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A lamp is connected in series with a capacitor. What do you observe on a dc source?
cards.back: When a dc source is connected to a capacitor, the capacitor gets charged and after charging no current flows in the circuit and the lamp will not glow.
cards.quote: When a dc source is connected to a capacitor, the capacitor gets charged and after charging no current flows in the circuit and the lamp will not glow.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a capacitor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A lamp is in series with a capacitor on an ac source. What happens when the capacitance is reduced?
cards.back: Reducing C will increase reactance and the lamp will shine less brightly than before.
cards.quote: Reducing C will increase reactance and the lamp will shine less brightly than before.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a capacitor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A bulb and an open coil inductor are on an ac source; an iron rod is inserted in the coil. What happens to the bulb?
cards.back: As a result, a larger fraction of the applied ac voltage appears across the inductor, leaving less voltage across the bulb. Therefore, the glow of the light bulb decreases.
cards.quote: As a result, a larger fraction of the applied ac voltage appears across the inductor, leaving less voltage across the bulb. Therefore, the glow of the light bulb decreases.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a capacitor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a series LCR circuit, how does the ac current compare in each element?
cards.back: Therefore, the ac current in each element is the same at any time, having the same amplitude and phase.
cards.quote: Therefore, the ac current in each element is the same at any time, having the same amplitude and phase.

source.section: AC voltage applied to a series LCR circuit

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By analogy to the resistance in a circuit, we introduce the ____ Z in an ac circuit
cards.back: By analogy to the resistance in a circuit, we introduce the impedance Z in an ac circuit
cards.quote: By analogy to the resistance in a circuit, we introduce the impedance Z in an ac circuit

source.section: AC voltage applied to a series LCR circuit

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a system's natural frequency?
cards.back: The phenomenon of resonance is common among systems that have a tendency to oscillate at a particular frequency. This frequency is called the system's natural frequency.
cards.quote: The phenomenon of resonance is common among systems that have a tendency to oscillate at a particular frequency. This frequency is called the system's natural frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens when a system is driven by an energy source at a frequency near its natural frequency?
cards.back: If such a system is driven by an energy source at a frequency that is near the natural frequency, the amplitude of oscillation is found to be large.
cards.quote: If such a system is driven by an energy source at a frequency that is near the natural frequency, the amplitude of oscillation is found to be large.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At resonant frequency, the current amplitude is ____
cards.back: At resonant frequency, the current amplitude is maximum
cards.quote: At resonant frequency, the current amplitude is maximum

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a radio tuned to a particular station, in terms of its tuning circuit?
cards.back: In tuning, we vary the capacitance of a capacitor in the tuning circuit such that the resonant frequency of the circuit becomes nearly equal to the frequency of the radio signal received.
cards.quote: In tuning, we vary the capacitance of a capacitor in the tuning circuit such that the resonant frequency of the circuit becomes nearly equal to the frequency of the radio signal received.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The metal detector works on the principle of ____ in ac circuits.
cards.back: The metal detector works on the principle of resonance in ac circuits.
cards.quote: The metal detector works on the principle of resonance in ac circuits.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can the voltages across the resistor and the capacitor in a series RC circuit not simply be added?
cards.back: the two voltages are not in the same phase. Therefore, they cannot be added like ordinary numbers.
cards.quote: the two voltages are not in the same phase. Therefore, they cannot be added like ordinary numbers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an ac circuit, while adding voltages across different elements, one should take care of their ____ properly.
cards.back: In an ac circuit, while adding voltages across different elements, one should take care of their phases properly.
cards.quote: In an ac circuit, while adding voltages across different elements, one should take care of their phases properly.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the average power dissipated in an ac circuit depend?
cards.back: So, the average power dissipated depends not only on the voltage and current but also on the cosine of the phase angle φ between them.
cards.quote: So, the average power dissipated depends not only on the voltage and current but also on the cosine of the phase angle φ between them.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The quantity cos φ is called the ____.
cards.back: The quantity cos φ is called the power factor.
cards.quote: The quantity cos φ is called the power factor.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the power factor in an RLC circuit measure?
cards.back: The power factor in a RLC circuit is a measure of how close the circuit is to expending the maximum power.
cards.quote: The power factor in a RLC circuit is a measure of how close the circuit is to expending the maximum power.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a purely resistive ac circuit, what are the phase angle, power factor and power dissipation?
cards.back: If the circuit contains only pure R, it is called resistive. In that case φ = 0, cos φ = 1. There is maximum power dissipation.
cards.quote: If the circuit contains only pure R, it is called resistive. In that case φ = 0, cos φ = 1. There is maximum power dissipation.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is wattless current?
cards.back: If the circuit contains only an inductor or capacitor, we know that the phase difference between voltage and current is π/2. Therefore, cos φ = 0, and no power is dissipated even though a current is flowing in the circuit. This current is sometimes referred to as wattless current.
cards.quote: If the circuit contains only an inductor or capacitor, we know that the phase difference between voltage and current is π/2. Therefore, cos φ = 0, and no power is dissipated even though a current is flowing in the circuit. This current is sometimes referred to as wattless current.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The only element that dissipates energy in an ac circuit is the ____.
cards.back: The only element that dissipates energy in an ac circuit is the resistive element.
cards.quote: The only element that dissipates energy in an ac circuit is the resistive element.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: That is, ____ is dissipated in a circuit (through R) at resonance.
cards.back: That is, maximum power is dissipated in a circuit (through R) at resonance.
cards.quote: That is, maximum power is dissipated in a circuit (through R) at resonance.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Power factor can often be improved by the use of a ____ of appropriate capacitance in the circuit.
cards.back: Power factor can often be improved by the use of a capacitor of appropriate capacitance in the circuit.
cards.quote: Power factor can often be improved by the use of a capacitor of appropriate capacitance in the circuit.

source.section: Power in AC circuit: the power factor

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which device transforms an alternating voltage, and on what principle does it work?
cards.back: This is done with a device called transformer using the principle of mutual induction.
cards.quote: This is done with a device called transformer using the principle of mutual induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a transformer consist of?
cards.back: A transformer consists of two sets of coils, insulated from each other. They are wound on a soft-iron core
cards.quote: A transformer consists of two sets of coils, insulated from each other. They are wound on a soft-iron core

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Often the primary coil is the ____ coil and the secondary coil is the ____ coil of the transformer.
cards.back: Often the primary coil is the input coil and the secondary coil is the output coil of the transformer.
cards.quote: Often the primary coil is the input coil and the secondary coil is the output coil of the transformer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a transformer induce an emf in the secondary coil?
cards.back: When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, the resulting current produces an alternating magnetic flux which links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
cards.quote: When an alternating voltage is applied to the primary, the resulting current produces an alternating magnetic flux which links the secondary and induces an emf in it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The value of this emf depends on the ____ in the secondary.
cards.back: The value of this emf depends on the number of turns in the secondary.
cards.quote: The value of this emf depends on the number of turns in the secondary.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an ideal transformer?
cards.back: We consider an ideal transformer in which the primary has negligible resistance and all the flux in the core links both primary and secondary windings.
cards.quote: We consider an ideal transformer in which the primary has negligible resistance and all the flux in the core links both primary and secondary windings.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If the transformer is assumed to be 100% efficient (no energy losses), the power input is equal to the ____
cards.back: If the transformer is assumed to be 100% efficient (no energy losses), the power input is equal to the power output
cards.quote: If the transformer is assumed to be 100% efficient (no energy losses), the power input is equal to the power output

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Although some energy is always lost, this is a good approximation, since a well designed transformer may have an efficiency of more than ____.
cards.back: Although some energy is always lost, this is a good approximation, since a well designed transformer may have an efficiency of more than 95%.
cards.quote: Although some energy is always lost, this is a good approximation, since a well designed transformer may have an efficiency of more than 95%.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name the three assumptions used to obtain the voltage relation of a transformer.
cards.quote: Note that the above relation has been obtained using three assumptions: (i) the primary resistance and current are small; (ii) the same flux links both the primary and the secondary as very little flux escapes from the core, and (iii) the secondary current is small.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If the secondary coil has turns less than the primary, we have a ____ transformer.
cards.back: If the secondary coil has turns less than the primary, we have a step-down transformer.
cards.quote: If the secondary coil has turns less than the primary, we have a step-down transformer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How can flux leakage in a transformer be reduced?
cards.back: It can be reduced by winding the primary and secondary coils one over the other.
cards.quote: It can be reduced by winding the primary and secondary coils one over the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is heat loss in the windings of a high current, low voltage transformer minimised?
cards.back: In high current, low voltage windings, these are minimised by using thick wire.
cards.quote: In high current, low voltage windings, these are minimised by using thick wire.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the eddy current loss in a transformer core reduced?
cards.back: The effect is reduced by using a laminated core.
cards.quote: The effect is reduced by using a laminated core.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is hysteresis loss in a transformer core kept to a minimum?
cards.back: The resulting expenditure of energy in the core appears as heat and is kept to a minimum by using a magnetic material which has a low hysteresis loss.
cards.quote: The resulting expenditure of energy in the core appears as heat and is kept to a minimum by using a magnetic material which has a low hysteresis loss.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The large scale transmission and distribution of electrical energy over long distances is done with the use of ____.
cards.back: The large scale transmission and distribution of electrical energy over long distances is done with the use of transformers.
cards.quote: The large scale transmission and distribution of electrical energy over long distances is done with the use of transformers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Motor vs generator: the energy input and output of each (motor first).
cards.back:
In a motor, electric energy is the input and mechanical energy is the output.
In a generator, mechanical energy is the input and electric energy is the output.
cards.quote:
In a motor, electric energy is the input and mechanical energy is the output.
In a generator, mechanical energy is the input and electric energy is the output.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does a step-up transformer not violate the law of conservation of energy?
cards.back: This does not violate the law of conservation of energy. The current is reduced by the same proportion.
cards.quote: This does not violate the law of conservation of energy. The current is reduced by the same proportion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who proposed the first model of the atom, and in which year?
cards.back: The first model of atom was proposed by J. J. Thomson in 1898.
cards.quote: The first model of atom was proposed by J. J. Thomson in 1898.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In Thomson's model, how are the positive charge and the electrons arranged?
cards.back: According to this model, the positive charge of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout the volume of the atom and the negatively charged electrons are embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon.
cards.quote: According to this model, the positive charge of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout the volume of the atom and the negatively charged electrons are embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What was Thomson's model of the atom picturesquely called?
cards.back: This model was picturesquely called plum pudding model of the atom.
cards.quote: This model was picturesquely called plum pudding model of the atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What kind of radiation do condensed matter and dense gases emit at all temperatures?
cards.back: We know that condensed matter (solids and liquids) and dense gases at all temperatures emit electromagnetic radiation in which a continuous distribution of several wavelengths is present, though with different intensities.
cards.quote: We know that condensed matter (solids and liquids) and dense gases at all temperatures emit electromagnetic radiation in which a continuous distribution of several wavelengths is present, though with different intensities.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What wavelengths does light from rarefied gases heated in a flame or excited in a glow tube contain?
cards.back: light emitted from rarefied gases heated in a flame, or excited electrically in a glow tube such as the familiar neon sign or mercury vapour light has only certain discrete wavelengths. The spectrum appears as a series of bright lines.
cards.quote: light emitted from rarefied gases heated in a flame, or excited electrically in a glow tube such as the familiar neon sign or mercury vapour light has only certain discrete wavelengths. The spectrum appears as a series of bright lines.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can radiation from a rarefied gas be considered due to individual atoms?
cards.back: In such gases, the average spacing between atoms is large. Hence, the radiation emitted can be considered due to individual atoms rather than because of interactions between atoms or molecules.
cards.quote: In such gases, the average spacing between atoms is large. Hence, the radiation emitted can be considered due to individual atoms rather than because of interactions between atoms or molecules.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the early nineteenth century, what was established about each element and its spectrum?
cards.back: In the early nineteenth century it was also established that each element is associated with a characteristic spectrum of radiation, for example, hydrogen always gives a set of lines with fixed relative position between the lines.
cards.quote: In the early nineteenth century it was also established that each element is associated with a characteristic spectrum of radiation, for example, hydrogen always gives a set of lines with fixed relative position between the lines.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who obtained a simple empirical formula for a group of lines of atomic hydrogen, and when?
cards.back: In 1885, Johann Jakob Balmer (1825 – 1898) obtained a simple empirical formula which gave the wavelengths of a group of lines emitted by atomic hydrogen.
cards.quote: In 1885, Johann Jakob Balmer (1825 – 1898) obtained a simple empirical formula which gave the wavelengths of a group of lines emitted by atomic hydrogen.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is Rutherford's planetary model of the atom also called?
cards.back: The explanation of the results led to the birth of Rutherford's planetary model of atom (also called the nuclear model of the atom).
cards.quote: The explanation of the results led to the birth of Rutherford's planetary model of atom (also called the nuclear model of the atom).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What could Rutherford's nuclear model not explain about the light emitted by atoms?
cards.back: Rutherford's nuclear model was a major step towards how we see the atom today. However, it could not explain why atoms emit light of only discrete wavelengths.
cards.quote: Rutherford's nuclear model was a major step towards how we see the atom today. However, it could not explain why atoms emit light of only discrete wavelengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who performed the alpha-particle scattering experiments, at whose suggestion, and when?
cards.back: At the suggestion of Ernst Rutherford, in 1911, H. Geiger and E. Marsden performed some experiments.
cards.quote: At the suggestion of Ernst Rutherford, in 1911, H. Geiger and E. Marsden performed some experiments.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did the rotatable detector in the Geiger-Marsden experiment consist of?
cards.back: The scattered alpha-particles were observed through a rotatable detector consisting of zinc sulphide screen and a microscope.
cards.quote: The scattered alpha-particles were observed through a rotatable detector consisting of zinc sulphide screen and a microscope.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did scattered α-particles produce on striking the zinc sulphide screen?
cards.back: The scattered alpha-particles on striking the screen produced brief light flashes or scintillations.
cards.quote: The scattered alpha-particles on striking the screen produced brief light flashes or scintillations.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is Rutherford credited with the discovery of the nucleus?
cards.back: This agreement supported the hypothesis of the nuclear atom. This is why Rutherford is credited with the discovery of the nucleus.
cards.quote: This agreement supported the hypothesis of the nuclear atom. This is why Rutherford is credited with the discovery of the nucleus.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Describe Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom.
cards.back: In Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom, the entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in the nucleus with the electrons some distance away. The electrons would be moving in orbits about the nucleus just as the planets do around the sun.
cards.quote: In Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom, the entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in the nucleus with the electrons some distance away. The electrons would be moving in orbits about the nucleus just as the planets do around the sun.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How far are the electrons from the nucleus compared with its size, and what does this imply?
cards.back: Thus, the electrons would seem to be at a distance from the nucleus of about 10,000 to 100,000 times the size of the nucleus itself. Thus, most of an atom is empty space.
cards.quote: Thus, the electrons would seem to be at a distance from the nucleus of about 10,000 to 100,000 times the size of the nucleus itself. Thus, most of an atom is empty space.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do most α-particles go right through a thin metal foil?
cards.back: With the atom being largely empty space, it is easy to see why most α-particles go right through a thin metal foil.
cards.quote: With the atom being largely empty space, it is easy to see why most α-particles go right through a thin metal foil.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What scatters an α-particle through a large angle when it comes near a nucleus?
cards.back: However, when α-particle happens to come near a nucleus, the intense electric field there scatters it through a large angle.
cards.quote: However, when α-particle happens to come near a nucleus, the intense electric field there scatters it through a large angle.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do atomic electrons not appreciably affect the α-particles?
cards.back: The atomic electrons, being so light, do not appreciably affect the α-particles.
cards.quote: The atomic electrons, being so light, do not appreciably affect the α-particles.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are α-particles, and how much positive charge do they carry?
cards.back: Alpha-particles are nuclei of helium atoms and, therefore, carry two units, 2e, of positive charge and have the mass of the helium atom.
cards.quote: Alpha-particles are nuclei of helium atoms and, therefore, carry two units, 2e, of positive charge and have the mass of the helium atom.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the charge of the gold nucleus, and what is Z for gold?
cards.back: The charge of the gold nucleus is Ze, where Z is the atomic number of the atom; for gold Z = 79.
cards.quote: The charge of the gold nucleus is Ze, where Z is the atomic number of the atom; for gold Z = 79.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which laws are used to compute the trajectory of an α-particle scattered by a nucleus?
cards.back: Under these assumptions, the trajectory of an alpha-particle can be computed employing Newton's second law of motion and the Coulomb's law for electrostatic force of repulsion between the alpha-particle and the positively charged nucleus.
cards.quote: Under these assumptions, the trajectory of an alpha-particle can be computed employing Newton's second law of motion and the Coulomb's law for electrostatic force of repulsion between the alpha-particle and the positively charged nucleus.

source.section: Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is Rutherford scattering a powerful way to determine?
cards.back: Rutherford scattering therefore, is a powerful way to determine an upper limit to the size of the nucleus.
cards.quote: Rutherford scattering therefore, is a powerful way to determine an upper limit to the size of the nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the classical Rutherford model picture the atom?
cards.back: The Rutherford nuclear model of the atom which involves classical concepts, pictures the atom as an electrically neutral sphere consisting of a very small, massive and positively charged nucleus at the centre surrounded by the revolving electrons in their respective dynamically stable orbits.
cards.quote: The Rutherford nuclear model of the atom which involves classical concepts, pictures the atom as an electrically neutral sphere consisting of a very small, massive and positively charged nucleus at the centre surrounded by the revolving electrons in their respective dynamically stable orbits.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a negative total energy of the electron in a hydrogen atom imply?
cards.back: The total energy of the electron is negative. This implies the fact that the electron is bound to the nucleus. If E were positive, an electron will not follow a closed orbit around the nucleus.
cards.quote: The total energy of the electron is negative. This implies the fact that the electron is bound to the nucleus. If E were positive, an electron will not follow a closed orbit around the nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an emission line spectrum?
cards.back: When an atomic gas or vapour is excited at low pressure, usually by passing an electric current through it, the emitted radiation has a spectrum which contains certain specific wavelengths only. A spectrum of this kind is termed as emission line spectrum and it consists of bright lines on a dark background.
cards.quote: When an atomic gas or vapour is excited at low pressure, usually by passing an electric current through it, the emitted radiation has a spectrum which contains certain specific wavelengths only. A spectrum of this kind is termed as emission line spectrum and it consists of bright lines on a dark background.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the emission line spectrum of a material called a fingerprint of the gas?
cards.back: Study of emission line spectra of a material can therefore serve as a type of "fingerprint" for identification of the gas.
cards.quote: Study of emission line spectra of a material can therefore serve as a type of "fingerprint" for identification of the gas.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When white light passes through a gas, dark lines appear. What do they correspond to, and what is this called?
cards.back: These dark lines correspond precisely to those wavelengths which were found in the emission line spectrum of the gas. This is called the absorption spectrum of the material of the gas.
cards.quote: These dark lines correspond precisely to those wavelengths which were found in the emission line spectrum of the gas. This is called the absorption spectrum of the material of the gas.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does classical electromagnetic theory predict for an accelerating charged particle?
cards.back: According to classical electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle emits radiation in the form of electromagnetic waves.
cards.quote: According to classical electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle emits radiation in the form of electromagnetic waves.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By classical theory, what would happen to an orbiting electron's energy and path?
cards.back: The energy of an accelerating electron should therefore, continuously decrease. The electron would spiral inward and eventually fall into the nucleus
cards.quote: The energy of an accelerating electron should therefore, continuously decrease. The electron would spiral inward and eventually fall into the nucleus

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By classical theory, what is the frequency of waves emitted by a revolving electron?
cards.back: according to the classical electromagnetic theory, the frequency of the electromagnetic waves emitted by the revolving electrons is equal to the frequency of revolution.
cards.quote: according to the classical electromagnetic theory, the frequency of the electromagnetic waves emitted by the revolving electrons is equal to the frequency of revolution.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why would a classical atom emit a continuous spectrum, contradicting observation?
cards.back: As the electrons spiral inwards, their angular velocities and hence their frequencies would change continuously, and so will the frequency of the light emitted. Thus, they would emit a continuous spectrum, in contradiction to the line spectrum actually observed.
cards.quote: As the electrons spiral inwards, their angular velocities and hence their frequencies would change continuously, and so will the frequency of the light emitted. Thus, they would emit a continuous spectrum, in contradiction to the line spectrum actually observed.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did Bohr conclude in 1913 about electromagnetic theory?
cards.back: Bohr, in 1913, concluded that in spite of the success of electromagnetic theory in explaining large-scale phenomena, it could not be applied to the processes at the atomic scale.
cards.quote: Bohr, in 1913, concluded that in spite of the success of electromagnetic theory in explaining large-scale phenomena, it could not be applied to the processes at the atomic scale.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In what form did Bohr give his theory?
cards.back: Bohr combined classical and early quantum concepts and gave his theory in the form of three postulates.
cards.quote: Bohr combined classical and early quantum concepts and gave his theory in the form of three postulates.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Bohr's first postulate.
cards.back: Bohr's first postulate was that an electron in an atom could revolve in certain stable orbits without the emission of radiant energy, contrary to the predictions of electromagnetic theory. According to this postulate, each atom has certain definite stable states in which it can exist, and each possible state has definite total energy. These are called the stationary states of the atom.
cards.quote: Bohr's first postulate was that an electron in an atom could revolve in certain stable orbits without the emission of radiant energy, contrary to the predictions of electromagnetic theory. According to this postulate, each atom has certain definite stable states in which it can exist, and each possible state has definite total energy. These are called the stationary states of the atom.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Bohr's second postulate.
cards.back: Bohr's second postulate defines these stable orbits. This postulate states that the electron revolves around the nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is some integral multiple of h/2π where h is the Planck's constant
cards.quote: Bohr's second postulate defines these stable orbits. This postulate states that the electron revolves around the nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is some integral multiple of h/2π where h is the Planck's constant

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What follows for the angular momentum of the orbiting electron from Bohr's second postulate?
cards.back: Thus the angular momentum (L) of the orbiting electron is quantised.
cards.quote: Thus the angular momentum (L) of the orbiting electron is quantised.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Bohr's third postulate.
cards.back: Bohr's third postulate incorporated into atomic theory the early quantum concepts that had been developed by Planck and Einstein. It states that an electron might make a transition from one of its specified non-radiating orbits to another of lower energy. When it does so, a photon is emitted having energy equal to the energy difference between the initial and final states.
cards.quote: Bohr's third postulate incorporated into atomic theory the early quantum concepts that had been developed by Planck and Einstein. It states that an electron might make a transition from one of its specified non-radiating orbits to another of lower energy. When it does so, a photon is emitted having energy equal to the energy difference between the initial and final states.

source.section: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which orbit is the energy of the hydrogen atom the least?
cards.back: The energy of an atom is the least (largest negative value) when its electron is revolving in an orbit closest to the nucleus i.e., the one for which n = 1.
cards.quote: The energy of an atom is the least (largest negative value) when its electron is revolving in an orbit closest to the nucleus i.e., the one for which n = 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the ground state of an atom?
cards.back: The lowest state of the atom, called the ground state, is that of the lowest energy, with the electron revolving in the orbit of smallest radius, the Bohr radius
cards.quote: The lowest state of the atom, called the ground state, is that of the lowest energy, with the electron revolving in the orbit of smallest radius, the Bohr radius

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the ionisation energy of the hydrogen atom?
cards.back: Therefore, the minimum energy required to free the electron from the ground state of the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV. It is called the ionisation energy of the hydrogen atom.
cards.quote: Therefore, the minimum energy required to free the electron from the ground state of the hydrogen atom is 13.6 eV. It is called the ionisation energy of the hydrogen atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At room temperature, most of the hydrogen atoms are in ____.
cards.back: At room temperature, most of the hydrogen atoms are in ground state.
cards.quote: At room temperature, most of the hydrogen atoms are in ground state.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is a hydrogen atom said to be in an excited state?
cards.back: When a hydrogen atom receives energy by processes such as electron collisions, the atom may acquire sufficient energy to raise the electron to higher energy states. The atom is then said to be in an excited state.
cards.quote: When a hydrogen atom receives energy by processes such as electron collisions, the atom may acquire sufficient energy to raise the electron to higher energy states. The atom is then said to be in an excited state.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the principal quantum number n label?
cards.back: The principal quantum number n labels the stationary states in the ascending order of energy.
cards.quote: The principal quantum number n labels the stationary states in the ascending order of energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are the lines in atomic spectra produced, and what are they called?
cards.back: The various lines in the atomic spectra are produced when electrons jump from higher energy state to a lower energy state and photons are emitted. These spectral lines are called emission lines.
cards.quote: The various lines in the atomic spectra are produced when electrons jump from higher energy state to a lower energy state and photons are emitted. These spectral lines are called emission lines.

source.section: The Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is absorption in an atom?
cards.back: when an atom absorbs a photon that has precisely the same energy needed by the electron in a lower energy state to make transitions to a higher energy state, the process is called absorption.
cards.quote: when an atom absorbs a photon that has precisely the same energy needed by the electron in a lower energy state to make transitions to a higher energy state, the process is called absorption.

source.section: The Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do the dark lines in the absorption spectrum of a rarefied gas indicate?
cards.back: Thus if photons with a continuous range of frequencies pass through a rarefied gas and then are analysed with a spectrometer, a series of dark spectral absorption lines appear in the continuous spectrum. The dark lines indicate the frequencies that have been absorbed by the atoms of the gas.
cards.quote: Thus if photons with a continuous range of frequencies pass through a rarefied gas and then are analysed with a spectrometer, a series of dark spectral absorption lines appear in the continuous spectrum. The dark lines indicate the frequencies that have been absorbed by the atoms of the gas.

source.section: The Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who explained the puzzle of Bohr's second postulate, and when?
cards.back: The French physicist Louis de Broglie explained this puzzle in 1923, ten years after Bohr proposed his model.
cards.quote: The French physicist Louis de Broglie explained this puzzle in 1923, ten years after Bohr proposed his model.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who experimentally verified the wave nature of electrons, and when?
cards.back: C. J. Davisson and L. H. Germer later experimentally verified the wave nature of electrons in 1927.
cards.quote: C. J. Davisson and L. H. Germer later experimentally verified the wave nature of electrons in 1927.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How did de Broglie argue the electron in a Bohr orbit must be seen?
cards.back: Louis de Broglie argued that the electron in its circular orbit, as proposed by Bohr, must be seen as a particle wave.
cards.quote: Louis de Broglie argued that the electron in its circular orbit, as proposed by Bohr, must be seen as a particle wave.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Under what conditions can particle waves lead to standing waves?
cards.back: In analogy to waves travelling on a string, particle waves too can lead to standing waves under resonant conditions.
cards.quote: In analogy to waves travelling on a string, particle waves too can lead to standing waves under resonant conditions.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did the de Broglie hypothesis provide an explanation for?
cards.back: Thus de Broglie hypothesis provided an explanation for Bohr's second postulate for the quantisation of angular momentum of the orbiting electron.
cards.quote: Thus de Broglie hypothesis provided an explanation for Bohr's second postulate for the quantisation of angular momentum of the orbiting electron.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the quantised electron orbits and energy states due to?
cards.back: The quantised electron orbits and energy states are due to the wave nature of the electron and only resonant standing waves can persist.
cards.quote: The quantised electron orbits and energy states are due to the wave nature of the electron and only resonant standing waves can persist.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does Bohr's model correctly predict for hydrogenic atoms?
cards.back: Bohr's model, involving classical trajectory picture (planet-like electron orbiting the nucleus), correctly predicts the gross features of the hydrogenic atoms, in particular, the frequencies of the radiation emitted or selectively absorbed.
cards.quote: Bohr's model, involving classical trajectory picture (planet-like electron orbiting the nucleus), correctly predicts the gross features of the hydrogenic atoms, in particular, the frequencies of the radiation emitted or selectively absorbed.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are hydrogenic atoms?
cards.back: Hydrogenic atoms are the atoms consisting of a nucleus with positive charge +Ze and a single electron, where Z is the proton number. Examples are hydrogen atom, singly ionised helium, doubly ionised lithium, and so forth.
cards.quote: Hydrogenic atoms are the atoms consisting of a nucleus with positive charge +Ze and a single electron, where Z is the proton number. Examples are hydrogen atom, singly ionised helium, doubly ionised lithium, and so forth.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can Bohr's model not be extended to atoms with more than one electron?
cards.back: Difficulty lies in the fact that each electron interacts not only with the positively charged nucleus but also with all other electrons.
cards.quote: Difficulty lies in the fact that each electron interacts not only with the positively charged nucleus but also with all other electrons.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the formulation of Bohr's model not include?
cards.back: The formulation of Bohr model involves electrical force between positively charged nucleus and electron. It does not include the electrical forces between electrons which necessarily appear in multi-electron atoms.
cards.quote: The formulation of Bohr model involves electrical force between positively charged nucleus and electron. It does not include the electrical forces between electrons which necessarily appear in multi-electron atoms.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What theory is needed for complex atoms?
cards.back: For complex atoms we have to use a new and radical theory based on Quantum Mechanics, which provides a more complete picture of the atomic structure.
cards.quote: For complex atoms we have to use a new and radical theory based on Quantum Mechanics, which provides a more complete picture of the atomic structure.

source.section: de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What charges does an atom, as a whole, contain?
cards.back: Atom, as a whole, is electrically neutral and therefore contains equal amount of positive and negative charges.
cards.quote: Atom, as a whole, is electrically neutral and therefore contains equal amount of positive and negative charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an atom in Thomson's model?
cards.back: In Thomson's model, an atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it.
cards.quote: In Thomson's model, an atom is a spherical cloud of positive charges with electrons embedded in it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where are the mass and positive charge of the atom in Rutherford's model?
cards.back: In Rutherford's model, most of the mass of the atom and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (typically one by ten thousand the size of an atom), and the electrons revolve around it.
cards.quote: In Rutherford's model, most of the mass of the atom and all its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (typically one by ten thousand the size of an atom), and the electrons revolve around it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name the two main difficulties of Rutherford's nuclear model in explaining the structure of the atom.
cards.back:
It predicts that atoms are unstable because the accelerated electrons revolving around the nucleus must spiral into the nucleus. This contradicts the stability of matter.
It cannot explain the characteristic line spectra of atoms of different elements.
cards.quote: Rutherford nuclear model has two main difficulties in explaining the structure of atom: (a) It predicts that atoms are unstable because the accelerated electrons revolving around the nucleus must spiral into the nucleus. This contradicts the stability of matter. (b) It cannot explain the characteristic line spectra of atoms of different elements.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a line spectrum?
cards.back: Atoms of most of the elements are stable and emit characteristic spectrum. The spectrum consists of a set of isolated parallel lines termed as line spectrum.
cards.quote: Atoms of most of the elements are stable and emit characteristic spectrum. The spectrum consists of a set of isolated parallel lines termed as line spectrum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens when an atom absorbs radiation of the same frequency it emits?
cards.back: An atom absorbs radiation of the same frequency the atom emits, in which case the electron is transferred to an orbit with a higher value of n.
cards.quote: An atom absorbs radiation of the same frequency the atom emits, in which case the electron is transferred to an orbit with a higher value of n.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the result of the quantisation condition of angular momentum for the electron orbits?
cards.back: As a result of the quantisation condition of angular momentum, the electron orbits the nucleus at only specific radii.
cards.quote: As a result of the quantisation condition of angular momentum, the electron orbits the nucleus at only specific radii.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the ground state energy of the hydrogen atom?
cards.back: The n = 1 state is called ground state. In hydrogen atom the ground state energy is −13.6 eV.
cards.quote: The n = 1 state is called ground state. In hydrogen atom the ground state energy is −13.6 eV.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are atoms excited to higher states?
cards.back: Higher values of n correspond to excited states (n > 1). Atoms are excited to these higher states by collisions with other atoms or electrons or by absorption of a photon of right frequency.
cards.quote: Higher values of n correspond to excited states (n > 1). Atoms are excited to these higher states by collisions with other atoms or electrons or by absorption of a photon of right frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do de Broglie's standing waves relate to Bohr's orbits?
cards.back: The orbits correspond to circular standing waves in which the circumference of the orbit equals a whole number of wavelengths.
cards.quote: The orbits correspond to circular standing waves in which the circumference of the orbit equals a whole number of wavelengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Thomson's model vs Rutherford's model: why is each unstable?
cards.back: Thomson's model is unstable electrostatically, while Rutherford's model is unstable because of electromagnetic radiation of orbiting electrons.
cards.quote: Thomson's model is unstable electrostatically, while Rutherford's model is unstable because of electromagnetic radiation of orbiting electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is quantising angular momentum natural in Bohr's second postulate?
cards.back: Note, h has dimensions of angular momentum, and for circular orbits, angular momentum is a very relevant quantity.
cards.quote: Note, h has dimensions of angular momentum, and for circular orbits, angular momentum is a very relevant quantity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What was inconsistent with the uncertainty principle in Bohr's model, and what replaced it?
cards.back: The orbital picture in Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom was inconsistent with the uncertainty principle. It was replaced by modern quantum mechanics in which Bohr's orbits are regions where the electron may be found with large probability.
cards.quote: The orbital picture in Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom was inconsistent with the uncertainty principle. It was replaced by modern quantum mechanics in which Bohr's orbits are regions where the electron may be found with large probability.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What foundation did Bohr lay by postulating specific non-radiating orbits?
cards.back: Bohr laid the foundation of the quantum theory by postulating specific orbits in which electrons do not radiate.
cards.quote: Bohr laid the foundation of the quantum theory by postulating specific orbits in which electrons do not radiate.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define electric current through a given area of a conductor.
cards.back: Current through a given area of a conductor is the net charge passing per unit time through the area.
cards.quote: Current through a given area of a conductor is the net charge passing per unit time through the area.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of electric current?
cards.back: In SI units, the unit of current is ampere.
cards.quote: In SI units, the unit of current is ampere.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An ampere is defined through ____ of currents that we will study in the following chapter.
cards.back: An ampere is defined through magnetic effects of currents that we will study in the following chapter.
cards.quote: An ampere is defined through magnetic effects of currents that we will study in the following chapter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charges in ____ constitute an electric current.
cards.back: Charges in motion constitute an electric current.
cards.quote: Charges in motion constitute an electric current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the typical order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances?
cards.back: An ampere is typically the order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances.
cards.quote: An ampere is typically the order of magnitude of currents in domestic appliances.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are conductors?
cards.back: In other materials, notably metals, some of the electrons are practically free to move within the bulk material. These materials, generally called conductors, develop electric currents in them when an electric field is applied.
cards.quote: In other materials, notably metals, some of the electrons are practically free to move within the bulk material. These materials, generally called conductors, develop electric currents in them when an electric field is applied.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the ____.
cards.back: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the negatively charged electrons.
cards.quote: If we consider solid conductors, then of course the atoms are tightly bound to each other so that the current is carried by the negatively charged electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which type of conductor can both positive and negative charges move?
cards.back: There are, however, other types of conductors like electrolytic solutions where positive and negative charges both can move.
cards.quote: There are, however, other types of conductors like electrolytic solutions where positive and negative charges both can move.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the ____ as before the collision.
cards.back: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the same speed as before the collision.
cards.quote: An electron colliding with an ion emerges with the same speed as before the collision.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are ____ that we shall study later in this chapter.
cards.back: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are cells or batteries that we shall study later in this chapter.
cards.quote: Mechanisms, which maintain a steady electric field are cells or batteries that we shall study later in this chapter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by ____ in ____
cards.back: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by G.S. Ohm in 1828
cards.quote: A basic law regarding flow of currents was discovered by G.S. Ohm in 1828

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Ohm's law.
cards.back: Ohm's law: The electric current I flowing through a substance is proportional to the voltage V across its ends
cards.quote: Ohm's law: The electric current I flowing through a substance is proportional to the voltage V across its ends

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of resistance?
cards.back: The SI units of resistance is ohm
cards.quote: The SI units of resistance is ohm

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the ____ of the conductor.
cards.back: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the dimensions of the conductor.
cards.quote: The resistance R not only depends on the material of the conductor but also on the dimensions of the conductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of a conductor depend on its length?
cards.back: In general, then resistance is proportional to length
cards.quote: In general, then resistance is proportional to length

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of a conductor depend on its cross-sectional area?
cards.back: In general, then the resistance R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area
cards.quote: In general, then the resistance R is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define current density.
cards.back: Current per unit area (taken normal to the current), I/A, is called current density and is denoted by j.
cards.quote: Current per unit area (taken normal to the current), I/A, is called current density and is denoted by j.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does current density j give?
cards.back: Current density j gives the amount of charge flowing per second per unit area normal to the flow
cards.quote: Current density j gives the amount of charge flowing per second per unit area normal to the flow

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be ____ since their directions are random.
cards.back: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero since their directions are random.
cards.quote: If we consider all the electrons, their average velocity will be zero since their directions are random.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the direction of drift velocity of electrons relative to the electric field?
cards.back: The direction of drift velocity of conduction electrons is opposite to the electric field direction, i.e., electrons drift in the direction of increasing potential.
cards.quote: The direction of drift velocity of conduction electrons is opposite to the electric field direction, i.e., electrons drift in the direction of increasing potential.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, ____ (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.
cards.back: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, almost instantly (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.
cards.quote: Electric field is established throughout the circuit, almost instantly (with the speed of light) causing at every point a local electron drift.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the absence of electric field, the paths are ____; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, ____.
cards.back: In the absence of electric field, the paths are straight lines; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, curved.
cards.quote: In the absence of electric field, the paths are straight lines; in the presence of electric field, the paths are, in general, curved.

source.section: Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mobility is defined as what?
cards.back: the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field
cards.quote: the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is mobility positive or negative?
cards.back: Mobility is positive.
cards.quote: Mobility is positive.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mobile charge carriers in a metal, an ionised gas and an electrolyte.
cards.back:
In metals, these mobile charge carriers are electrons
in an ionised gas, they are electrons and positive charged ions
in an electrolyte, these can be both positive and negative ions
cards.quote: In metals, these mobile charge carriers are electrons; in an ionised gas, they are electrons and positive charged ions; in an electrolyte, these can be both positive and negative ions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Three ways in which Ohm's law fails.
cards.back:
(a) V depends on I non-linearly.
(b) the relation between V and I depends on the sign of V for the same absolute value of V.
(c) The relation between V and I is non-unique.
cards.quote: It fails if (a) V depends on I non-linearly. (b) the relation between V and I depends on the sign of V for the same absolute value of V. (c) The relation between V and I is non-unique.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is ____ of nature.
cards.back: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is not a fundamental law of nature.
cards.quote: Ohm's law is obeyed by many substances, but it is not a fundamental law of nature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which device shows a V-I relation that depends on the sign of V?
cards.back: This happens, for example, in a diode which we will study in Chapter 14.
cards.quote: This happens, for example, in a diode which we will study in Chapter 14.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which material shows a V-I relation with more than one V for the same current I?
cards.back: A material exhibiting such behaviour is GaAs.
cards.quote: A material exhibiting such behaviour is GaAs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is ____ i.e., R is independent of V.
cards.back: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is linear i.e., R is independent of V.
cards.quote: The Ohm's law asserts that the plot of I versus V is linear i.e., R is independent of V.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: V = IR defines resistance. To which devices may it be applied?
cards.back: This equation defines resistance and it may be applied to all conducting devices whether they obey Ohm's law or not.
cards.quote: This equation defines resistance and it may be applied to all conducting devices whether they obey Ohm's law or not.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which of a resistor and a diode obeys Ohm's law?
cards.back: A resistor obeys Ohm's law while a diode does not.
cards.quote: A resistor obeys Ohm's law while a diode does not.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If the field becomes ____, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.
cards.back: If the field becomes too strong, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.
cards.quote: If the field becomes too strong, there are departures from Ohm's law in all cases.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Current is a ____ although we represent current with an arrow.
cards.back: Current is a scalar although we represent current with an arrow.
cards.quote: Current is a scalar although we represent current with an arrow.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Currents do not obey the law of ____.
cards.back: Currents do not obey the law of vector addition.
cards.quote: Currents do not obey the law of vector addition.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Classification of materials by resistivity, in increasing order.
cards.back:
conductors
semiconductors
insulators
cards.quote: The materials are classified as conductors, semiconductors and insulators depending on their resistivities, in an increasing order of their values.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically ____ with a rise in temperature.
cards.back: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically decreasing with a rise in temperature.
cards.quote: In between the two are the semiconductors. These, however, have resistivities characteristically decreasing with a rise in temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable ____.
cards.back: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable impurities.
cards.quote: The resistivities of semiconductors can be decreased by adding small amount of suitable impurities.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where do semiconductors like Si and Ge lie on the resistivity scale?
cards.back: Semiconductors like Si and Ge lie roughly in the middle range of resistivity on a logarithmic scale.
cards.quote: Semiconductors like Si and Ge lie roughly in the middle range of resistivity on a logarithmic scale.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the carriers of current in most substances, and in ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids?
cards.back: In most substances, the carriers of current are electrons; in some cases, for example, ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids, positive and negative ions carry the electric current.
cards.quote: In most substances, the carriers of current are electrons; in some cases, for example, ionic crystals and electrolytic liquids, positive and negative ions carry the electric current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The temperature coefficient of resistivity is defined as what?
cards.back: the fractional increase in resistivity per unit increase in temperature
cards.quote: the fractional increase in resistivity per unit increase in temperature

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which alloy of nickel, iron and chromium shows a very weak dependence of resistivity on temperature?
cards.back: Some materials like Nichrome (which is an alloy of nickel, iron and chromium) exhibit a very weak dependence of resistivity with temperature.
cards.quote: Some materials like Nichrome (which is an alloy of nickel, iron and chromium) exhibit a very weak dependence of resistivity with temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors ____ with increasing temperatures.
cards.back: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors decrease with increasing temperatures.
cards.quote: Unlike metals, the resistivities of semiconductors decrease with increasing temperatures.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in ____.
cards.back: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in more frequent collisions.
cards.quote: As we increase temperature, average speed of the electrons, which act as the carriers of current, increases resulting in more frequent collisions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor ____.
cards.back: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor heats up.
cards.quote: During collisions, the energy gained by the charges thus is shared with the atoms. The atoms vibrate more vigorously, i.e., the conductor heats up.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define power dissipated in a conductor.
cards.back: The energy dissipated per unit time is the power dissipated
cards.quote: The energy dissipated per unit time is the power dissipated

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: power dissipated in terms of potential difference V and current I.
cards.back: P=IV
cards.quote: P=IV

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the power loss in a conductor of resistance R carrying a current I called?
cards.back: "ohmic loss"
cards.quote: as the power loss ("ohmic loss") in a conductor of resistance R carrying a current I.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a ____ lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.
cards.back: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a transformer lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.
cards.quote: Using electricity at such voltages is not safe and hence at the other end, a device called a transformer lowers the voltage to a value suitable for use.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Basically a cell has two ____, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)
cards.back: Basically a cell has two electrodes, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)
cards.quote: Basically a cell has two electrodes, called the positive (P) and the negative (N)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the electromotive force (emf) of a source.
cards.back: The work done per unit charge by the source in taking the charge from lower to higher potential energy (i.e., from one terminal of the source to the other) is called the electromotive force, or emf, of the source.
cards.quote: The work done per unit charge by the source in taking the charge from lower to higher potential energy (i.e., from one terminal of the source to the other) is called the electromotive force, or emf, of the source.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the emf is ____; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.
cards.back: Note that the emf is not a force; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.
cards.quote: Note that the emf is not a force; it is the voltage difference between the two terminals of a source in open circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: To maintain a steady current, we must have a ____ in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.
cards.back: To maintain a steady current, we must have a closed circuit in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.
cards.quote: To maintain a steady current, we must have a closed circuit in which an external agency moves electric charge from lower to higher potential energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The electrolyte through which a current flows has a finite resistance r, called the ____.
cards.back: The electrolyte through which a current flows has a finite resistance r, called the internal resistance.
cards.quote: The electrolyte through which a current flows has a finite resistance r, called the internal resistance.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The internal resistance of dry cells, however, is much ____ than the common electrolytic cells.
cards.back: The internal resistance of dry cells, however, is much higher than the common electrolytic cells.
cards.quote: The internal resistance of dry cells, however, is much higher than the common electrolytic cells.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: And like resistors, one can, for calculating currents and voltages in a circuit, replace a combination of cells by an ____.
cards.back: And like resistors, one can, for calculating currents and voltages in a circuit, replace a combination of cells by an equivalent cell.
cards.quote: And like resistors, one can, for calculating currents and voltages in a circuit, replace a combination of cells by an equivalent cell.

source.section: Cells in series and in parallel

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Rule for n cells in series: equivalent emf and equivalent internal resistance.
cards.back:
The equivalent emf of a series combination of n cells is just the sum of their individual emf's
The equivalent internal resistance of a series combination of n cells is just the sum of their internal resistances
cards.quote: (i) The equivalent emf of a series combination of n cells is just the sum of their individual emf's, and (ii) The equivalent internal resistance of a series combination of n cells is just the sum of their internal resistances.

source.section: Cells in series and in parallel

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the two rules for analysis of electric circuits called?
cards.back: Two rules, called Kirchhoff's rules, are very useful for analysis of electric circuits.
cards.quote: Two rules, called Kirchhoff's rules, are very useful for analysis of electric circuits.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If ultimately I is determined to be ____, the actual current in the resistor is in the direction of the arrow.
cards.back: If ultimately I is determined to be positive, the actual current in the resistor is in the direction of the arrow.
cards.quote: If ultimately I is determined to be positive, the actual current in the resistor is in the direction of the arrow.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If I turns out to be ____, the current actually flows in a direction opposite to the arrow.
cards.back: If I turns out to be negative, the current actually flows in a direction opposite to the arrow.
cards.quote: If I turns out to be negative, the current actually flows in a direction opposite to the arrow.

cards.subject: physics
