cards.front: State Kirchhoff's junction rule.
cards.back: Junction rule: At any junction, the sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to the sum of currents leaving the junction
cards.quote: Junction rule: At any junction, the sum of the currents entering the junction is equal to the sum of currents leaving the junction

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Kirchhoff's loop rule.
cards.back: Loop rule: The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells in the loop is zero
cards.quote: Loop rule: The algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells in the loop is zero

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is ____ at any junction or at any point in a line.
cards.back: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is no accumulation of charges at any junction or at any point in a line.
cards.quote: The proof of this rule follows from the fact that when currents are steady, there is no accumulation of charges at any junction or at any point in a line.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on ____
cards.back: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on conservation of charge
cards.quote: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on conservation of charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a galvanometer, as used in the Wheatstone bridge?
cards.back: a device to detect currents
cards.quote: a galvanometer G (which is a device to detect currents)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The Wheatstone bridge and its balance condition provide a practical method for determination of an ____.
cards.back: The Wheatstone bridge and its balance condition provide a practical method for determination of an unknown resistance.
cards.quote: The Wheatstone bridge and its balance condition provide a practical method for determination of an unknown resistance.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which practical device uses the Wheatstone bridge principle?
cards.back: A practical device using this principle is called the meter bridge.
cards.quote: A practical device using this principle is called the meter bridge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Define the work function of a metal.
cards.back: A certain minimum amount of energy is required to be given to an electron to pull it out from the surface of the metal. This minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is called the work function of the metal.
cards.quote: A certain minimum amount of energy is required to be given to an electron to pull it out from the surface of the metal. This minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is called the work function of the metal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is one electron volt (the unit of work function)?
cards.back: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron when it has been accelerated by a potential difference of 1 volt
cards.quote: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron when it has been accelerated by a potential difference of 1 volt

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: ____: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal.
cards.back: Thermionic emission: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal.
cards.quote: Thermionic emission: By suitably heating, sufficient thermal energy can be imparted to the free electrons to enable them to come out of the metal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who discovered photoelectric emission, and in which year?
cards.back: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz (1857-1894), during his electromagnetic wave experiments.
cards.quote: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz (1857-1894), during his electromagnetic wave experiments.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which two scientists investigated photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902?
cards.back: Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard investigated the phenomenon of photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902.
cards.quote: Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard investigated the phenomenon of photoelectric emission in detail during 1886-1902.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is the threshold frequency (Hallwachs and Lenard's observation)?
cards.back: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency.
cards.quote: Hallwachs and Lenard also observed that when ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value, called the threshold frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which metals respond only to ultraviolet light (short wavelength) for photoelectric emission?
cards.back: It was found that certain metals like zinc, cadmium, magnesium, etc., responded only to ultraviolet light, having short wavelength, to cause electron emission from the surface.
cards.quote: It was found that certain metals like zinc, cadmium, magnesium, etc., responded only to ultraviolet light, having short wavelength, to cause electron emission from the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which alkali metals are sensitive even to visible light in photoelectric emission?
cards.back: However, some alkali metals such as lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium were sensitive even to visible light.
cards.quote: However, some alkali metals such as lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium were sensitive even to visible light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: Photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons by metals when illuminated by light of suitable frequency.
cards.quote: Photoelectric effect is the phenomenon of emission of electrons by metals when illuminated by light of suitable frequency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of ____ into ____.
cards.back: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of light energy into electrical energy.
cards.quote: Photoelectric effect involves conversion of light energy into electrical energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The polarity of the plates C and A can be reversed by a ____.
cards.back: The polarity of the plates C and A can be reversed by a commutator.
cards.quote: The polarity of the plates C and A can be reversed by a commutator.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the four factors with which photocurrent variation is studied in the experimental arrangement.
cards.back:
intensity of radiation
frequency of incident radiation
the potential difference between the plates A and C
the nature of the material of plate C
cards.quote: We can use the experimental arrangement of Fig. 11.1 to study the variation of photocurrent with (a) intensity of radiation, (b) frequency of incident radiation, (c) the potential difference between the plates A and C, and (d) the nature of the material of plate C.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What is saturation current in the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: This maximum value of the photoelectric current is called saturation current. Saturation current corresponds to the case when all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter plate C reach the collector plate A.
cards.quote: This maximum value of the photoelectric current is called saturation current. Saturation current corresponds to the case when all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter plate C reach the collector plate A.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the ____.
cards.back: All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the same energy.
cards.quote: All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the same energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: We obtain different values of stopping potential but the same value of the ____ for incident radiation of different frequencies.
cards.back: We obtain different values of stopping potential but the same value of the saturation current for incident radiation of different frequencies.
cards.quote: We obtain different values of stopping potential but the same value of the saturation current for incident radiation of different frequencies.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The energy of the emitted electrons depends on the ____ of the incident radiations.
cards.back: The energy of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency of the incident radiations.
cards.quote: The energy of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency of the incident radiations.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: If we plot a graph between the frequency of incident radiation and the corresponding stopping potential for different metals we get a ____
cards.back: If we plot a graph between the frequency of incident radiation and the corresponding stopping potential for different metals we get a straight line
cards.quote: If we plot a graph between the frequency of incident radiation and the corresponding stopping potential for different metals we get a straight line

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies ____ with the frequency of incident radiation, but is ____ of its intensity.
cards.back: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies linearly with the frequency of incident radiation, but is independent of its intensity.
cards.quote: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies linearly with the frequency of incident radiation, but is independent of its intensity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Define threshold frequency.
cards.back: For a given photosensitive material, there exists a certain minimum cut-off frequency of the incident radiation, called the threshold frequency, below which no emission of photoelectrons takes place, no matter how intense the incident light is.
cards.quote: For a given photosensitive material, there exists a certain minimum cut-off frequency of the incident radiation, called the threshold frequency, below which no emission of photoelectrons takes place, no matter how intense the incident light is.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the factors on which the photoelectric current depends.
cards.back:
the intensity of incident light
the potential difference applied between the two electrodes
the nature of the emitter material
cards.quote: Photoelectric current depends on (i) the intensity of incident light, (ii) the potential difference applied between the two electrodes, and (iii) the nature of the emitter material.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the factors on which the stopping potential depends.
cards.back:
the frequency of incident light
the nature of the emitter material
cards.quote: The stopping potential (Vo) depends on (i) the frequency of incident light, and (ii) the nature of the emitter material.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In this picture, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons on the surface is then expected to increase with increase in ____.
cards.back: In this picture, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons on the surface is then expected to increase with increase in intensity.
cards.quote: In this picture, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons on the surface is then expected to increase with increase in intensity.

source.section: Photoelectric effect and wave theory of light

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In short, the ____ is unable to explain the most basic features of photoelectric emission.
cards.back: In short, the wave picture is unable to explain the most basic features of photoelectric emission.
cards.quote: In short, the wave picture is unable to explain the most basic features of photoelectric emission.

source.section: Photoelectric effect and wave theory of light

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation in 1905 to explain the photoelectric effect?
cards.back: In 1905, Albert Einstein (1879 -1955) proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation to explain photoelectric effect.
cards.quote: In 1905, Albert Einstein (1879 -1955) proposed a radically new picture of electromagnetic radiation to explain photoelectric effect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called ____ of energy of radiation.
cards.back: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called quanta of energy of radiation.
cards.quote: Radiation energy is built up of discrete units - the so called quanta of energy of radiation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the ____ incident per second.
cards.back: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the number of photons incident per second.
cards.quote: Note that the intensity of light of a given frequency is determined by the number of photons incident per second.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Low intensity does not mean ____ in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.
cards.back: Low intensity does not mean delay in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.
cards.quote: Low intensity does not mean delay in emission, since the basic elementary process is the same.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the ____ as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.back: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the energy conservation law as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.quote: Einstein's photoelectric equation is in accordance with the energy conservation law as applied to the photon absorption by an electron in the metal.
cards.note: The equation: maximum kinetic energy = photon energy (Planck's constant times frequency) minus the work function.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The stopping potential is directly related to the ____ of electrons emitted
cards.back: The stopping potential is directly related to the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted
cards.quote: The stopping potential is directly related to the maximum kinetic energy of electrons emitted
cards.note: Stopping potential times the electron charge equals the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Which scientist performed experiments in 1906-1916 aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation?
cards.back: During 1906-1916, Millikan performed a series of experiments on photoelectric effect, aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation.
cards.quote: During 1906-1916, Millikan performed a series of experiments on photoelectric effect, aimed at disproving Einstein's photoelectric equation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What did Millikan determine from the slope of the stopping potential versus frequency line for sodium?
cards.back: He measured the slope of the straight line obtained for sodium, similar to that shown in Fig. 11.5. Using the known value of e, he determined the value of Planck's constant h.
cards.quote: He measured the slope of the straight line obtained for sodium, similar to that shown in Fig. 11.5. Using the known value of e, he determined the value of Planck's constant h.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation in 1916?
cards.back: In this way, in 1916, Millikan proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation, instead of disproving it.
cards.quote: In this way, in 1916, Millikan proved the validity of Einstein's photoelectric equation, instead of disproving it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Whose 1924 experiment on scattering of X-rays from electrons further confirmed the particle-like behaviour of light?
cards.back: The particle-like behaviour of light was further confirmed, in 1924, by the experiment of A.H. Compton (1892-1962) on scattering of X-rays from electrons.
cards.quote: The particle-like behaviour of light was further confirmed, in 1924, by the experiment of A.H. Compton (1892-1962) on scattering of X-rays from electrons.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of ____ called photons.
cards.back: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of particles called photons.
cards.quote: In interaction of radiation with matter, radiation behaves as if it is made up of particles called photons.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Photons are ____ and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
cards.back: Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
cards.quote: Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

source.section: Particle nature of light: the photon

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Name the phenomena in which the wave nature of light shows up.
cards.back:
interference
diffraction
polarisation
cards.quote: The wave nature of light shows up in the phenomena of interference, diffraction and polarisation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the ____.
cards.back: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the nature of the experiment.
cards.quote: Whether a particle or wave description is best suited for understanding an experiment depends on the nature of the experiment.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: Who put forward the hypothesis in 1924 that moving particles of matter display wave-like properties?
cards.back: In 1924, the French physicist Louis Victor de Broglie (pronounced as de Broy) (1892-1987) put forward the bold hypothesis that moving particles of matter should display wave-like properties under suitable conditions.
cards.quote: In 1924, the French physicist Louis Victor de Broglie (pronounced as de Broy) (1892-1987) put forward the bold hypothesis that moving particles of matter should display wave-like properties under suitable conditions.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - ____, must have symmetrical character.
cards.back: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - matter and energy, must have symmetrical character.
cards.quote: He reasoned that nature was symmetrical and that the two basic physical entities - matter and energy, must have symmetrical character.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: What are matter waves (de Broglie waves)?
cards.back: The waves associated with the moving material particles are called matter waves or de Broglie waves.
cards.quote: The waves associated with the moving material particles are called matter waves or de Broglie waves.
cards.note: De Broglie wavelength = Planck's constant divided by the momentum (mass times speed) of the particle.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
cards.front: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the ____ of the material particle.
cards.back: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the charge and nature of the material particle.
cards.quote: The de Broglie wavelength is independent of the charge and nature of the material particle.
cards.note: The wavelength depends only on the particle's momentum (mass and speed), not on its charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does electrostatics deal with?
cards.back: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges.
cards.quote: Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does static mean?
cards.back: Static means anything that does not move or change with time.
cards.quote: Static means anything that does not move or change with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word ____ meaning amber.
cards.back: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word elektron meaning amber.
cards.quote: The name electricity is coined from the Greek word elektron meaning amber.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) ____ charges repel and (ii) ____ charges attract each other.
cards.back: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) like charges repel and (ii) unlike charges attract each other.
cards.quote: There are two kinds of electrification and we find that (i) like charges repel and (ii) unlike charges attract each other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the polarity of charge?
cards.back: The property which differentiates the two kinds of charges is called the polarity of charge.
cards.quote: The property which differentiates the two kinds of charges is called the polarity of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who named the two kinds of charges positive and negative?
cards.back: Therefore, the charges were named as positive and negative by the American scientist Benjamin Franklin.
cards.quote: Therefore, the charges were named as positive and negative by the American scientist Benjamin Franklin.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By convention, which bodies carry positive charge and which negative charge?
cards.back: By convention, the charge on glass rod or cat's fur is called positive and that on plastic rod or silk is termed negative.
cards.quote: By convention, the charge on glass rod or cat's fur is called positive and that on plastic rod or silk is termed negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is an object said to be electrified, and when electrically neutral?
cards.back: If an object possesses an electric charge, it is said to be electrified or charged. When it has no charge it is said to be electrically neutral.
cards.quote: If an object possesses an electric charge, it is said to be electrified or charged. When it has no charge it is said to be electrically neutral.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the ____.
cards.back: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the gold-leaf electroscope.
cards.quote: A simple apparatus to detect charge on a body is the gold-leaf electroscope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they ____.
cards.back: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they diverge.
cards.quote: When a charged object touches the metal knob at the top of the rod, charge flows on to the leaves and they diverge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which everyday forces are basically electrical in nature?
cards.back: Forces that hold the molecules together, forces that hold atoms together in a solid, the adhesive force of glue, forces associated with surface tension, all are basically electrical in nature, arising from the forces between charged particles.
cards.quote: Forces that hold the molecules together, forces that hold atoms together in a solid, the adhesive force of glue, forces associated with surface tension, all are basically electrical in nature, arising from the forces between charged particles.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In solids, some of the ____, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.
cards.back: In solids, some of the electrons, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.
cards.quote: In solids, some of the electrons, being less tightly bound in the atom, are the charges which are transferred from one body to the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a body become positively charged and how negatively charged?
cards.back: A body can thus be charged positively by losing some of its electrons. Similarly, a body can be charged negatively by gaining electrons.
cards.quote: A body can thus be charged positively by losing some of its electrons. Similarly, a body can be charged negatively by gaining electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a glass rod is rubbed with silk, what is transferred and which becomes positive?
cards.back: When we rub a glass rod with silk, some of the electrons from the rod are transferred to the silk cloth. Thus the rod gets positively charged and the silk gets negatively charged.
cards.quote: When we rub a glass rod with silk, some of the electrons from the rod are transferred to the silk cloth. Thus the rod gets positively charged and the silk gets negatively charged.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: No new charge is ____ in the process of rubbing.
cards.back: No new charge is created in the process of rubbing.
cards.quote: No new charge is created in the process of rubbing.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: To electrify a neutral body, we need to ____ or remove one kind of charge.
cards.back: To electrify a neutral body, we need to add or remove one kind of charge.
cards.quote: To electrify a neutral body, we need to add or remove one kind of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are insulators? Name some.
cards.back: Most of the non-metals like glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood offer high resistance to the passage of electricity through them. They are called insulators.
cards.quote: Most of the non-metals like glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood offer high resistance to the passage of electricity through them. They are called insulators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Conductor vs insulator: where does transferred charge go?
cards.back: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.
cards.quote: When some charge is transferred to a conductor, it readily gets distributed over the entire surface of the conductor. In contrast, if some charge is put on an insulator, it stays at the same place.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the third category of materials besides conductors and insulators?
cards.back: There is a third category called semiconductors, which offer resistance to the movement of charges which is intermediate between the conductors and insulators.
cards.quote: There is a third category called semiconductors, which offer resistance to the movement of charges which is intermediate between the conductors and insulators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When are charged bodies treated as point charges?
cards.back: If the sizes of charged bodies are very small as compared to the distances between them, we treat them as point charges. All the charge content of the body is assumed to be concentrated at one point in space.
cards.quote: If the sizes of charged bodies are very small as compared to the distances between them, we treat them as point charges. All the charge content of the body is assumed to be concentrated at one point in space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charge has magnitude but no ____, similar to mass.
cards.back: Charge has magnitude but no direction, similar to mass.
cards.quote: Charge has magnitude but no direction, similar to mass.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mass vs charge: the difference in sign.
cards.back: Mass of a body is always positive whereas a charge can be either positive or negative.
cards.quote: Mass of a body is always positive whereas a charge can be either positive or negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the total charge of an isolated system of charged bodies when charges get redistributed?
cards.back: Within an isolated system consisting of many charged bodies, due to interactions among the bodies, charges may get redistributed but it is found that the total charge of the isolated system is always conserved.
cards.quote: Within an isolated system consisting of many charged bodies, due to interactions among the bodies, charges may get redistributed but it is found that the total charge of the isolated system is always conserved.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Nature creates charged particles: what does a neutron turn into, and why is total charge conserved?
cards.back: Sometimes nature creates charged particles: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The proton and electron thus created have equal and opposite charges and the total charge is zero before and after the creation.
cards.quote: Sometimes nature creates charged particles: a neutron turns into a proton and an electron. The proton and electron thus created have equal and opposite charges and the total charge is zero before and after the creation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is quantisation of charge?
cards.back: The fact that electric charge is always an integral multiple of e is termed as quantisation of charge.
cards.quote: The fact that electric charge is always an integral multiple of e is termed as quantisation of charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are ____ multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.
cards.back: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are integral multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.
cards.quote: Experimentally it is established that all free charges are integral multiples of a basic unit of charge denoted by e.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: charge on a body in terms of the basic unit of charge e.
cards.back: q = ne where n is any integer, positive or negative.
cards.quote: q = ne where n is any integer, positive or negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who first suggested quantisation of charge, through which experimental laws?
cards.back: The quantisation of charge was first suggested by the experimental laws of electrolysis discovered by English experimentalist Faraday.
cards.quote: The quantisation of charge was first suggested by the experimental laws of electrolysis discovered by English experimentalist Faraday.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who experimentally demonstrated quantisation of charge, and in which year?
cards.back: It was experimentally demonstrated by Millikan in 1912.
cards.quote: It was experimentally demonstrated by Millikan in 1912.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of charge and its symbol?
cards.back: In the International System (SI) of Units, a unit of charge is called a coulomb and is denoted by the symbol C.
cards.quote: In the International System (SI) of Units, a unit of charge is called a coulomb and is denoted by the symbol C.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define one coulomb in terms of current.
cards.back: In terms of this definition, one coulomb is the charge flowing through a wire in 1 s if the current is 1 A (ampere)
cards.quote: In terms of this definition, one coulomb is the charge flowing through a wire in 1 s if the current is 1 A (ampere)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can quantisation of charge not be ignored at the microscopic level?
cards.back: However, at the microscopic level, where the charges involved are of the order of a few tens or hundreds of e, i.e., they can be counted, they appear in discrete lumps and quantisation of charge cannot be ignored.
cards.quote: However, at the microscopic level, where the charges involved are of the order of a few tens or hundreds of e, i.e., they can be counted, they appear in discrete lumps and quantisation of charge cannot be ignored.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is Coulomb's law a quantitative statement about?
cards.back: Coulomb's law is a quantitative statement about the force between two point charges.
cards.quote: Coulomb's law is a quantitative statement about the force between two point charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Coulomb's law in words (how the force varies with distance and with charges).
cards.back: Coulomb measured the force between two point charges and found that it varied inversely as the square of the distance between the charges and was directly proportional to the product of the magnitude of the two charges and acted along the line joining the two charges.
cards.quote: Coulomb measured the force between two point charges and found that it varied inversely as the square of the distance between the charges and was directly proportional to the product of the magnitude of the two charges and acted along the line joining the two charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which device did Coulomb use to measure the force between two charged metallic spheres?
cards.back: Coulomb used a torsion balance for measuring the force between two charged metallic spheres.
cards.quote: Coulomb used a torsion balance for measuring the force between two charged metallic spheres.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a torsion balance?
cards.back: A torsion balance is a sensitive device to measure force.
cards.quote: A torsion balance is a sensitive device to measure force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State the principle of superposition for electric forces.
cards.back: Experimentally, it is verified that force on any charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of all the forces on that charge due to the other charges, taken one at a time. The individual forces are unaffected due to the presence of other charges. This is termed as the principle of superposition.
cards.quote: Experimentally, it is verified that force on any charge due to a number of other charges is the vector sum of all the forces on that charge due to the other charges, taken one at a time. The individual forces are unaffected due to the presence of other charges. This is termed as the principle of superposition.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: All of electrostatics is basically a consequence of Coulomb's law and the ____ principle.
cards.back: All of electrostatics is basically a consequence of Coulomb's law and the superposition principle.
cards.quote: All of electrostatics is basically a consequence of Coulomb's law and the superposition principle.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of electric field?
cards.back: Equation (1.8) defines the SI unit of electric field as N/C
cards.quote: Equation (1.8) defines the SI unit of electric field as N/C

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are a source charge and a test charge?
cards.back: The charge Q, which is producing the electric field, is called a source charge and the charge q, which tests the effect of a source charge, is called a test charge.
cards.quote: The charge Q, which is producing the electric field, is called a source charge and the charge q, which tests the effect of a source charge, is called a test charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the electric field E due to Q, though defined operationally in terms of some test charge q, is ____ of q.
cards.back: Note that the electric field E due to Q, though defined operationally in terms of some test charge q, is independent of q.
cards.quote: Note that the electric field E due to Q, though defined operationally in terms of some test charge q, is independent of q.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the direction of the electric field for a positive and for a negative source charge?
cards.back: For a positive charge, the electric field will be directed radially outwards from the charge. On the other hand, if the source charge is negative, the electric field vector, at each point, points radially inwards.
cards.quote: For a positive charge, the electric field will be directed radially outwards from the charge. On the other hand, if the source charge is negative, the electric field vector, at each point, points radially inwards.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the term field in physics generally refer to?
cards.back: The term field in physics generally refers to a quantity that is defined at every point in space and may vary from point to point.
cards.quote: The term field in physics generally refers to a quantity that is defined at every point in space and may vary from point to point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric field is a ____, since force is a vector quantity.
cards.back: Electric field is a vector field, since force is a vector quantity.
cards.quote: Electric field is a vector field, since force is a vector quantity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric field is a characteristic of the system of charges and is independent of the ____ that you place at a point to determine the field.
cards.back: Electric field is a characteristic of the system of charges and is independent of the test charge that you place at a point to determine the field.
cards.quote: Electric field is a characteristic of the system of charges and is independent of the test charge that you place at a point to determine the field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who first introduced the concept of field?
cards.back: The concept of field was first introduced by Faraday and is now among the central concepts in physics.
cards.quote: The concept of field was first introduced by Faraday and is now among the central concepts in physics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Now the magnitude of the field is represented by the ____ of field lines.
cards.back: Now the magnitude of the field is represented by the density of field lines.
cards.quote: Now the magnitude of the field is represented by the density of field lines.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who invented the picture of field lines, and what did he call them?
cards.back: The picture of field lines was invented by Faraday to develop an intuitive non-mathematical way of visualising electric fields around charged configurations. Faraday called them lines of force.
cards.quote: The picture of field lines was invented by Faraday to develop an intuitive non-mathematical way of visualising electric fields around charged configurations. Faraday called them lines of force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The field lines crowd where the field is strong and are spaced apart where it is ____.
cards.back: The field lines crowd where the field is strong and are spaced apart where it is weak.
cards.quote: The field lines crowd where the field is strong and are spaced apart where it is weak.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do the field lines of a single positive and a single negative charge run?
cards.back: The field lines of a single positive charge are radially outward while those of a single negative charge are radially inward.
cards.quote: The field lines of a single positive charge are radially outward while those of a single negative charge are radially inward.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Name the properties of electric field lines.
cards.back:
Field lines start from positive charges and end at negative charges. If there is a single charge, they may start or end at infinity.
In a charge-free region, electric field lines can be taken to be continuous curves without any breaks.
Two field lines can never cross each other.
Electrostatic field lines do not form any closed loops.
cards.quote: (i) Field lines start from positive charges and end at negative charges. If there is a single charge, they may start or end at infinity. (ii) In a charge-free region, electric field lines can be taken to be continuous curves without any breaks. (iii) Two field lines can never cross each other. (If they did, the field at the point of intersection will not have a unique direction, which is absurd.) (iv) Electrostatic field lines do not form any closed loops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Two field lines can never ____ each other. (If they did, the field at the point of intersection will not have a unique direction, which is absurd.)
cards.back: Two field lines can never cross each other. (If they did, the field at the point of intersection will not have a unique direction, which is absurd.)
cards.quote: Two field lines can never cross each other. (If they did, the field at the point of intersection will not have a unique direction, which is absurd.)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electrostatic field lines do not form any ____. This follows from the conservative nature of electric field (Chapter 2).
cards.back: Electrostatic field lines do not form any closed loops. This follows from the conservative nature of electric field (Chapter 2).
cards.quote: Electrostatic field lines do not form any closed loops. This follows from the conservative nature of electric field (Chapter 2).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the number of field lines crossing a unit area normal to the field measure?
cards.back: In the picture of electric field lines described above, we saw that the number of field lines crossing a unit area, placed normal to the field at a point is a measure of the strength of electric field at that point.
cards.quote: In the picture of electric field lines described above, we saw that the number of field lines crossing a unit area, placed normal to the field at a point is a measure of the strength of electric field at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The vector associated with every area element of a closed surface is taken to be in the direction of the ____.
cards.back: The vector associated with every area element of a closed surface is taken to be in the direction of the outward normal.
cards.quote: The vector associated with every area element of a closed surface is taken to be in the direction of the outward normal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The total charge of the electric dipole is obviously ____.
cards.back: The total charge of the electric dipole is obviously zero.
cards.quote: The total charge of the electric dipole is obviously zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In most molecules, the centres of positive charges and of negative charges lie at the same place. Therefore, their dipole moment is ____.
cards.back: In most molecules, the centres of positive charges and of negative charges lie at the same place. Therefore, their dipole moment is zero.
cards.quote: In most molecules, the centres of positive charges and of negative charges lie at the same place. Therefore, their dipole moment is zero.
cards.note: CO2 and CH4 are the examples NCERT gives of such molecules.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are polar molecules?
cards.back: But in some molecules, the centres of negative charges and of positive charges do not coincide. Therefore they have a permanent electric dipole moment, even in the absence of an electric field. Such molecules are called polar molecules.
cards.quote: But in some molecules, the centres of negative charges and of positive charges do not coincide. Therefore they have a permanent electric dipole moment, even in the absence of an electric field. Such molecules are called polar molecules.
cards.note: The water molecule is NCERT's example of a polar molecule.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By permanent dipole, we mean that p exists irrespective of E; it has not been ____ by E.
cards.back: By permanent dipole, we mean that p exists irrespective of E; it has not been induced by E.
cards.quote: By permanent dipole, we mean that p exists irrespective of E; it has not been induced by E.

source.section: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the net force on a dipole in a uniform external field, and what does it experience instead?
cards.back: The net force on the dipole is zero, since E is uniform. However, the charges are separated, so the forces act at different points, resulting in a torque on the dipole.
cards.quote: The net force on the dipole is zero, since E is uniform. However, the charges are separated, so the forces act at different points, resulting in a torque on the dipole.

source.section: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a non-uniform field, in which direction is the net force on a dipole when p is parallel and when antiparallel to E?
cards.back: It is easily seen that when p is parallel to E, the dipole has a net force in the direction of increasing field. When p is antiparallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of decreasing field.
cards.quote: It is easily seen that when p is parallel to E, the dipole has a net force in the direction of increasing field. When p is antiparallel to E, the net force on the dipole is in the direction of decreasing field.

source.section: Dipole in a Uniform External Field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Using which two results can the electric field be found for any charge distribution?
cards.back: In short, using Coulomb's law and the superposition principle, electric field can be determined for any charge distribution, discrete or continuous or part discrete and part continuous.
cards.quote: In short, using Coulomb's law and the superposition principle, electric field can be determined for any charge distribution, discrete or continuous or part discrete and part continuous.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The law implies that the total electric flux through a closed surface is ____ if no charge is enclosed by the surface.
cards.back: The law implies that the total electric flux through a closed surface is zero if no charge is enclosed by the surface.
cards.quote: The law implies that the total electric flux through a closed surface is zero if no charge is enclosed by the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Gauss's law is true for any closed surface, no matter what its ____ or size.
cards.back: Gauss's law is true for any closed surface, no matter what its shape or size.
cards.quote: Gauss's law is true for any closed surface, no matter what its shape or size.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The surface that we choose for the application of Gauss's law is called the ____.
cards.back: The surface that we choose for the application of Gauss's law is called the Gaussian surface.
cards.quote: The surface that we choose for the application of Gauss's law is called the Gaussian surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why must a Gaussian surface not pass through a discrete charge?
cards.back: However, take care not to let the Gaussian surface pass through any discrete charge. This is because electric field due to a system of discrete charges is not well defined at the location of any charge.
cards.quote: However, take care not to let the Gaussian surface pass through any discrete charge. This is because electric field due to a system of discrete charges is not well defined at the location of any charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Gauss's law is often useful towards a much easier calculation of the electrostatic field when the system has some ____.
cards.back: Gauss's law is often useful towards a much easier calculation of the electrostatic field when the system has some symmetry.
cards.quote: Gauss's law is often useful towards a much easier calculation of the electrostatic field when the system has some symmetry.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Finally, Gauss's law is based on the ____ dependence on distance contained in the Coulomb's law.
cards.back: Finally, Gauss's law is based on the inverse square dependence on distance contained in the Coulomb's law.
cards.quote: Finally, Gauss's law is based on the inverse square dependence on distance contained in the Coulomb's law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In short, the electric field is everywhere radial in the plane cutting the wire normally, and its magnitude depends only on the ____ r.
cards.back: In short, the electric field is everywhere radial in the plane cutting the wire normally, and its magnitude depends only on the radial distance r.
cards.quote: In short, the electric field is everywhere radial in the plane cutting the wire normally, and its magnitude depends only on the radial distance r.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Further, the assumption that the wire is infinitely ____ is crucial.
cards.back: Further, the assumption that the wire is infinitely long is crucial.
cards.quote: Further, the assumption that the wire is infinitely long is crucial.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The three basic properties of electric charge.
cards.back:
quantisation
additivity
conservation
cards.quote: Electric charge has three basic properties: quantisation, additivity and conservation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does additivity of electric charges mean?
cards.back: Additivity of electric charges means that the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum (i.e., the sum taking into account proper signs) of all individual charges in the system.
cards.quote: Additivity of electric charges means that the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum (i.e., the sum taking into account proper signs) of all individual charges in the system.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does conservation of electric charge mean?
cards.back: Conservation of electric charges means that the total charge of an isolated system remains unchanged with time.
cards.quote: Conservation of electric charges means that the total charge of an isolated system remains unchanged with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric and magnetic forces determine the properties of atoms, molecules and ____ matter.
cards.back: Electric and magnetic forces determine the properties of atoms, molecules and bulk matter.
cards.quote: Electric and magnetic forces determine the properties of atoms, molecules and bulk matter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the mobile charges in metals, and in electrolytes?
cards.back: In metals, the mobile charges are electrons; in electrolytes both positive and negative ions are mobile.
cards.quote: In metals, the mobile charges are electrons; in electrolytes both positive and negative ions are mobile.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Like Coulomb force, electric field also satisfies ____ principle.
cards.back: Like Coulomb force, electric field also satisfies superposition principle.
cards.quote: Like Coulomb force, electric field also satisfies superposition principle.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an electric field line?
cards.back: An electric field line is a curve drawn in such a way that the tangent at each point on the curve gives the direction of electric field at that point.
cards.quote: An electric field line is a curve drawn in such a way that the tangent at each point on the curve gives the direction of electric field at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In regions of constant electric field, the field lines are uniformly spaced ____ straight lines.
cards.back: In regions of constant electric field, the field lines are uniformly spaced parallel straight lines.
cards.quote: In regions of constant electric field, the field lines are uniformly spaced parallel straight lines.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an electric dipole?
cards.back: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges q and −q separated by some distance 2a.
cards.quote: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges q and −q separated by some distance 2a.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the magnitude and direction of the dipole moment vector of an electric dipole?
cards.back: Its dipole moment vector p has magnitude 2qa and is in the direction of the dipole axis from −q to q.
cards.quote: Its dipole moment vector p has magnitude 2qa and is in the direction of the dipole axis from −q to q.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what property is the superposition principle for electric forces based?
cards.back: The principle is based on the property that the forces with which two charges attract or repel each other are not affected by the presence of a third (or more) additional charge(s).
cards.quote: The principle is based on the property that the forces with which two charges attract or repel each other are not affected by the presence of a third (or more) additional charge(s).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Coulomb force vs gravitational force: the difference in sign.
cards.back: But gravitational force has only one sign (always attractive), while Coulomb force can be of both signs (attractive and repulsive), allowing possibility of cancellation of electric forces.
cards.quote: But gravitational force has only one sign (always attractive), while Coulomb force can be of both signs (attractive and repulsive), allowing possibility of cancellation of electric forces.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Coulomb force and gravitational force follow the same ____ law.
cards.back: Coulomb force and gravitational force follow the same inverse-square law.
cards.quote: Coulomb force and gravitational force follow the same inverse-square law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In SI units, how is the unit of charge defined?
cards.back: In SI units, however, what is defined is the unit of current (A) via its magnetic effect (Ampere's law) and the unit of charge (coulomb) is simply defined by (1C = 1 A s).
cards.quote: In SI units, however, what is defined is the unit of current (A) via its magnetic effect (Ampere's law) and the unit of charge (coulomb) is simply defined by (1C = 1 A s).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Charge is not only a scalar (or invariant) under rotation; it is also invariant for frames of reference in ____ motion.
cards.back: Charge is not only a scalar (or invariant) under rotation; it is also invariant for frames of reference in relative motion.
cards.quote: Charge is not only a scalar (or invariant) under rotation; it is also invariant for frames of reference in relative motion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is electromagnetic induction?
cards.back: The phenomenon in which electric current is generated by varying magnetic fields is appropriately called electromagnetic induction.
cards.quote: The phenomenon in which electric current is generated by varying magnetic fields is appropriately called electromagnetic induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Whose experiments around 1830 showed that changing magnetic fields induce currents in closed coils?
cards.back: The experiments of Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in USA, conducted around 1830
cards.quote: The experiments of Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in USA, conducted around 1830, demonstrated conclusively that electric currents were induced in closed coils when subjected to changing magnetic fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When the magnet is pulled away from the coil, the galvanometer shows deflection in the ____, which indicates reversal of the current's direction.
cards.back: When the magnet is pulled away from the coil, the galvanometer shows deflection in the opposite direction, which indicates reversal of the current's direction.
cards.quote: When the magnet is pulled away from the coil, the galvanometer shows deflection in the opposite direction, which indicates reversal of the current's direction.

source.section: The experiments of Faraday and Henry

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If the key is held pressed continuously, there is ____ in the galvanometer.
cards.back: If the key is held pressed continuously, there is no deflection in the galvanometer.
cards.quote: If the key is held pressed continuously, there is no deflection in the galvanometer.

source.section: The experiments of Faraday and Henry

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?
cards.back: SI unit of magnetic flux is weber (Wb)
cards.quote: SI unit of magnetic flux is weber (Wb)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is magnetic flux a scalar or a vector quantity?
cards.back: Magnetic flux is a scalar quantity.
cards.quote: Magnetic flux is a scalar quantity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: From the experimental observations, Faraday arrived at a conclusion that an emf is induced in a coil when magnetic flux through the coil ____.
cards.back: From the experimental observations, Faraday arrived at a conclusion that an emf is induced in a coil when magnetic flux through the coil changes with time.
cards.quote: From the experimental observations, Faraday arrived at a conclusion that an emf is induced in a coil when magnetic flux through the coil changes with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The common point in all these observations is that the ____ of magnetic flux through a circuit induces emf in it.
cards.back: The common point in all these observations is that the time rate of change of magnetic flux through a circuit induces emf in it.
cards.quote: The common point in all these observations is that the time rate of change of magnetic flux through a circuit induces emf in it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
cards.back: The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit.
cards.quote: The magnitude of the induced emf in a circuit is equal to the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The induced emf can be increased by increasing the ____ N of a closed coil.
cards.back: The induced emf can be increased by increasing the number of turns N of a closed coil.
cards.quote: The induced emf can be increased by increasing the number of turns N of a closed coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The flux can also be altered by changing the ____ of a coil (that is, by shrinking it or stretching it) in a magnetic field
cards.back: The flux can also be altered by changing the shape of a coil (that is, by shrinking it or stretching it) in a magnetic field
cards.quote: The flux can also be altered by changing the shape of a coil (that is, by shrinking it or stretching it) in a magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who deduced, in 1834, the rule that gives the polarity of the induced emf?
cards.back: In 1834, German physicist Heinrich Friedrich Lenz (1804-1865) deduced a rule, known as Lenz's law which gives the polarity of the induced emf in a clear and concise fashion.
cards.quote: In 1834, German physicist Heinrich Friedrich Lenz (1804-1865) deduced a rule, known as Lenz's law which gives the polarity of the induced emf in a clear and concise fashion.

source.section: Lenz's law and conservation of energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Lenz's law.
cards.back: The polarity of induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
cards.quote: The polarity of induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

source.section: Lenz's law and conservation of energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If this can happen, one could construct a perpetual-motion machine by a suitable arrangement. This violates the law of ____ and hence can not happen.
cards.back: If this can happen, one could construct a perpetual-motion machine by a suitable arrangement. This violates the law of conservation of energy and hence can not happen.
cards.quote: If this can happen, one could construct a perpetual-motion machine by a suitable arrangement. This violates the law of conservation of energy and hence can not happen.

source.section: Lenz's law and conservation of energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where does the energy spent by the person go? This energy is dissipated by ____ produced by the induced current.
cards.back: Where does the energy spent by the person go? This energy is dissipated by Joule heating produced by the induced current.
cards.quote: Where does the energy spent by the person go? This energy is dissipated by Joule heating produced by the induced current.

source.section: Lenz's law and conservation of energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The induced emf Blv is called ____.
cards.back: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf.
cards.quote: The induced emf Blv is called motional emf.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In terms of work and charge, what is emf?
cards.back: emf is the work done per unit charge
cards.quote: Since emf is the work done per unit charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the ____.
cards.back: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the stationary charge.
cards.quote: Conversely, a bar magnet in motion (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on the stationary charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are ____.
cards.back: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are in parallel.
cards.quote: The number of spokes is immaterial because the emf's across the spokes are in parallel.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the ____ is linked with all the turns.
cards.back: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the same magnetic flux is linked with all the turns.
cards.quote: For a closely wound coil of N turns, the same magnetic flux is linked with all the turns.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define inductance.
cards.back: Inductance is the ratio of the flux-linkage to current.
cards.quote: Inductance is the ratio of the flux-linkage to current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: We shall see that inductance depends only on the ____ and intrinsic material properties.
cards.back: We shall see that inductance depends only on the geometry of the coil and intrinsic material properties.
cards.quote: We shall see that inductance depends only on the geometry of the coil and intrinsic material properties.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is inductance a scalar or a vector quantity?
cards.back: Inductance is a scalar quantity.
cards.quote: Inductance is a scalar quantity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of inductance, and its symbol?
cards.back: The SI unit of inductance is henry and is denoted by H.
cards.quote: The SI unit of inductance is henry and is denoted by H.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In whose honour is the SI unit of inductance named?
cards.back: It is named in honour of Joseph Henry who discovered electromagnetic induction in USA, independently of Faraday in England.
cards.quote: It is named in honour of Joseph Henry who discovered electromagnetic induction in USA, independently of Faraday in England.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the ____ and mutual inductance of the two coils.
cards.back: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.
cards.quote: The magnitude of the induced emf depends upon the rate of change of current and mutual inductance of the two coils.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is self-induction?
cards.back: It is also possible that emf is induced in a single isolated coil due to change of flux through the coil by means of varying the current through the same coil. This phenomenon is called self-induction.
cards.quote: It is also possible that emf is induced in a single isolated coil due to change of flux through the coil by means of varying the current through the same coil. This phenomenon is called self-induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its ____ and on the ____ of the medium.
cards.back: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry and on the permeability of the medium.
cards.quote: The self-inductance of the coil depends on its geometry and on the permeability of the medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The self-induced emf is also called the ____ as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
cards.back: The self-induced emf is also called the back emf as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.
cards.quote: The self-induced emf is also called the back emf as it opposes any change in the current in a circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of ____. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
cards.back: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of inertia. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.
cards.quote: Physically, the self-inductance plays the role of inertia. It is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the ____.
cards.back: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the same coil.
cards.quote: When a current in a coil changes, it induces a back emf in the same coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An exceptionally important application is the generation of ____ (ac).
cards.back: An exceptionally important application is the generation of alternating currents (ac).
cards.quote: An exceptionally important application is the generation of alternating currents (ac).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who is credited with the development of the ac generator?
cards.back: The Yugoslav inventor Nicola Tesla is credited with the development of the machine.
cards.quote: The Yugoslav inventor Nicola Tesla is credited with the development of the machine.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An ac generator converts ____ into electrical energy.
cards.back: An ac generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
cards.quote: An ac generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The axis of rotation of the coil is ____ to the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.back: The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: The axis of rotation of the coil is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The coil (called ____) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.
cards.back: The coil (called armature) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.
cards.quote: The coil (called armature) is mechanically rotated in the uniform magnetic field by some external means.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The rotation of the coil causes the ____ through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.
cards.back: The rotation of the coil causes the magnetic flux through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.
cards.quote: The rotation of the coil causes the magnetic flux through it to change, so an emf is induced in the coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of ____.
cards.back: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of slip rings and brushes.
cards.quote: The ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit by means of slip rings and brushes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called ____ (ac).
cards.back: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called alternating current (ac).
cards.quote: The direction of the current changes periodically and therefore the current is called alternating current (ac).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of commercial generators, by how the armature is made to rotate.
cards.back:
hydro-electric generators
thermal generators
nuclear power generators
cards.quote: In commercial generators, the mechanical energy required for rotation of the armature is provided by water falling from a height, for example, from dams. These are called hydro-electric generators. Alternatively, water is heated to produce steam using coal or other sources. The steam at high pressure produces the rotation of the armature. These are called thermal generators. Instead of coal, if a nuclear fuel is used, we get nuclear power generators.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the ____ which are rotated.
cards.back: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the electromagnets which are rotated.
cards.quote: In most generators, the coils are held stationary and it is the electromagnets which are rotated.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the frequency of rotation in generators in India, and in the USA?
cards.back: The frequency of rotation is 50 Hz in India. In certain countries such as USA, it is 60 Hz.
cards.quote: The frequency of rotation is 50 Hz in India. In certain countries such as USA, it is 60 Hz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of ____.
cards.back: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of electromagnetic induction.
cards.quote: In an ac generator, mechanical energy is converted to electrical energy by virtue of electromagnetic induction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a closed circuit, electric currents are induced so as to ____ the changing magnetic flux.
cards.back: In a closed circuit, electric currents are induced so as to oppose the changing magnetic flux.
cards.quote: In a closed circuit, electric currents are induced so as to oppose the changing magnetic flux.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell noticed an ____ in the Ampere's circuital law.
cards.back: Maxwell noticed an inconsistency in the Ampere's circuital law.
cards.quote: Maxwell noticed an inconsistency in the Ampere's circuital law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the ____ to remove this inconsistency.
cards.back: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the displacement current to remove this inconsistency.
cards.quote: He suggested the existence of an additional current, called by him, the displacement current to remove this inconsistency.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are electromagnetic waves (Maxwell's most important prediction)?
cards.back: (coupled) time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate in space
cards.quote: The most important prediction to emerge from Maxwell's equations is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which are (coupled) time-varying electric and magnetic fields that propagate in space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of ____.
cards.back: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of electricity, magnetism and light.
cards.quote: Maxwell's work thus unified the domain of electricity, magnetism and light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a ____ must also produce a magnetic field.
cards.back: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field.
cards.quote: Maxwell showed that for logical consistency, a changing electric field must also produce a magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the ____ and the ____.
cards.back: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the conduction current and the displacement current.
cards.quote: "the total current passing through any surface of which the closed loop is the perimeter" is the sum of the conduction current and the displacement current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the generalised Ampere's circuital law (with displacement current) known as?
cards.back: Ampere-Maxwell law
cards.quote: and is known as Ampere-Maxwell law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In all respects, the displacement current has ____ as the conduction current.
cards.back: In all respects, the displacement current has the same physical effects as the conduction current.
cards.quote: In all respects, the displacement current has the same physical effects as the conduction current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In some cases, for example, ____ in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.
cards.back: In some cases, for example, steady electric fields in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.
cards.quote: In some cases, for example, steady electric fields in a conducting wire, the displacement current may be zero since the electric field E does not change with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is ____ due to time-varying electric fields.
cards.back: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is only a displacement current due to time-varying electric fields.
cards.quote: Most interestingly, there may be large regions of space where there is no conduction current, but there is only a displacement current due to time-varying electric fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In such a region, we expect a ____, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!
cards.back: In such a region, we expect a magnetic field, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!
cards.quote: In such a region, we expect a magnetic field, though there is no (conduction) current source nearby!

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the ____.
cards.back: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
cards.quote: Faraday's law of induction states that there is an induced emf equal to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
blanks: rate of change of magnetic flux

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the ____, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.
cards.back: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.
cards.quote: One very important consequence of this symmetry is the existence of electromagnetic waves, which we discuss qualitatively in the next section.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Neither ____ nor ____ (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.
cards.back: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.
cards.quote: Neither stationary charges nor charges in uniform motion (steady currents) can be sources of electromagnetic waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus ____, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.
cards.back: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus regenerate each other, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.
cards.quote: The oscillating electric and magnetic fields thus regenerate each other, so to speak, as the wave propagates through the space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the ____.
cards.back: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge.
cards.quote: The frequency of the electromagnetic wave naturally equals the frequency of oscillation of the charge.
blanks: frequency of oscillation of the charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate ____ in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.
cards.back: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate sinusoidally in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.
cards.quote: Electric and magnetic fields oscillate sinusoidally in space and time in an electromagnetic wave.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are electromagnetic waves, in terms of oscillations of fields?
cards.back: They are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space, or vacuum.
cards.quote: They are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space, or vacuum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important ____.
cards.back: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important fundamental constant.
cards.quote: The velocity of electromagnetic waves in free space or vacuum is an important fundamental constant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the velocity of em waves in vacuum depend on wavelength?
