cards.back: this velocity is the same (independent of wavelength) to within a few metres per second
cards.quote: It has been shown by experiments on electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths that this velocity is the same (independent of wavelength) to within a few metres per second

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to ____ from one place to another.
cards.back: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to carry energy from one place to another.
cards.quote: The great technological importance of electromagnetic waves stems from their capability to carry energy from one place to another.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have ____ in free space.
cards.back: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have the same velocity c in free space.
cards.quote: Electromagnetic waves other than light also have the same velocity c in free space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the ____ (Fig. 8.4).
cards.back: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the electromagnetic spectrum (Fig. 8.4).
cards.quote: The classification of em waves according to frequency is the electromagnetic spectrum (Fig. 8.4).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There is ____ between one kind of wave and the next.
cards.back: There is no sharp division between one kind of wave and the next.
cards.quote: There is no sharp division between one kind of wave and the next.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are ____.
cards.back: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are produced and/or detected.
cards.quote: The classification is based roughly on how the waves are produced and/or detected.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an ____.
cards.back: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an infinite range of wavelengths.
cards.quote: The spectrum of electromagnetic waves stretches, in principle, over an infinite range of wavelengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Radio waves are used in which communication systems?
cards.back: radio and television communication systems
cards.quote: They are used in radio and television communication systems.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from ____ to ____.
cards.back: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from 530 kHz to 1710 kHz.
cards.quote: The AM (amplitude modulated) band is from 530 kHz to 1710 kHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: TV waves range from 54 MHz to ____.
cards.back: TV waves range from 54 MHz to 890 MHz.
cards.quote: TV waves range from 54 MHz to 890 MHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from ____ to ____.
cards.back: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.
cards.quote: The FM (frequency modulated) radio band extends from 88 MHz to 108 MHz.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ____ band.
cards.back: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band.
cards.quote: Cellular phones use radio waves to transmit voice communication in the ultrahigh frequency (UHF) band.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are microwaves produced?
cards.back: by special vacuum tubes (called klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes)
cards.quote: Microwaves (short-wavelength radio waves), with frequencies in the gigahertz (GHz) range, are produced by special vacuum tubes (called klystrons, magnetrons and Gunn diodes).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the ____ used in aircraft navigation.
cards.back: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the radar systems used in aircraft navigation.
cards.quote: Due to their short wavelengths, they are suitable for the radar systems used in aircraft navigation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as ____.
cards.back: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves.
cards.quote: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared lamps are used in ____.
cards.back: Infrared lamps are used in physical therapy.
cards.quote: Infrared lamps are used in physical therapy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the ____.
cards.back: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the greenhouse effect.
cards.quote: Infrared radiation also plays an important role in maintaining the earth's warmth or average temperature through the greenhouse effect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe ____.
cards.back: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe growth of crops.
cards.quote: Infrared detectors are used in Earth satellites, both for military purposes and to observe growth of crops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which household devices use infrared from light emitting diodes?
cards.back: the remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets, video recorders and hi-fi systems
cards.quote: Electronic devices (for example semiconductor light emitting diodes) also emit infrared and are widely used in the remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets, video recorders and hi-fi systems.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more ____, causing tanning of the skin.
cards.back: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more melanin, causing tanning of the skin.
cards.quote: Exposure to UV radiation induces the production of more melanin, causing tanning of the skin.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: UV radiation is absorbed by ____. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.
cards.back: UV radiation is absorbed by ordinary glass. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.
cards.quote: UV radiation is absorbed by ordinary glass. Hence, one cannot get tanned or sunburn through glass windows.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by ____.
cards.back: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by welding arcs.
cards.quote: Welders wear special glass goggles or face masks with glass windows to protect their eyes from large amount of UV produced by welding arcs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: UV lamps are used to kill germs in ____.
cards.back: UV lamps are used to kill germs in water purifiers.
cards.quote: UV lamps are used to kill germs in water purifiers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a ____ by high energy electrons.
cards.back: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a metal target by high energy electrons.
cards.quote: One common way to generate X-rays is to bombard a metal target by high energy electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: X-rays are used as a ____ in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.
cards.back: X-rays are used as a diagnostic tool in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.
cards.quote: X-rays are used as a diagnostic tool in medicine and as a treatment for certain forms of cancer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Because X-rays ____ and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.
cards.back: Because X-rays damage or destroy living tissues and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.
cards.quote: Because X-rays damage or destroy living tissues and organisms, care must be taken to avoid unnecessary or over exposure.

cards.back: Rapid acceleration and decelerations of electrons in aerials

cards.back: Klystron valve or magnetron valve

cards.back: Vibration of atoms and molecules

cards.front: Table 8.1: how is ultraviolet produced?

cards.front: Table 8.1: how are X-rays produced?
cards.back: X-ray tubes or inner shell electrons

cards.front: Table 8.1: how are gamma rays produced?
cards.back: Radioactive decay of the nucleus
cards.quote: Radioactive decay of the nucleus

cards.front: Table 8.1: wavelength range of radio waves?

cards.front: Table 8.1: wavelength range of microwaves?
cards.back: 0.1m to 1 mm

cards.front: Table 8.1: wavelength range of infrared?
cards.back: 1mm to 700 nm

cards.front: Table 8.1: wavelength range of visible light?
cards.back: 700 nm to 400 nm

cards.front: Table 8.1: how are radio waves detected?

cards.front: Table 8.1: how are microwaves detected?

Thermopiles
Bolometer
Infrared photographic film

cards.front: Table 8.1: name the detectors of X-rays.

Photographic film
Geiger tubes
Ionisation chamber

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The basic difference between various types of electromagnetic waves lies in their ____ since all of them travel through vacuum with the same speed.
cards.back: The basic difference between various types of electromagnetic waves lies in their wavelengths or frequencies since all of them travel through vacuum with the same speed.
cards.quote: The basic difference between various types of electromagnetic waves lies in their wavelengths or frequencies since all of them travel through vacuum with the same speed.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Consequently, the waves differ considerably in their ____.
cards.back: Consequently, the waves differ considerably in their mode of interaction with matter.
cards.quote: Consequently, the waves differ considerably in their mode of interaction with matter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A transmitting antenna can most efficiently radiate waves having a wavelength of ____.
cards.back: A transmitting antenna can most efficiently radiate waves having a wavelength of about the same size as the antenna.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Infrared waves, with frequencies lower than those of visible light, vibrate not only the electrons, but ____ of a substance.
cards.back: Infrared waves, with frequencies lower than those of visible light, vibrate not only the electrons, but entire atoms or molecules of a substance.
cards.quote: Infrared waves, with frequencies lower than those of visible light, vibrate not only the electrons, but entire atoms or molecules of a substance.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The centre of sensitivity of our eyes coincides with the ____.
cards.back: The centre of sensitivity of our eyes coincides with the centre of the wavelength distribution of the sun.

cards.front: Besides conduction current, what is also a source of magnetic field (Maxwell's generalisation)?

cards.quote: but also the time rate of change of electric field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An electric field changing with time gives rise to a magnetic field: a consequence of what?
cards.back: the displacement current being a source of a magnetic field
cards.quote: a consequence of the displacement current being a source of a magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: UV radiations can be focussed into very narrow beams for high precision applications such as ____ (Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) eye surgery.
cards.back: UV radiations can be focussed into very narrow beams for high precision applications such as LASIK (Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) eye surgery.
cards.quote: UV radiations can be focussed into very narrow beams for high precision applications such as LASIK (Laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) eye surgery.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are visible rays?
cards.back: It is the most familiar form of electromagnetic waves. It is the part of the spectrum that is detected by the human eye.
cards.quote: It is the most familiar form of electromagnetic waves. It is the part of the spectrum that is detected by the human eye.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Coulomb force between two (stationary) charges is also a ____ force.
cards.back: Coulomb force between two (stationary) charges is also a conservative force.
cards.quote: Coulomb force between two (stationary) charges is also a conservative force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge between two points depend?
cards.back: It means that the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge from one point to another depends only on the initial and the final points and is independent of the path taken to go from one point to the other.
cards.quote: It means that the work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge from one point to another depends only on the initial and the final points and is independent of the path taken to go from one point to the other.
cards.note: Path independence is the fundamental characteristic of a conservative force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define electric potential energy difference between two points.
cards.back: Therefore, we can define electric potential energy difference between two points as the work required to be done by an external force in moving (without accelerating) charge q from one point to another for electric field of any arbitrary charge configuration.
cards.quote: Therefore, we can define electric potential energy difference between two points as the work required to be done by an external force in moving (without accelerating) charge q from one point to another for electric field of any arbitrary charge configuration.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at ____.
cards.back: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at infinity.
cards.quote: A convenient choice is to have electrostatic potential energy zero at infinity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the potential energy of a charge q at a point in an electric field.
cards.back: Potential energy of charge q at a point (in the presence of field due to any charge configuration) is the work done by the external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in bringing the charge q from infinity to that point.
cards.quote: Potential energy of charge q at a point (in the presence of field due to any charge configuration) is the work done by the external force (equal and opposite to the electric force) in bringing the charge q from infinity to that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the electrostatic potential at a point in an electrostatic field.
cards.back: In other words, the electrostatic potential (V) at any point in a region with electrostatic field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point.
cards.quote: In other words, the electrostatic potential (V) at any point in a region with electrostatic field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the ____ that is physically significant.
cards.back: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the potential difference that is physically significant.
cards.quote: Note, as before, that it is not the actual value of potential but the potential difference that is physically significant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the sign of the potential (V) due to a negative point charge Q?
cards.back: For Q < 0, V < 0, i.e., work done (by the external force) per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to the point is negative.
cards.quote: For Q < 0, V < 0, i.e., work done (by the external force) per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to the point is negative.

source.section: Potential due to a Point Charge

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the dipole moment vector p of an electric dipole characterised (magnitude and direction)?
cards.back: It is characterised by a dipole moment vector p whose magnitude is q × 2a and which points in the direction from −q to q
cards.quote: It is characterised by a dipole moment vector p whose magnitude is q × 2a and which points in the direction from −q to q

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the ____ principle.
cards.back: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the superposition principle.
cards.quote: Since potential is related to the work done by the field, electrostatic potential also follows the superposition principle.

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Besides the distance r, what else does the potential due to a dipole depend on?
cards.back: The potential due to a dipole depends not just on r but also on the angle between the position vector r and the dipole moment vector p.
cards.quote: The potential due to a dipole depends not just on r but also on the angle between the position vector r and the dipole moment vector p.

source.section: Potential due to an Electric Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By the superposition principle, how is the potential at P due to a system of charges obtained?
cards.back: By the superposition principle, the potential V at P due to the total charge configuration is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to the individual charges
cards.quote: By the superposition principle, the potential V at P due to the total charge configuration is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to the individual charges

source.section: Potential due to a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Uniformly charged spherical shell: what is the potential inside the shell?
cards.back: The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface
cards.quote: The electric field inside the shell is zero. This implies (Section 2.6) that potential is constant inside the shell (as no work is done in moving a charge inside the shell), and, therefore, equals its value at the surface

source.section: Potential due to a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define an equipotential surface.
cards.back: An equipotential surface is a surface with a constant value of potential at all points on the surface.
cards.quote: An equipotential surface is a surface with a constant value of potential at all points on the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do the equipotential surfaces of a single point charge look like?
cards.back: Thus, equipotential surfaces of a single point charge are concentric spherical surfaces centred at the charge.
cards.quote: Thus, equipotential surfaces of a single point charge are concentric spherical surfaces centred at the charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the equipotential surface through a point oriented relative to the electric field at that point?
cards.back: This is true in general: for any charge configuration, equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field at that point.
cards.quote: This is true in general: for any charge configuration, equipotential surface through a point is normal to the electric field at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the equipotential surfaces for a uniform electric field along the x-axis?
cards.back: For a uniform electric field E, say, along the x-axis, the equipotential surfaces are planes normal to the x-axis, i.e., planes parallel to the y-z plane
cards.quote: For a uniform electric field E, say, along the x-axis, the equipotential surfaces are planes normal to the x-axis, i.e., planes parallel to the y-z plane

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which direction does the electric field point with respect to the potential?
cards.back: Electric field is in the direction in which the potential decreases steepest.
cards.quote: Electric field is in the direction in which the potential decreases steepest.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the magnitude of the electric field related to the potential?
cards.back: Its magnitude is given by the change in the magnitude of potential per unit displacement normal to the equipotential surface at the point.
cards.quote: Its magnitude is given by the change in the magnitude of potential per unit displacement normal to the equipotential surface at the point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the potential energy stored in a system of charges.
cards.back: Potential energy stored in a system of charges is the work done (by an external agency) in assembling the charges at their locations.
cards.quote: Potential energy stored in a system of charges is the work done (by an external agency) in assembling the charges at their locations.

source.section: Potential Energy of a System of Charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to a point P in an external field, and where is it stored?
cards.back: Thus, work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to the point P in the external field is qV. This work is stored in the form of potential energy of q.
cards.quote: Thus, work done in bringing a charge q from infinity to the point P in the external field is qV. This work is stored in the form of potential energy of q.

source.section: Potential Energy in an External Field

cards.note: V is the external potential at P.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a dipole experience in a uniform electric field?
cards.back: in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque
cards.quote: in a uniform electric field, the dipole experiences no net force; but experiences a torque

source.section: Potential Energy of a Dipole in an External Field

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When does a dipole in a uniform field eventually align with the field?
cards.back: Only if there is a dissipative mechanism, the oscillations are damped and the dipole eventually aligns with E.
cards.quote: Only if there is a dissipative mechanism, the oscillations are damped and the dipole eventually aligns with E.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the potential due to a charge q at its own location?
cards.back: Potential due to a charge q at its own location is not defined – it is infinite.
cards.quote: Potential due to a charge q at its own location is not defined – it is infinite.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do conductors contain, and what are the charge carriers in metallic conductors?
cards.back: Conductors contain mobile charge carriers. In metallic conductors, these charge carriers are electrons.
cards.quote: Conductors contain mobile charge carriers. In metallic conductors, these charge carriers are electrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which electrons are free to move in a metal?
cards.back: In a metal, the outer (valence) electrons part away from their atoms and are free to move.
cards.quote: In a metal, the outer (valence) electrons part away from their atoms and are free to move.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the static situation, what is the electric field inside a conductor?
cards.back: In the static situation, when there is no current inside or on the surface of the conductor, the electric field is zero everywhere inside the conductor.
cards.quote: In the static situation, when there is no current inside or on the surface of the conductor, the electric field is zero everywhere inside the conductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is the electrostatic field directed at the surface of a charged conductor?
cards.back: Thus electrostatic field at the surface of a charged conductor must be normal to the surface at every point.
cards.quote: Thus electrostatic field at the surface of a charged conductor must be normal to the surface at every point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where can the excess charge on a charged conductor reside in the static situation?
cards.back: When the conductor is charged, the excess charge can reside only on the surface in the static situation.
cards.quote: When the conductor is charged, the excess charge can reside only on the surface in the static situation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What can be said about the electrostatic potential throughout a conductor and on its surface?
cards.back: Electrostatic potential is constant throughout the volume of the conductor and has the same value (as inside) on its surface
cards.quote: Electrostatic potential is constant throughout the volume of the conductor and has the same value (as inside) on its surface

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a system of conductors, how is the potential of each conductor characterised?
cards.back: In a system of conductors of arbitrary size, shape and charge configuration, each conductor is characterised by a constant value of potential, but this constant may differ from one conductor to the other.
cards.quote: In a system of conductors of arbitrary size, shape and charge configuration, each conductor is characterised by a constant value of potential, but this constant may differ from one conductor to the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A bird perching on a bare high power line is unharmed, but a man on the ground touching it gets a fatal shock. Why?
cards.back: Current passes only when there is difference in potential.
cards.quote: Current passes only when there is difference in potential.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are dielectrics?
cards.back: Dielectrics are non-conducting substances. In contrast to conductors, they have no (or negligible number of) charge carriers.
cards.quote: Dielectrics are non-conducting substances. In contrast to conductors, they have no (or negligible number of) charge carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does an external field induce a dipole moment in a dielectric?
cards.back: It turns out that the external field induces dipole moment by stretching or re-orienting molecules of the dielectric.
cards.quote: It turns out that the external field induces dipole moment by stretching or re-orienting molecules of the dielectric.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of molecules of a substance (by charge distribution).
cards.back:
polar
non-polar
cards.quote: The molecules of a substance may be polar or non-polar.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a non-polar molecule?
cards.back: In a non-polar molecule, the centres of positive and negative charges coincide. The molecule then has no permanent (or intrinsic) dipole moment.
cards.quote: In a non-polar molecule, the centres of positive and negative charges coincide. The molecule then has no permanent (or intrinsic) dipole moment.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a polar molecule?
cards.back: a polar molecule is one in which the centres of positive and negative charges are separated (even when there is no external field). Such molecules have a permanent dipole moment.
cards.quote: a polar molecule is one in which the centres of positive and negative charges are separated (even when there is no external field). Such molecules have a permanent dipole moment.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Polar or non-polar, what does a dielectric develop in the presence of an external field?
cards.back: Thus in either case, whether polar or non-polar, a dielectric develops a net dipole moment in the presence of an external field.
cards.quote: Thus in either case, whether polar or non-polar, a dielectric develops a net dipole moment in the presence of an external field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define polarisation of a dielectric.
cards.back: The dipole moment per unit volume is called polarisation and is denoted by P.
cards.quote: The dipole moment per unit volume is called polarisation and is denoted by P.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the polarised dielectric affect the field inside it?
cards.back: Clearly, the field produced by these surface charges opposes the external field. The total field in the dielectric is, thereby, reduced from the case when no dielectric is present.
cards.quote: Clearly, the field produced by these surface charges opposes the external field. The total field in the dielectric is, thereby, reduced from the case when no dielectric is present.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a capacitor?
cards.back: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator.
cards.quote: A capacitor is a system of two conductors separated by an insulator.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: capacitance of a capacitor.
cards.back: C = Q/V, where Q and −Q are the charges on the two conductors and V is the potential difference between them.
cards.quote: Its capacitance is defined by C = Q/V, where Q and −Q are the charges on the two conductors and V is the potential difference between them.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the capacitance of a capacitor depend (in vacuum)?
cards.back: The capacitance C depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the system of two conductors.
cards.quote: The capacitance C depends only on the geometrical configuration (shape, size, separation) of the system of two conductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of capacitance?
cards.back: The SI unit of capacitance is 1 farad
cards.quote: The SI unit of capacitance is 1 farad

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a parallel plate capacitor?
cards.back: A parallel plate capacitor consists of two large plane parallel conducting plates separated by a small distance
cards.quote: A parallel plate capacitor consists of two large plane parallel conducting plates separated by a small distance

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Parallel plate capacitor: what is the direction and nature of the field between the plates?
cards.back: The direction of electric field is from the positive to the negative plate. Thus, the electric field is localised between the two plates and is uniform throughout.
cards.quote: The direction of electric field is from the positive to the negative plate. Thus, the electric field is localised between the two plates and is uniform throughout.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the 'fringing of the field' at the edges of a parallel plate capacitor?
cards.back: The field lines bend outward at the edges -- an effect called 'fringing of the field'.
cards.quote: The field lines bend outward at the edges -- an effect called 'fringing of the field'.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the dielectric constant of a substance.
cards.back: Thus, the dielectric constant of a substance is the factor (>1) by which the capacitance increases from its vacuum value, when the dielectric is inserted fully between the plates of a capacitor.
cards.quote: Thus, the dielectric constant of a substance is the factor (>1) by which the capacitance increases from its vacuum value, when the dielectric is inserted fully between the plates of a capacitor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the net field and the potential difference between the plates when a dielectric fills the gap?
cards.back: The net electric field inside the dielectric and hence the potential difference between the plates is thus reduced.
cards.quote: The net electric field inside the dielectric and hence the potential difference between the plates is thus reduced.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Capacitors in series: what is the same on each capacitor?
cards.back: Thus, in the series combination, charges on the two plates (±Q) are the same on each capacitor.
cards.quote: Thus, in the series combination, charges on the two plates (±Q) are the same on each capacitor.
cards.note: For series: the reciprocal of the effective capacitance is the sum of the reciprocals of the individual capacitances.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Capacitors in parallel: what is the same across each capacitor?
cards.back: In this case, the same potential difference is applied across both the capacitors.
cards.quote: In this case, the same potential difference is applied across both the capacitors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since electrostatic force is ____, this work is stored in the form of potential energy of the system.
cards.back: Since electrostatic force is conservative, this work is stored in the form of potential energy of the system.
cards.quote: Since electrostatic force is conservative, this work is stored in the form of potential energy of the system.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where can the potential energy of a charged capacitor be viewed as stored?
cards.back: It is possible to view the potential energy of the capacitor as 'stored' in the electric field between the plates.
cards.quote: It is possible to view the potential energy of the capacitor as 'stored' in the electric field between the plates.
cards.note: Energy stored = one half x charge x voltage (one half x C x V squared, or Q squared over 2C).

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The earth behaves as a magnet with the magnetic field pointing approximately from the geographic ____ to the north.
cards.back: The earth behaves as a magnet with the magnetic field pointing approximately from the geographic south to the north.
cards.quote: The earth behaves as a magnet with the magnetic field pointing approximately from the geographic south to the north.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: When a bar magnet is freely suspended, it points in the ____ direction.
cards.back: When a bar magnet is freely suspended, it points in the north-south direction.
cards.quote: When a bar magnet is freely suspended, it points in the north-south direction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Which tip of a freely suspended bar magnet is the north pole and which is the south pole?
cards.back: The tip which points to the geographic north is called the north pole and the tip which points to the geographic south is called the south pole of the magnet.
cards.quote: The tip which points to the geographic north is called the north pole and the tip which points to the geographic south is called the south pole of the magnet.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What force acts between like poles, and between unlike poles, of two magnets?
cards.back: There is a repulsive force when north poles ( or south poles ) of two magnets are brought close together. Conversely, there is an attractive force between the north pole of one magnet and the south pole of the other.
cards.quote: There is a repulsive force when north poles ( or south poles ) of two magnets are brought close together. Conversely, there is an attractive force between the north pole of one magnet and the south pole of the other.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Unlike electric charges, isolated magnetic north and south poles known as magnetic ____ do not exist.
cards.back: Unlike electric charges, isolated magnetic north and south poles known as magnetic monopoles do not exist.
cards.quote: Unlike electric charges, isolated magnetic north and south poles known as magnetic monopoles do not exist.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What do we get if a bar magnet is broken into two halves?
cards.back: If a bar magnet is broken into two halves, we get two similar bar magnets with somewhat weaker properties.
cards.quote: If a bar magnet is broken into two halves, we get two similar bar magnets with somewhat weaker properties.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What does the iron-filings pattern around a bar magnet suggest about its poles?
cards.back: The pattern of iron filings suggests that the magnet has two poles similar to the positive and negative charge of an electric dipole.
cards.quote: The pattern of iron filings suggests that the magnet has two poles similar to the positive and negative charge of an electric dipole.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Magnetic field lines of a magnet vs electric dipole field lines: how do they begin and end?
cards.back: The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous closed loops. This is unlike the electric dipole where these field lines begin from a positive charge and end on the negative charge or escape to infinity.
cards.quote: The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous closed loops. This is unlike the electric dipole where these field lines begin from a positive charge and end on the negative charge or escape to infinity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous ____.
cards.back: The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous closed loops.
cards.quote: The magnetic field lines of a magnet (or a solenoid) form continuous closed loops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The ____ to the field line at a given point represents the direction of the net magnetic field B at that point.
cards.back: The tangent to the field line at a given point represents the direction of the net magnetic field B at that point.
cards.quote: The tangent to the field line at a given point represents the direction of the net magnetic field B at that point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The magnetic field lines ____, for if they did, the direction of the magnetic field would not be unique at the point of intersection.
cards.back: The magnetic field lines do not intersect, for if they did, the direction of the magnetic field would not be unique at the point of intersection.
cards.quote: The magnetic field lines do not intersect, for if they did, the direction of the magnetic field would not be unique at the point of intersection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Why does NCERT avoid calling magnetic field lines 'magnetic lines of force'?
cards.back: In some textbooks the magnetic field lines are called magnetic lines of force. This nomenclature is avoided since it can be confusing. Unlike electrostatics the field lines in magnetism do not indicate the direction of the force on a (moving) charge.
cards.quote: In some textbooks the magnetic field lines are called magnetic lines of force. This nomenclature is avoided since it can be confusing. Unlike electrostatics the field lines in magnetism do not indicate the direction of the force on a (moving) charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: How can a compass needle be used to plot magnetic field lines?
cards.back: One way is to place a small magnetic compass needle at various positions and note its orientation. This gives us an idea of the magnetic field direction at various points in space.
cards.quote: One way is to place a small magnetic compass needle at various positions and note its orientation. This gives us an idea of the magnetic field direction at various points in space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What does the resemblance of field lines of a bar magnet and a solenoid suggest?
cards.back: The resemblance of magnetic field lines for a bar magnet and a solenoid suggest that a bar magnet may be thought of as a large number of circulating currents in analogy with a solenoid.
cards.quote: The resemblance of magnetic field lines for a bar magnet and a solenoid suggest that a bar magnet may be thought of as a large number of circulating currents in analogy with a solenoid.

source.section: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Cutting a bar magnet in half is like cutting a solenoid. What do we get?
cards.back: Cutting a bar magnet in half is like cutting a solenoid. We get two smaller solenoids with weaker magnetic properties.
cards.quote: Cutting a bar magnet in half is like cutting a solenoid. We get two smaller solenoids with weaker magnetic properties.

source.section: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is Ampere's hypothesis about magnetic phenomena?
cards.back: We mentioned Ampere's hypothesis that all magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of circulating currents.
cards.quote: We mentioned Ampere's hypothesis that all magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of circulating currents.

source.section: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: How is the magnetic moment of a bar magnet related to that of an equivalent solenoid?
cards.back: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is thus equal to the magnetic moment of an equivalent solenoid that produces the same magnetic field.
cards.quote: The magnetic moment of a bar magnet is thus equal to the magnetic moment of an equivalent solenoid that produces the same magnetic field.

source.section: Bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What does a magnetised needle experience in a uniform magnetic field?
cards.back: A magnetised needle in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque but no net force.
cards.quote: A magnetised needle in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque but no net force.

source.section: The dipole in a uniform magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Example: an iron nail near a bar magnet feels a force as well as a torque. Why?
cards.back: No force if the field is uniform. The iron nail experiences a non-uniform field due to the bar magnet. There is induced magnetic moment in the nail, therefore, it experiences both force and torque.
cards.quote: No force if the field is uniform. The iron nail experiences a non-uniform field due to the bar magnet. There is induced magnetic moment in the nail, therefore, it experiences both force and torque.

source.section: The dipole in a uniform magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Example: a bar magnet is cut transverse to its length, or along its length. What results?
cards.back: In either case, one gets two magnets, each with a north and south pole.
cards.quote: In either case, one gets two magnets, each with a north and south pole.

source.section: The dipole in a uniform magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Example: must every magnetic configuration have a north pole and a south pole? (think of a toroid)
cards.back: Not necessarily. True only if the source of the field has a net non-zero magnetic moment. This is not so for a toroid or even for a straight infinite conductor.
cards.quote: Not necessarily. True only if the source of the field has a net non-zero magnetic moment. This is not so for a toroid or even for a straight infinite conductor.

source.section: The dipole in a uniform magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In a bar magnet the intensity of the magnetic field is the ____ at the two ends (poles) and ____ at the central region.
cards.back: In a bar magnet the intensity of the magnetic field is the strongest at the two ends (poles) and weakest at the central region.
cards.quote: In a bar magnet the intensity of the magnetic field is the strongest at the two ends (poles) and weakest at the central region.

source.section: The dipole in a uniform magnetic field

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: State Gauss's law for magnetism.
cards.back: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.
cards.quote: Gauss's law for magnetism is: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: There are no ____ of B; the simplest magnetic element is a ____ or a current loop.
cards.back: There are no sources or sinks of B; the simplest magnetic element is a dipole or a current loop.
cards.quote: There are no sources or sinks of B; the simplest magnetic element is a dipole or a current loop.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: All magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of an arrangement of ____ and/or current loops.
cards.back: All magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of an arrangement of dipoles and/or current loops.
cards.quote: All magnetic phenomena can be explained in terms of an arrangement of dipoles and/or current loops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Why can magnetic field lines never cross each other?
cards.back: Magnetic field lines (like electric field lines) can never cross each other, because otherwise the direction of field at the point of intersection is ambiguous.
cards.quote: Magnetic field lines (like electric field lines) can never cross each other, because otherwise the direction of field at the point of intersection is ambiguous.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What must a closed loop of static magnetic field line enclose?
cards.back: Magnetostatic field lines can never form closed loops around empty space. A closed loop of static magnetic field line must enclose a region across which a current is passing.
cards.quote: Magnetostatic field lines can never form closed loops around empty space. A closed loop of static magnetic field line must enclose a region across which a current is passing.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Example: can a system have magnetic moments even though its net charge is zero?
cards.back: Yes. The average of the charge in the system may be zero. Yet, the mean of the magnetic moments due to various current loops may not be zero.
cards.quote: Yes. The average of the charge in the system may be zero. Yet, the mean of the magnetic moments due to various current loops may not be zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What happens to the magnetic moments of circulating electrons in a bulk material?
cards.back: We have seen that a circulating electron in an atom has a magnetic moment. In a bulk material, these moments add up vectorially and they can give a net magnetic moment which is non-zero.
cards.quote: We have seen that a circulating electron in an atom has a magnetic moment. In a bulk material, these moments add up vectorially and they can give a net magnetic moment which is non-zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define magnetisation M of a sample.
cards.back: We define magnetisation M of a sample to be equal to its net magnetic moment per unit volume
cards.quote: We define magnetisation M of a sample to be equal to its net magnetic moment per unit volume

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In a magnetic material, which part of the total field is represented by H and which by M?
cards.back: We have partitioned the contribution to the total magnetic field inside the sample into two parts: one, due to external factors such as the current in the solenoid. This is represented by H. The other is due to the specific nature of the magnetic material, namely M.
cards.quote: We have partitioned the contribution to the total magnetic field inside the sample into two parts: one, due to external factors such as the current in the solenoid. This is represented by H. The other is due to the specific nature of the magnetic material, namely M.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Magnetic susceptibility is a dimensionless quantity. What is it a measure of?
cards.back: It is a measure of how a magnetic material responds to an external field.
cards.quote: It is a measure of how a magnetic material responds to an external field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the magnetic susceptibility of diamagnetic materials (size and sign)?
cards.back: It is small and negative for materials, which are termed diamagnetic.
cards.quote: It is small and negative for materials, which are termed diamagnetic.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Relative magnetic permeability is a dimensionless quantity. What is it the analog of in electrostatics?
cards.back: It is the analog of the dielectric constant in electrostatics.
cards.quote: It is the analog of the dielectric constant in electrostatics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Into which three classes are magnetic materials broadly classified?
cards.back:
diamagnetic
paramagnetic
ferromagnetic
cards.quote: Magnetic materials are broadly classified as: diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define diamagnetic substances.
cards.back: Diamagnetic substances are those which have tendency to move from stronger to the weaker part of the external magnetic field.
cards.quote: Diamagnetic substances are those which have tendency to move from stronger to the weaker part of the external magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The field lines are repelled or expelled and the field inside the material is ____.
cards.back: The field lines are repelled or expelled and the field inside the material is reduced.
cards.quote: The field lines are repelled or expelled and the field inside the material is reduced.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from ____ field.
cards.back: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from high to low field.
cards.quote: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from high to low field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Diamagnetic substances are the ones in which resultant magnetic moment in an atom is ____.
cards.back: Diamagnetic substances are the ones in which resultant magnetic moment in an atom is zero.
cards.quote: Diamagnetic substances are the ones in which resultant magnetic moment in an atom is zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Name some diamagnetic materials (NCERT).
cards.back:
bismuth
copper
lead
silicon
nitrogen (at STP)
water
sodium chloride
cards.quote: Some diamagnetic materials are bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, nitrogen (at STP), water and sodium chloride.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In which substances is diamagnetism present, and why is it usually not seen?
cards.back: Diamagnetism is present in all the substances. However, the effect is so weak in most cases that it gets shifted by other effects like paramagnetism, ferromagnetism, etc.
cards.quote: Diamagnetism is present in all the substances. However, the effect is so weak in most cases that it gets shifted by other effects like paramagnetism, ferromagnetism, etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What are the most exotic diamagnetic materials, and what do they exhibit?
cards.back: The most exotic diamagnetic materials are superconductors. These are metals, cooled to very low temperatures which exhibits both perfect conductivity and perfect diamagnetism.
cards.quote: The most exotic diamagnetic materials are superconductors. These are metals, cooled to very low temperatures which exhibits both perfect conductivity and perfect diamagnetism.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the Meissner effect?
cards.back: The phenomenon of perfect diamagnetism in superconductors is called the Meissner effect, after the name of its discoverer.
cards.quote: The phenomenon of perfect diamagnetism in superconductors is called the Meissner effect, after the name of its discoverer.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What does a superconductor do to a magnet?
cards.back: A superconductor repels a magnet and (by Newton's third law) is repelled by the magnet.
cards.quote: A superconductor repels a magnet and (by Newton's third law) is repelled by the magnet.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Name an application of superconducting magnets given in NCERT.
cards.back: Superconducting magnets can be gainfully exploited in variety of situations, for example, for running magnetically levitated superfast trains.
cards.quote: Superconducting magnets can be gainfully exploited in variety of situations, for example, for running magnetically levitated superfast trains.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define paramagnetic substances.
cards.back: Paramagnetic substances are those which get weakly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field.
cards.quote: Paramagnetic substances are those which get weakly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Paramagnetic substances tend to move from which region of an external field to which?
cards.back: They have tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get weakly attracted to a magnet.
cards.quote: They have tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get weakly attracted to a magnet.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) of a paramagnetic material possess a ____ magnetic dipole moment of their own.
cards.back: The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) of a paramagnetic material possess a permanent magnetic dipole moment of their own.
cards.quote: The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) of a paramagnetic material possess a permanent magnetic dipole moment of their own.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: On account of the ceaseless random ____ of the atoms, no net magnetisation is seen.
cards.back: On account of the ceaseless random thermal motion of the atoms, no net magnetisation is seen.
cards.quote: On account of the ceaseless random thermal motion of the atoms, no net magnetisation is seen.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The field lines gets concentrated inside the material, and the field inside is ____.
cards.back: The field lines gets concentrated inside the material, and the field inside is enhanced.
cards.quote: The field lines gets concentrated inside the material, and the field inside is enhanced.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from ____.
cards.back: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from weak field to strong.
cards.quote: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, the bar will tend to move from weak field to strong.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Name some paramagnetic materials (NCERT).
cards.back:
aluminium
sodium
calcium
oxygen (at STP)
copper chloride
cards.quote: Some paramagnetic materials are aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen (at STP) and copper chloride.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: As the field is increased or the temperature is lowered, the magnetisation increases until it reaches the ____
cards.back: As the field is increased or the temperature is lowered, the magnetisation increases until it reaches the saturation value
cards.quote: As the field is increased or the temperature is lowered, the magnetisation increases until it reaches the saturation value

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define ferromagnetic substances.
cards.back: Ferromagnetic substances are those which gets strongly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field.
cards.quote: Ferromagnetic substances are those which gets strongly magnetised when placed in an external magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Ferromagnetic substances tend to move from which region of an external field to which?
cards.back: They have strong tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get strongly attracted to a magnet.
cards.quote: They have strong tendency to move from a region of weak magnetic field to strong magnetic field, i.e., they get strongly attracted to a magnet.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is a domain in a ferromagnetic material?
cards.back: The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) in a ferromagnetic material possess a dipole moment as in a paramagnetic material. However, they interact with one another in such a way that they spontaneously align themselves in a common direction over a macroscopic volume called domain.
cards.quote: The individual atoms (or ions or molecules) in a ferromagnetic material possess a dipole moment as in a paramagnetic material. However, they interact with one another in such a way that they spontaneously align themselves in a common direction over a macroscopic volume called domain.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In a non-uniform magnetic field, where does a ferromagnetic sample tend to move?
cards.back: In non-uniform magnetic field, the sample tends to move towards the region of high field.
cards.quote: In non-uniform magnetic field, the sample tends to move towards the region of high field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What are hard magnetic materials (hard ferromagnets)?
cards.back: In some ferromagnetic materials the magnetisation persists. Such materials are called hard magnetic materials or hard ferromagnets.
cards.quote: In some ferromagnetic materials the magnetisation persists. Such materials are called hard magnetic materials or hard ferromagnets.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Name examples of hard magnetic materials (NCERT).
cards.back: Alnico, an alloy of iron, aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper, is one such material. The naturally occurring lodestone is another.
cards.quote: Alnico, an alloy of iron, aluminium, nickel, cobalt and copper, is one such material. The naturally occurring lodestone is another.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What are soft ferromagnetic materials? Give an example.
cards.back: On the other hand, there is a class of ferromagnetic materials in which the magnetisation disappears on removal of the external field. Soft iron is one such material. Appropriately enough, such materials are called soft ferromagnetic materials.
cards.quote: On the other hand, there is a class of ferromagnetic materials in which the magnetisation disappears on removal of the external field. Soft iron is one such material. Appropriately enough, such materials are called soft ferromagnetic materials.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Name the ferromagnetic elements listed in NCERT.
cards.back:
iron
cobalt
nickel
gadolinium
cards.quote: There are a number of elements, which are ferromagnetic: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the relative magnetic permeability of ferromagnetic materials?
cards.back: The relative magnetic permeability is >1000!
cards.quote: The relative magnetic permeability is >1000!

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What happens to a ferromagnet at high enough temperature?
cards.back: The ferromagnetic property depends on temperature. At high enough temperature, a ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet.
cards.quote: The ferromagnetic property depends on temperature. At high enough temperature, a ferromagnet becomes a paramagnet.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define permanent magnets.
cards.back: Substances, which at room temperature, retain their ferromagnetic property for a long period of time are called permanent magnets.
cards.quote: Substances, which at room temperature, retain their ferromagnetic property for a long period of time are called permanent magnets.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Electric dipole vs magnetic dipole: what is each built up of?
cards.back: an electric dipole is built up of two elementary units -- the charges (or electric monopoles). In magnetism, a magnetic dipole (or a current loop) is the most elementary element.
cards.quote: an electric dipole is built up of two elementary units -- the charges (or electric monopoles). In magnetism, a magnetic dipole (or a current loop) is the most elementary element.

source.section: Circular Current Loop as a Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What happens if you slice a magnet in half, and how does this differ from charges?
cards.back: Magnetic monopoles do not exist. If you slice a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets. On the other hand, isolated positive and negative charges exist.
cards.quote: Magnetic monopoles do not exist. If you slice a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets. On the other hand, isolated positive and negative charges exist.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What did a current loop's field and torque lead Ampere to suggest?
cards.back: This led Ampere to suggest that all magnetism is due to circulating currents.
cards.quote: This led Ampere to suggest that all magnetism is due to circulating currents.

source.section: Circular Current Loop as a Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What follows from the non-existence of magnetic monopoles for field lines?
cards.back: A consequence of the fact that magnetic monopoles do not exist is that the magnetic field lines are continuous and form closed loops. In contrast, the electrostatic lines of force begin on a positive charge and terminate on the negative charge (or fade out at infinity).
cards.quote: A consequence of the fact that magnetic monopoles do not exist is that the magnetic field lines are continuous and form closed loops. In contrast, the electrostatic lines of force begin on a positive charge and terminate on the negative charge (or fade out at infinity).

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Which material is a perfect diamagnet?
cards.back: There exists a perfect diamagnet, namely, a superconductor. This is a metal at very low temperatures.
cards.quote: There exists a perfect diamagnet, namely, a superconductor. This is a metal at very low temperatures.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Diamagnetism is ____. It is present in all materials. But it is weak and hard to detect if the substance is para- or ferromagnetic.
cards.back: Diamagnetism is universal. It is present in all materials. But it is weak and hard to detect if the substance is para- or ferromagnetic.
cards.quote: Diamagnetism is universal. It is present in all materials. But it is weak and hard to detect if the substance is para- or ferromagnetic.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What did Hans Christian Oersted observe in 1820, and why was it important?
cards.back: He observed that a compass needle suffers a deflection when placed near a wire carrying an electric current. This discovery gave the first empirical evidence of a connection between electric and magnetic phenomena.
cards.quote: He observed that a compass needle suffers a deflection when placed near a wire carrying an electric current. This discovery gave the first empirical evidence of a connection between electric and magnetic phenomena.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Oersted concluded that moving charges or currents produced a ____ in the surrounding space.
cards.back: Oersted concluded that moving charges or currents produced a magnetic field in the surrounding space.
cards.quote: Oersted concluded that moving charges or currents produced a magnetic field in the surrounding space.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Iron filings sprinkled around the wire arrange themselves in ____ with the wire as the centre
cards.back: Iron filings sprinkled around the wire arrange themselves in concentric circles with the wire as the centre
cards.quote: Iron filings sprinkled around the wire arrange themselves in concentric circles with the wire as the centre

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Just as static charges produce an electric field, the currents or moving charges produce (in addition) a ____, denoted by B (r), again a vector field.
cards.back: Just as static charges produce an electric field, the currents or moving charges produce (in addition) a magnetic field, denoted by B (r), again a vector field.
cards.quote: Just as static charges produce an electric field, the currents or moving charges produce (in addition) a magnetic field, denoted by B (r), again a vector field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define the Lorentz force.
cards.back: The total force on a charge q moving with velocity v in the presence of magnetic and electric fields B and E, respectively is called the Lorentz force.
cards.quote: The total force on a charge q moving with velocity v in the presence of magnetic and electric fields B and E, respectively is called the Lorentz force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Who first gave the expression for the force on a charge in electric and magnetic fields?
cards.back: This force was given first by H.A. Lorentz based on the extensive experiments of Ampere and others.
cards.quote: This force was given first by H.A. Lorentz based on the extensive experiments of Ampere and others.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Force on a negative charge is ____ to that on a positive charge.
cards.back: Force on a negative charge is opposite to that on a positive charge.
cards.quote: Force on a negative charge is opposite to that on a positive charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The force acts in a (sideways) direction ____ to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
cards.back: The force acts in a (sideways) direction perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.
cards.quote: The force acts in a (sideways) direction perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Only a ____ charge feels the magnetic force.
cards.back: Only a moving charge feels the magnetic force.
cards.quote: Only a moving charge feels the magnetic force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: How is the direction of the magnetic force on a moving charge given?
cards.back: Its direction is given by the screw rule or right hand rule for vector (or cross) product
cards.quote: Its direction is given by the screw rule or right hand rule for vector (or cross) product

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: When is the magnitude of magnetic field B said to be 1 SI unit (one tesla)?
cards.back: The magnitude of magnetic field B is 1 SI unit, when the force acting on a unit charge (1 C), moving perpendicular to B with a speed 1m/s, is one newton.
cards.quote: The magnitude of magnetic field B is 1 SI unit, when the force acting on a unit charge (1 C), moving perpendicular to B with a speed 1m/s, is one newton.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: After whom is the SI unit of magnetic field, the tesla, named?
cards.back: This unit is called tesla ( T ) named after Nikola Tesla
cards.quote: This unit is called tesla ( T ) named after Nikola Tesla

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the smaller, non-SI unit of magnetic field called?
cards.back: Tesla is a rather large unit. A smaller unit (non-SI) called gauss
cards.quote: Tesla is a rather large unit. A smaller unit (non-SI) called gauss

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: B is the ____ magnetic field. It is not the field produced by the current-carrying rod.
cards.back: B is the external magnetic field. It is not the field produced by the current-carrying rod.
cards.quote: B is the external magnetic field. It is not the field produced by the current-carrying rod.

source.section: Magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In the case of motion of a charge in a magnetic field, the magnetic force is ____ to the velocity of the particle.
cards.back: In the case of motion of a charge in a magnetic field, the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity of the particle.
cards.quote: In the case of motion of a charge in a magnetic field, the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity of the particle.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The particle will describe a ____ if v and B are perpendicular to each other
cards.back: The particle will describe a circle if v and B are perpendicular to each other
cards.quote: The particle will describe a circle if v and B are perpendicular to each other

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The motion in a plane perpendicular to B is as before a circular one, thereby producing a ____ motion
cards.back: The motion in a plane perpendicular to B is as before a circular one, thereby producing a helical motion
cards.quote: The motion in a plane perpendicular to B is as before a circular one, thereby producing a helical motion

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the cyclotron frequency?
cards.back: In a uniform magnetic field B, a charge q executes a circular orbit in a plane normal to B. Its frequency of uniform circular motion is called the cyclotron frequency
cards.quote: In a uniform magnetic field B, a charge q executes a circular orbit in a plane normal to B. Its frequency of uniform circular motion is called the cyclotron frequency

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define the pitch of the helical path of a charged particle in a magnetic field.
cards.back: The distance moved along the magnetic field in one rotation is called pitch p.
cards.quote: The distance moved along the magnetic field in one rotation is called pitch p.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: All magnetic fields that we know are due to currents (or moving charges) and due to ____ of particles.
cards.back: All magnetic fields that we know are due to currents (or moving charges) and due to intrinsic magnetic moments of particles.
cards.quote: All magnetic fields that we know are due to currents (or moving charges) and due to intrinsic magnetic moments of particles.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: State the Biot-Savart law (magnitude of the field dB due to a current element).
cards.back: According to Biot-Savart's law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB is proportional to the current I, the element length |dl|, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance r.
cards.quote: According to Biot-Savart's law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB is proportional to the current I, the element length |dl|, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance r.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: We call μ0 the ____ of free space (or vacuum).
cards.back: We call μ0 the permeability of free space (or vacuum).
cards.quote: We call μ0 the permeability of free space (or vacuum).

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Electrostatic field vs magnetic field: the nature of the source.
cards.back: The electrostatic field is produced by a scalar source, namely, the electric charge. The magnetic field is produced by a vector source I dl.
cards.quote: The electrostatic field is produced by a scalar source, namely, the electric charge. The magnetic field is produced by a vector source I dl.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Electrostatic field vs magnetic field: the direction of the field with respect to the source.
cards.back: The electrostatic field is along the displacement vector joining the source and the field point. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane containing the displacement vector r and the current element I dl.
cards.quote: The electrostatic field is along the displacement vector joining the source and the field point. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane containing the displacement vector r and the current element I dl.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: There is an ____ in the Biot-Savart law which is not present in the electrostatic case.
cards.back: There is an angle dependence in the Biot-Savart law which is not present in the electrostatic case.
cards.quote: There is an angle dependence in the Biot-Savart law which is not present in the electrostatic case.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: When the components perpendicular to the x-axis are summed over, they ____ and we obtain a null result.
cards.back: When the components perpendicular to the x-axis are summed over, they cancel out and we obtain a null result.
cards.quote: When the components perpendicular to the x-axis are summed over, they cancel out and we obtain a null result.

source.section: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The magnetic field lines due to a circular wire form ____
cards.back: The magnetic field lines due to a circular wire form closed loops
cards.quote: The magnetic field lines due to a circular wire form closed loops

source.section: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: State the right-hand thumb rule for the direction of the magnetic field of a circular current loop.
cards.back: Curl the palm of your right hand around the circular wire with the fingers pointing in the direction of the current. The right-hand thumb gives the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: Curl the palm of your right hand around the circular wire with the fingers pointing in the direction of the current. The right-hand thumb gives the direction of the magnetic field.

source.section: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Field at the centre of a semicircular current arc compared with a full circular loop (same radius and current).
cards.back: Hence direction of B for a semicircular arc is given by the right-hand rule and magnitude is half that of a circular loop.
cards.quote: Hence direction of B for a semicircular arc is given by the right-hand rule and magnitude is half that of a circular loop.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Amperian loop: what are the three possibilities for B at each point of the loop?
cards.back:
B is tangential to the loop and is a non-zero constant B
B is normal to the loop
B vanishes
cards.quote: it is possible to choose the loop (called an amperian loop) such that at each point of the loop, either (i) B is tangential to the loop and is a non-zero constant B, or (ii) B is normal to the loop, or (iii) B vanishes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Ampere's law is to Biot-Savart law, what ____ is to Coulomb's law.
cards.back: Ampere's law is to Biot-Savart law, what Gauss's law is to Coulomb's law.
cards.quote: Ampere's law is to Biot-Savart law, what Gauss's law is to Coulomb's law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: We also note that Ampere's circuital law holds for ____ which do not fluctuate with time.
