cards.back: We also note that Ampere's circuital law holds for steady currents which do not fluctuate with time.
cards.quote: We also note that Ampere's circuital law holds for steady currents which do not fluctuate with time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The field is ____ proportional to the current and ____ proportional to the distance from the (infinitely long) current source.
cards.back: The field is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance from the (infinitely long) current source.
cards.quote: The field is directly proportional to the current and inversely proportional to the distance from the (infinitely long) current source.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Magnetic field lines vs electrostatic field lines: how do they begin and end?
cards.back: These lines called magnetic field lines form closed loops. This is unlike the electrostatic field lines which originate from positive charges and end at negative charges.
cards.quote: These lines called magnetic field lines form closed loops. This is unlike the electrostatic field lines which originate from positive charges and end at negative charges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: State the right-hand rule for the direction of the magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying wire.
cards.back: Grasp the wire in your right hand with your extended thumb pointing in the direction of the current. Your fingers will curl around in the direction of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: Grasp the wire in your right hand with your extended thumb pointing in the direction of the current. Your fingers will curl around in the direction of the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The field lines are circles ____ with the wire.
cards.back: The field lines are circles concentric with the wire.
cards.quote: The field lines are circles concentric with the wire.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is meant by a long solenoid?
cards.back: By long solenoid we mean that the solenoid's length is large compared to its radius.
cards.quote: By long solenoid we mean that the solenoid's length is large compared to its radius.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Finite solenoid: the field at the interior mid-point vs the exterior mid-point.
cards.back: the field at the interior mid-point P is uniform, strong and along the axis of the solenoid. The field at the exterior mid-point Q is weak and moreover is along the axis of the solenoid with no perpendicular or normal component.
cards.quote: the field at the interior mid-point P is uniform, strong and along the axis of the solenoid. The field at the exterior mid-point Q is weak and moreover is along the axis of the solenoid with no perpendicular or normal component.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The field outside the solenoid approaches zero. We shall assume that the field outside is zero. The field inside becomes everywhere ____ to the axis.
cards.back: The field outside the solenoid approaches zero. We shall assume that the field outside is zero. The field inside becomes everywhere parallel to the axis.
cards.quote: The field outside the solenoid approaches zero. We shall assume that the field outside is zero. The field inside becomes everywhere parallel to the axis.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The solenoid is commonly used to obtain a ____.
cards.back: The solenoid is commonly used to obtain a uniform magnetic field.
cards.quote: The solenoid is commonly used to obtain a uniform magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: We shall see in the next chapter that a large field is possible by inserting a ____ inside the solenoid.
cards.back: We shall see in the next chapter that a large field is possible by inserting a soft iron core inside the solenoid.
cards.quote: We shall see in the next chapter that a large field is possible by inserting a soft iron core inside the solenoid.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the rule for the force between two parallel and between two antiparallel currents?
cards.back: Parallel currents attract, and antiparallel currents repel.
cards.quote: Parallel currents attract, and antiparallel currents repel.

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Like (same sign) charges ____ each other, but like (parallel) currents ____ each other.
cards.back: Like (same sign) charges repel each other, but like (parallel) currents attract each other.
cards.quote: Like (same sign) charges repel each other, but like (parallel) currents attract each other.

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The above expression is used to define the ampere (A), which is one of the ____ SI base units.
cards.back: The above expression is used to define the ampere (A), which is one of the seven SI base units.
cards.quote: The above expression is used to define the ampere (A), which is one of the seven SI base units.

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: In which year was the present definition of the ampere adopted?
cards.back: This definition of the ampere was adopted in 1946.
cards.quote: This definition of the ampere was adopted in 1946.

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: An instrument called the ____ is used to measure this mechanical force.
cards.back: An instrument called the current balance is used to measure this mechanical force.
cards.quote: An instrument called the current balance is used to measure this mechanical force.

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define one coulomb in terms of the ampere.
cards.back: When a steady current of 1A is set up in a conductor, the quantity of charge that flows through its cross-section in 1s is one coulomb (1C).
cards.quote: When a steady current of 1A is set up in a conductor, the quantity of charge that flows through its cross-section in 1s is one coulomb (1C).

source.section: Force Between Two Parallel Currents, the Ampere

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: State the right-hand thumb rule for the direction of the magnetic moment of a current loop.
cards.back: curl the palm of your right hand along the loop with the fingers pointing in the direction of the current. The thumb sticking out gives the direction of m (and A)
cards.quote: curl the palm of your right hand along the loop with the fingers pointing in the direction of the current. The thumb sticking out gives the direction of m (and A)

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: A coil whose magnetic moment m is parallel or antiparallel to B: what state is it in?
cards.back: This indicates a state of equilibrium as there is no torque on the coil (this also applies to any object with a magnetic moment m).
cards.quote: This indicates a state of equilibrium as there is no torque on the coil (this also applies to any object with a magnetic moment m).

source.section: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Current loop in a magnetic field: equilibrium when m is parallel vs antiparallel to B.
cards.back: When m and B are parallel the equilibrium is a stable one. Any small rotation of the coil produces a torque which brings it back to its original position. When they are antiparallel, the equilibrium is unstable as any rotation produces a torque which increases with the amount of rotation.
cards.quote: When m and B are parallel the equilibrium is a stable one. Any small rotation of the coil produces a torque which brings it back to its original position. When they are antiparallel, the equilibrium is unstable as any rotation produces a torque which increases with the amount of rotation.

source.section: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: The presence of this torque is also the reason why a small magnet or any magnetic dipole ____ itself with the external magnetic field.
cards.back: The presence of this torque is also the reason why a small magnet or any magnetic dipole aligns itself with the external magnetic field.
cards.quote: The presence of this torque is also the reason why a small magnet or any magnetic dipole aligns itself with the external magnetic field.

source.section: Torque on Current Loop, Magnetic Dipole

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: A current loop free to turn in a uniform external field: its orientation of stable equilibrium.
cards.back: Orientation of stable equilibrium is one where the area vector A of the loop is in the direction of external magnetic field.
cards.quote: Orientation of stable equilibrium is one where the area vector A of the loop is in the direction of external magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Why does a flexible irregular current loop in an external magnetic field become circular?
cards.back: It assumes circular shape with its plane normal to the field to maximise flux, since for a given perimeter, a circle encloses greater area than any other shape.
cards.quote: It assumes circular shape with its plane normal to the field to maximise flux, since for a given perimeter, a circle encloses greater area than any other shape.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Describe the construction of a moving coil galvanometer.
cards.back: The galvanometer consists of a coil, with many turns, free to rotate about a fixed axis (Fig. 4.20), in a uniform radial magnetic field. There is a cylindrical soft iron core which not only makes the field radial but also increases the strength of the magnetic field.
cards.quote: The galvanometer consists of a coil, with many turns, free to rotate about a fixed axis (Fig. 4.20), in a uniform radial magnetic field. There is a cylindrical soft iron core which not only makes the field radial but also increases the strength of the magnetic field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is the torsional constant k of the spring in a moving coil galvanometer?
cards.back: k is the torsional constant of the spring; i.e. the restoring torque per unit twist.
cards.quote: k is the torsional constant of the spring; i.e. the restoring torque per unit twist.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer.
cards.back: the deflection per unit current
cards.quote: galvanometer as the deflection per unit current

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: A convenient way for the manufacturer to increase the sensitivity is to increase the ____ N.
cards.back: A convenient way for the manufacturer to increase the sensitivity is to increase the number of turns N.
cards.quote: A convenient way for the manufacturer to increase the sensitivity is to increase the number of turns N.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Why can a galvanometer not be used as such as an ammeter? Give the two reasons.
cards.back:
Galvanometer is a very sensitive device, it gives a full-scale deflection for a current of the order of μA.
For measuring currents, the galvanometer has to be connected in series, and as it has a large resistance, this will change the value of the current in the circuit.
cards.quote: This is for two reasons: (i) Galvanometer is a very sensitive device, it gives a full-scale deflection for a current of the order of μA. (ii) For measuring currents, the galvanometer has to be connected in series, and as it has a large resistance, this will change the value of the current in the circuit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: What is a shunt resistance, and how is it connected to the galvanometer?
cards.back: one attaches a small resistance rs, called shunt resistance, in parallel with the galvanometer coil; so that most of the current passes through the shunt
cards.quote: one attaches a small resistance rs, called shunt resistance, in parallel with the galvanometer coil; so that most of the current passes through the shunt

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Define the voltage sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer.
cards.back: We define the voltage sensitivity as the deflection per unit voltage.
cards.quote: We define the voltage sensitivity as the deflection per unit voltage.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: An interesting point to note is that increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the ____.
cards.back: An interesting point to note is that increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity.
cards.quote: An interesting point to note is that increasing the current sensitivity may not necessarily increase the voltage sensitivity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Converting a moving coil galvanometer into an ammeter vs into a voltmeter.
cards.back: A moving coil galvanometer can be converted into a ammeter by introducing a shunt resistance rs, of small value in parallel. It can be converted into a voltmeter by introducing a resistance of a large value in series.
cards.quote: A moving coil galvanometer can be converted into a ammeter by introducing a shunt resistance rs, of small value in parallel. It can be converted into a voltmeter by introducing a resistance of a large value in series.

cards.subject: physics
cards.unit: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
cards.front: Ampere's Circuital law is not independent of the Biot-Savart law. It can be ____ from the Biot-Savart law.
cards.back: Ampere's Circuital law is not independent of the Biot-Savart law. It can be derived from the Biot-Savart law.
cards.quote: Ampere's Circuital law is not independent of the Biot-Savart law. It can be derived from the Biot-Savart law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How much of the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?
cards.back: More than 99.9% mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.
cards.quote: More than 99.9% mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Atomic masses in u are close to integral multiples of the mass of which atom?
cards.back: The atomic masses of various elements expressed in atomic mass unit (u) are close to being integral multiples of the mass of a hydrogen atom.
cards.quote: The atomic masses of various elements expressed in atomic mass unit (u) are close to being integral multiples of the mass of a hydrogen atom.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which instrument is used for accurate measurement of atomic masses?
cards.back: Accurate measurement of atomic masses is carried out with a mass spectrometer
cards.quote: Accurate measurement of atomic masses is carried out with a mass spectrometer

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are isotopes?
cards.back: The measurement of atomic masses reveals the existence of different types of atoms of the same element, which exhibit the same chemical properties, but differ in mass. Such atomic species of the same element differing in mass are called isotopes.
cards.quote: The measurement of atomic masses reveals the existence of different types of atoms of the same element, which exhibit the same chemical properties, but differ in mass. Such atomic species of the same element differing in mass are called isotopes.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the word 'isotope' mean in Greek?
cards.back: In Greek, isotope means the same place, i.e. they occur in the same place in the periodic table of elements.
cards.quote: In Greek, isotope means the same place, i.e. they occur in the same place in the periodic table of elements.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The atomic mass of an element is a ____ of the masses of its isotopes and calculated in accordance to the relative abundances of the isotopes.
cards.back: The atomic mass of an element is a weighted average of the masses of its isotopes and calculated in accordance to the relative abundances of the isotopes.
cards.quote: The atomic mass of an element is a weighted average of the masses of its isotopes and calculated in accordance to the relative abundances of the isotopes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The nucleus of the lightest atom of hydrogen, which has a relative abundance of 99.985%, is called the ____.
cards.back: The nucleus of the lightest atom of hydrogen, which has a relative abundance of 99.985%, is called the proton.
cards.quote: The nucleus of the lightest atom of hydrogen, which has a relative abundance of 99.985%, is called the proton.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: After the proton, what are the other two isotopes of hydrogen called?
cards.back: The other two isotopes of hydrogen are called deuterium and tritium.
cards.quote: The other two isotopes of hydrogen are called deuterium and tritium.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does tritium not occur naturally?
cards.back: Tritium nuclei, being unstable, do not occur naturally and are produced artificially in laboratories.
cards.quote: Tritium nuclei, being unstable, do not occur naturally and are produced artificially in laboratories.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What charge does a proton carry, and is it stable?
cards.back: A proton carries one unit of fundamental charge and is stable.
cards.quote: A proton carries one unit of fundamental charge and is stable.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is it now known that the nucleus does not contain electrons?
cards.back: It was earlier thought that the nucleus may contain electrons, but this was ruled out later using arguments based on quantum theory.
cards.quote: It was earlier thought that the nucleus may contain electrons, but this was ruled out later using arguments based on quantum theory.

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since the atom is neutral, what is the charge of the nucleus of atomic number Z?
cards.back: (+Ze)
cards.quote: since the atom is neutral, the charge of the nucleus is (+Ze)

source.section: Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the atomic number Z.
cards.back: The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the atomic nucleus of an element.
cards.quote: The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the atomic nucleus of an element.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did the 1:2:3 ratio of masses of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium nuclei imply?
cards.back: But the masses of the nuclei of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium are in the ratio of 1:2:3. Therefore, the nuclei of deuterium and tritium must contain, in addition to a proton, some neutral matter.
cards.quote: But the masses of the nuclei of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium are in the ratio of 1:2:3. Therefore, the nuclei of deuterium and tritium must contain, in addition to a proton, some neutral matter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who verified in 1932 that nuclei contain neutral matter, and by what experiment?
cards.back: This hypothesis was verified in 1932 by James Chadwick who observed emission of neutral radiation when beryllium nuclei were bombarded with alpha-particles
cards.quote: This hypothesis was verified in 1932 by James Chadwick who observed emission of neutral radiation when beryllium nuclei were bombarded with alpha-particles

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did Chadwick assume the neutral radiation consisted of?
cards.back: The clue to this puzzle, which Chadwick satisfactorily solved, was to assume that the neutral radiation consists of a new type of neutral particles called neutrons.
cards.quote: The clue to this puzzle, which Chadwick satisfactorily solved, was to assume that the neutral radiation consists of a new type of neutral particles called neutrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the mass of a neutron compare with that of a proton?
cards.back: A nucleus contains a neutral particle called neutron. Its mass is almost the same as that of proton
cards.quote: A nucleus contains a neutral particle called neutron. Its mass is almost the same as that of proton

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For what discovery was Chadwick awarded the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics?
cards.back: Chadwick was awarded the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of the neutron.
cards.quote: Chadwick was awarded the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of the neutron.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Free neutron vs free proton: the difference in stability.
cards.back: A free neutron, unlike a free proton, is unstable.
cards.quote: A free neutron, unlike a free proton, is unstable.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Into what does a free neutron decay, and what is its mean life?
cards.back: It decays into a proton, an electron and a antineutrino (another elementary particle), and has a mean life of about 1000s. It is, however, stable inside the nucleus.
cards.quote: It decays into a proton, an electron and a antineutrino (another elementary particle), and has a mean life of about 1000s. It is, however, stable inside the nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Composition of a nucleus: what is Z?
cards.back: Z - atomic number = number of protons
cards.quote: Z - atomic number = number of protons

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Composition of a nucleus: what is N?
cards.back: N - neutron number = number of neutrons
cards.quote: N - neutron number = number of neutrons

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Composition of a nucleus: what is the mass number A?
cards.back: A - mass number = Z + N = total number of protons and neutrons
cards.quote: A - mass number = Z + N = total number of protons and neutrons

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a nucleon?
cards.back: One also uses the term nucleon for a proton or a neutron. Thus the number of nucleons in an atom is its mass number A.
cards.quote: One also uses the term nucleon for a proton or a neutron. Thus the number of nucleons in an atom is its mass number A.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do the nuclei of isotopes of a given element differ?
cards.back: The nuclei of isotopes of a given element contain the same number of protons, but differ from each other in their number of neutrons.
cards.quote: The nuclei of isotopes of a given element contain the same number of protons, but differ from each other in their number of neutrons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How many protons and neutrons are in a deuterium nucleus?
cards.back: contains one proton and one neutron
cards.quote: contains one proton and one neutron

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How many protons and neutrons are in a tritium nucleus?
cards.back: contains one proton and two neutrons
cards.quote: contains one proton and two neutrons

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do isotopes have identical chemical behaviour?
cards.back: As the atoms of isotopes have identical electronic structure they have identical chemical behaviour and are placed in the same location in the periodic table.
cards.quote: As the atoms of isotopes have identical electronic structure they have identical chemical behaviour and are placed in the same location in the periodic table.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: All nuclides with same mass number A are called ____.
cards.back: All nuclides with same mass number A are called isobars.
cards.quote: All nuclides with same mass number A are called isobars.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are isotones?
cards.back: Nuclides with same neutron number N but different atomic number Z
cards.quote: Nuclides with same neutron number N but different atomic number Z

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Isotopes, isobars and isotones: what do the nuclides share?
cards.back:
Nuclides with the same atomic number Z, but different neutron number N are called isotopes.
Nuclides with the same A are isobars and those with the same N are isotones.
cards.quote: Nuclides with the same atomic number Z, but different neutron number N are called isotopes. Nuclides with the same A are isobars and those with the same N are isotones.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who postulated and established the existence of the atomic nucleus?
cards.back: Rutherford was the pioneer who postulated and established the existence of the atomic nucleus.
cards.quote: Rutherford was the pioneer who postulated and established the existence of the atomic nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who performed the classic scattering experiment on thin gold foils at Rutherford's suggestion?
cards.back: Geiger and Marsden
cards.quote: At Rutherford's suggestion, Geiger and Marsden performed their classic experiment

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did Rutherford assume was solely responsible for the scattering of alpha-particles by a gold sheet?
cards.back: the coulomb repulsive force
cards.quote: by assuming that the coulomb repulsive force was solely responsible for scattering

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Different nuclei are like what, in terms of density?
cards.back: Different nuclei are like a drop of liquid of constant density.
cards.quote: Different nuclei are like a drop of liquid of constant density.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Matter in which astrophysical object has a density comparable to nuclear density?
cards.back: neutron stars (an astrophysical object)
cards.quote: The density of matter in neutron stars (an astrophysical object) is comparable to this density.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Does the density of nuclear matter depend on the size of the nucleus? What about the mass density of the atom?
cards.back: The density of nuclear matter is independent of the size of the nucleus. The mass density of the atom does not follow this rule.
cards.quote: The density of nuclear matter is independent of the size of the nucleus. The mass density of the atom does not follow this rule.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do electron and alpha-particle scattering give slightly different nuclear radii?
cards.back: electron scattering senses the charge distribution of the nucleus, whereas alpha and similar particles sense the nuclear matter.
cards.quote: electron scattering senses the charge distribution of the nucleus, whereas alpha and similar particles sense the nuclear matter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did Einstein show about mass and energy?
cards.back: Einstein showed that mass is another form of energy and one can convert mass-energy into other forms of energy, say kinetic energy and vice-versa.
cards.quote: Einstein showed that mass is another form of energy and one can convert mass-energy into other forms of energy, say kinetic energy and vice-versa.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What was presumed about mass and energy before the theory of special relativity?
cards.back: Before the advent of this theory of special relativity it was presumed that mass and energy were conserved separately in a reaction.
cards.quote: Before the advent of this theory of special relativity it was presumed that mass and energy were conserved separately in a reaction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a reaction, when are the initial energy and the final energy equal?
cards.back: In a reaction the conservation law of energy states that the initial energy and the final energy are equal provided the energy associated with mass is also included.
cards.quote: In a reaction the conservation law of energy states that the initial energy and the final energy are equal provided the energy associated with mass is also included.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: After Einstein, what law replaces the separate laws of conservation of mass and of energy?
cards.back: we cannot any longer speak of separate laws of conservation of mass and conservation of energy, but we have to speak of a unified law of conservation of mass and energy.
cards.quote: we cannot any longer speak of separate laws of conservation of mass and conservation of energy, but we have to speak of a unified law of conservation of mass and energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define mass defect.
cards.back: The difference in mass of a nucleus and its constituents is called the mass defect
cards.quote: The difference in mass of a nucleus and its constituents is called the mass defect

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the nuclear binding energy a convenient measure of?
cards.back: Although we cannot tear apart a nucleus in this way, the nuclear binding energy is still a convenient measure of how well a nucleus is held together.
cards.quote: Although we cannot tear apart a nucleus in this way, the nuclear binding energy is still a convenient measure of how well a nucleus is held together.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What can binding energy per nucleon be thought of as?
cards.back: We can think of binding energy per nucleon as the average energy per nucleon needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons.
cards.quote: We can think of binding energy per nucleon as the average energy per nucleon needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the binding energy per nucleon in the mass number range A = 30 to 170?
cards.back: In the mass number range A = 30 to 170, the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant, about 8 MeV/nucleon.
cards.quote: In the mass number range A = 30 to 170, the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant, about 8 MeV/nucleon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What conclusion about the nuclear force follows from the binding energy of a few MeV per nucleon?
cards.back: The force is attractive and sufficiently strong to produce a binding energy of a few MeV per nucleon.
cards.quote: The force is attractive and sufficiently strong to produce a binding energy of a few MeV per nucleon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The constancy of the binding energy in the range 30 < A < 170 is a consequence of the fact that the nuclear force is ____.
cards.back: The constancy of the binding energy in the range 30 < A < 170 is a consequence of the fact that the nuclear force is short-ranged.
cards.quote: The constancy of the binding energy in the range 30 < A < 170 is a consequence of the fact that the nuclear force is short-ranged.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the saturation property of the nuclear force?
cards.back: The property that a given nucleon influences only nucleons close to it is also referred to as saturation property of the nuclear force.
cards.quote: The property that a given nucleon influences only nucleons close to it is also referred to as saturation property of the nuclear force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens in energy terms if a nucleus with A = 240 breaks into two A = 120 nuclei?
cards.back: A very heavy nucleus, say A = 240, has lower binding energy per nucleon compared to that of a nucleus with A = 120. Thus if a nucleus A = 240 breaks into two A = 120 nuclei, nucleons get more tightly bound. This implies energy would be released in the process.
cards.quote: A very heavy nucleus, say A = 240, has lower binding energy per nucleon compared to that of a nucleus with A = 120. Thus if a nucleus A = 240 breaks into two A = 120 nuclei, nucleons get more tightly bound. This implies energy would be released in the process.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens in energy terms when two very light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus?
cards.back: The binding energy per nucleon of the fused heavier nuclei is more than the binding energy per nucleon of the lighter nuclei. This means that the final system is more tightly bound than the initial system. Again energy would be released in such a process of fusion.
cards.quote: The binding energy per nucleon of the fused heavier nuclei is more than the binding energy per nucleon of the lighter nuclei. This means that the final system is more tightly bound than the initial system. Again energy would be released in such a process of fusion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which force determines the motion of atomic electrons?
cards.back: The force that determines the motion of atomic electrons is the familiar Coulomb force.
cards.quote: The force that determines the motion of atomic electrons is the familiar Coulomb force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What must the nuclear binding force be strong enough to do?
cards.back: It must be strong enough to overcome the repulsion between the (positively charged) protons and to bind both protons and neutrons into the tiny nuclear volume.
cards.quote: It must be strong enough to overcome the repulsion between the (positively charged) protons and to bind both protons and neutrons into the tiny nuclear volume.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The nuclear force is much ____ than the Coulomb force acting between charges or the gravitational forces between masses.
cards.back: The nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force acting between charges or the gravitational forces between masses.
cards.quote: The nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force acting between charges or the gravitational forces between masses.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the gravitational force compare with the Coulomb force?
cards.back: The gravitational force is much weaker than even Coulomb force.
cards.quote: The gravitational force is much weaker than even Coulomb force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The nuclear force between two nucleons falls rapidly to zero as their distance is more than a few ____.
cards.back: The nuclear force between two nucleons falls rapidly to zero as their distance is more than a few femtometres.
cards.quote: The nuclear force between two nucleons falls rapidly to zero as their distance is more than a few femtometres.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Between two nucleons, when is the nuclear force attractive and when repulsive?
cards.back: This means that the force is attractive for distances larger than 0.8 fm and repulsive if they are separated by distances less than 0.8 fm.
cards.quote: This means that the force is attractive for distances larger than 0.8 fm and repulsive if they are separated by distances less than 0.8 fm.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the nuclear force between nn, pn and pp pairs compare, and does it depend on charge?
cards.back: The nuclear force between neutron-neutron, proton-neutron and proton-proton is approximately the same. The nuclear force does not depend on the electric charge.
cards.quote: The nuclear force between neutron-neutron, proton-neutron and proton-proton is approximately the same. The nuclear force does not depend on the electric charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Does the nuclear force have a simple mathematical form like Coulomb's law?
cards.back: Unlike Coulomb's law or the Newton's law of gravitation there is no simple mathematical form of the nuclear force.
cards.quote: Unlike Coulomb's law or the Newton's law of gravitation there is no simple mathematical form of the nuclear force.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What binds neutrons and protons in a nucleus, and does it distinguish between them?
cards.back: Neutrons and protons are bound in a nucleus by the short-range strong nuclear force. The nuclear force does not distinguish between neutron and proton.
cards.quote: Neutrons and protons are bound in a nucleus by the short-range strong nuclear force. The nuclear force does not distinguish between neutron and proton.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When will there be a net energy release in a nuclear transformation?
cards.back: if nuclei with less total binding energy transform to nuclei with greater binding energy, there will be a net energy release.
cards.quote: if nuclei with less total binding energy transform to nuclei with greater binding energy, there will be a net energy release.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is energy released in nuclear transmutation?
cards.back: Energy is released when less tightly bound nuclei are transmuted into more tightly bound nuclei.
cards.quote: Energy is released when less tightly bound nuclei are transmuted into more tightly bound nuclei.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What underlies conventional energy sources such as coal or petroleum?
cards.back: Exothermic chemical reactions underlie conventional energy sources such as coal or petroleum.
cards.quote: Exothermic chemical reactions underlie conventional energy sources such as coal or petroleum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Chemical vs nuclear reactions: the difference in the energy involved.
cards.back: Here the energies involved are in the range of electron volts. On the other hand, in a nuclear reaction, the energy release is of the order of MeV.
cards.quote: Here the energies involved are in the range of electron volts. On the other hand, in a nuclear reaction, the energy release is of the order of MeV.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For the same quantity of matter, how much more energy do nuclear sources produce than chemical sources?
cards.back: Thus for the same quantity of matter, nuclear sources produce a million times more energy than a chemical source.
cards.quote: Thus for the same quantity of matter, nuclear sources produce a million times more energy than a chemical source.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is nuclear fission?
cards.back: when a heavy nucleus decays into two or more intermediate mass fragments (fission)
cards.quote: when a heavy nucleus decays into two or more intermediate mass fragments (fission)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which most important neutron-induced nuclear reaction is described in NCERT?
cards.back: A most important neutron-induced nuclear reaction is fission.
cards.quote: A most important neutron-induced nuclear reaction is fission.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the order of energy released per fissioning nucleus of uranium?
cards.back: The energy released (the Q value) in the fission reaction of nuclei like uranium is of the order of 200 MeV per fissioning nucleus.
cards.quote: The energy released (the Q value) in the fission reaction of nuclei like uranium is of the order of 200 MeV per fissioning nucleus.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In what form does the disintegration energy in fission first appear, and where does it end up?
cards.back: The disintegration energy in fission events first appears as the kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons. Eventually it is transferred to the surrounding matter appearing as heat.
cards.quote: The disintegration energy in fission events first appears as the kinetic energy of the fragments and neutrons. Eventually it is transferred to the surrounding matter appearing as heat.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the source of energy in nuclear reactors?
cards.back: The source of energy in nuclear reactors, which produce electricity, is nuclear fission.
cards.quote: The source of energy in nuclear reactors, which produce electricity, is nuclear fission.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the source of the enormous energy released in an atom bomb?
cards.back: The enormous energy released in an atom bomb comes from uncontrolled nuclear fission.
cards.quote: The enormous energy released in an atom bomb comes from uncontrolled nuclear fission.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is nuclear fusion, and what is its importance in stars?
cards.back: In fusion, lighter nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus. Fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium nuclei is the source of energy of all stars including our sun.
cards.quote: In fusion, lighter nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus. Fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium nuclei is the source of energy of all stars including our sun.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is energy released when two light nuclei fuse to form a larger nucleus?
cards.back: When two light nuclei fuse to form a larger nucleus, energy is released, since the larger nucleus is more tightly bound, as seen from the binding energy curve in Fig.13.1.
cards.quote: When two light nuclei fuse to form a larger nucleus, energy is released, since the larger nucleus is more tightly bound, as seen from the binding energy curve in Fig.13.1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the fusion of two protons, what is formed and how much energy is released?
cards.back: two protons combine to form a deuteron and a positron with a release of 0.42 MeV energy
cards.quote: two protons combine to form a deuteron and a positron with a release of 0.42 MeV energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What must happen to the two nuclei for fusion to take place?
cards.back: For fusion to take place, the two nuclei must come close enough so that attractive short-range nuclear force is able to affect them.
cards.quote: For fusion to take place, the two nuclei must come close enough so that attractive short-range nuclear force is able to affect them.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why must nuclei have enough energy for fusion to take place?
cards.back: However, since they are both positively charged particles, they experience coulomb repulsion. They, therefore, must have enough energy to overcome this coulomb barrier.
cards.quote: However, since they are both positively charged particles, they experience coulomb repulsion. They, therefore, must have enough energy to overcome this coulomb barrier.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the height of the coulomb barrier depend?
cards.back: The height of the barrier depends on the charges and radii of the two interacting nuclei.
cards.quote: The height of the barrier depends on the charges and radii of the two interacting nuclei.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is thermonuclear fusion?
cards.back: When fusion is achieved by raising the temperature of the system so that particles have enough kinetic energy to overcome the coulomb repulsive behaviour, it is called thermonuclear fusion.
cards.quote: When fusion is achieved by raising the temperature of the system so that particles have enough kinetic energy to overcome the coulomb repulsive behaviour, it is called thermonuclear fusion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the source of energy output in the interior of stars?
cards.back: Thermonuclear fusion is the source of energy output in the interior of stars.
cards.quote: Thermonuclear fusion is the source of energy output in the interior of stars.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the fuel in the sun?
cards.back: Thus, the fuel in the sun is the hydrogen in its core.
cards.quote: Thus, the fuel in the sun is the hydrogen in its core.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the proton-proton cycle, what energy is released when four hydrogen atoms combine to form one helium atom?
cards.back: a release of 26.7 MeV of energy
cards.quote: a release of 26.7 MeV of energy

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For how much longer is there enough hydrogen in the sun to keep it going?
cards.back: it is estimated that there is enough hydrogen in the sun to keep it going for another 5 billion years.
cards.quote: it is estimated that there is enough hydrogen in the sun to keep it going for another 5 billion years.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What will happen to the sun after its hydrogen burning stops?
cards.back: After that, the hydrogen burning will stop and the sun will begin to cool and will start to collapse under gravity, which will raise the core temperature. The outer envelope of the sun will expand, turning it into the so called red giant.
cards.quote: After that, the hydrogen burning will stop and the sun will begin to cool and will start to collapse under gravity, which will raise the core temperature. The outer envelope of the sun will expand, turning it into the so called red giant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At the temperatures needed for controlled fusion, what is the fuel?
cards.back: At these temperatures, the fuel is a mixture of positive ions and electrons (plasma).
cards.quote: At these temperatures, the fuel is a mixture of positive ions and electrons (plasma).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the challenge in controlled fusion reactors?
cards.back: The challenge is to confine this plasma, since no container can stand such a high temperature.
cards.quote: The challenge is to confine this plasma, since no container can stand such a high temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the binding energy curve show about exothermic nuclear reactions?
cards.back: The nature of the binding energy (per nucleon) curve shows that exothermic nuclear reactions are possible, when two light nuclei fuse or when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission into nuclei with intermediate mass.
cards.quote: The nature of the binding energy (per nucleon) curve shows that exothermic nuclear reactions are possible, when two light nuclei fuse or when a heavy nucleus undergoes fission into nuclei with intermediate mass.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does fusion require very high temperatures?
cards.back: For fusion, the light nuclei must have sufficient initial energy to overcome the coulomb potential barrier. That is why fusion requires very high temperatures.
cards.quote: For fusion, the light nuclei must have sufficient initial energy to overcome the coulomb potential barrier. That is why fusion requires very high temperatures.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What wavelength range of the electromagnetic spectrum is called light?
cards.back: Electromagnetic radiation belonging to this region of the spectrum (wavelength of about 400 nm to 750 nm) is called light.
cards.quote: Electromagnetic radiation belonging to this region of the spectrum (wavelength of about 400 nm to 750 nm) is called light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The speed of light in vacuum is the ____ speed attainable in nature.
cards.back: The speed of light in vacuum is the highest speed attainable in nature.
cards.quote: The speed of light in vacuum is the highest speed attainable in nature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State the laws of reflection.
cards.back:
The angle of reflection (i.e., the angle between reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface or the mirror) equals the angle of incidence (angle between incident ray and the normal).
the incident ray, reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence lie in the same plane
cards.quote: The angle of reflection (i.e., the angle between reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface or the mirror) equals the angle of incidence (angle between incident ray and the normal). Also that the incident ray, reflected ray and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence lie in the same plane (Fig. 9.1).

source.section: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the pole of a spherical mirror and the optical centre of a spherical lens?
cards.back: the geometric centre of a spherical mirror is called its pole while that of a spherical lens is called its optical centre.
cards.quote: the geometric centre of a spherical mirror is called its pole while that of a spherical lens is called its optical centre.

source.section: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the principal axis of a spherical mirror?
cards.back: The line joining the pole and the centre of curvature of the spherical mirror is known as the principal axis.
cards.quote: The line joining the pole and the centre of curvature of the spherical mirror is known as the principal axis.

source.section: Reflection of Light by Spherical Mirrors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are paraxial rays?
cards.back: We assume that the rays are paraxial, i.e., they are incident at points close to the pole P of the mirror and make small angles with the principal axis.
cards.quote: We assume that the rays are paraxial, i.e., they are incident at points close to the pole P of the mirror and make small angles with the principal axis.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Principal focus of a concave mirror and of a convex mirror.
cards.back: The reflected rays converge at a point F on the principal axis of a concave mirror [Fig. 9.3(a)]. For a convex mirror, the reflected rays appear to diverge from a point F on its principal axis [Fig. 9.3(b)]. The point F is called the principal focus of the mirror.
cards.quote: The reflected rays converge at a point F on the principal axis of a concave mirror [Fig. 9.3(a)]. For a convex mirror, the reflected rays appear to diverge from a point F on its principal axis [Fig. 9.3(b)]. The point F is called the principal focus of the mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the focal plane of a mirror?
cards.back: If the parallel paraxial beam of light were incident, making some angle with the principal axis, the reflected rays would converge (or appear to diverge) from a point in a plane through F normal to the principal axis. This is called the focal plane of the mirror [Fig. 9.3(c)].
cards.quote: If the parallel paraxial beam of light were incident, making some angle with the principal axis, the reflected rays would converge (or appear to diverge) from a point in a plane through F normal to the principal axis. This is called the focal plane of the mirror [Fig. 9.3(c)].

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the focal length of a mirror.
cards.back: The distance between the focus F and the pole P of the mirror is called the focal length of the mirror, denoted by f.
cards.quote: The distance between the focus F and the pole P of the mirror is called the focal length of the mirror, denoted by f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: focal length f of a spherical mirror in terms of its radius of curvature R.
cards.back: f = R/2, where R is the radius of curvature of the mirror.
cards.quote: f = R/2, where R is the radius of curvature of the mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is meant by the image of a point?
cards.back: If rays emanating from a point actually meet at another point after reflection and/or refraction, that point is called the image of the first point.
cards.quote: If rays emanating from a point actually meet at another point after reflection and/or refraction, that point is called the image of the first point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Real image vs virtual image: when is each formed?
cards.back: The image is real if the rays actually converge to the point; it is virtual if the rays do not actually meet but appear to diverge from the point when produced backwards.
cards.quote: The image is real if the rays actually converge to the point; it is virtual if the rays do not actually meet but appear to diverge from the point when produced backwards.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An image is thus a ____ with the object established through reflection and/or refraction.
cards.back: An image is thus a point-to-point correspondence with the object established through reflection and/or refraction.
cards.quote: An image is thus a point-to-point correspondence with the object established through reflection and/or refraction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mirror ray diagram: a ray from the object parallel to the principal axis. Where does the reflected ray go?
cards.back: The ray from the point which is parallel to the principal axis. The reflected ray goes through the focus of the mirror.
cards.quote: The ray from the point which is parallel to the principal axis. The reflected ray goes through the focus of the mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mirror ray diagram: a ray passing through the centre of curvature. What does the reflected ray do?
cards.back: The reflected ray simply retraces the path.
cards.quote: curvature of a concave mirror or appearing to pass through it for a convex mirror. The reflected ray simply retraces the path.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mirror ray diagram: a ray passing through (or directed towards) the focus. What does the reflected ray do?
cards.back: The reflected ray is parallel to the principal axis.
cards.quote: The ray passing through (or directed towards) the focus of the concave mirror or appearing to pass through (or directed towards) the focus of a convex mirror. The reflected ray is parallel to the principal axis.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Mirror ray diagram: a ray incident at any angle at the pole. How does it reflect?
cards.back: The reflected ray follows laws of reflection.
cards.quote: The ray incident at any angle at the pole. The reflected ray follows laws of reflection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define linear magnification (m) produced by a mirror.
cards.back: We define linear magnification (m) as the ratio of the height of the image (h′) to the height of the object (h)
cards.quote: We define linear magnification (m) as the ratio of the height of the image (h′) to the height of the object (h)
cards.note: For a mirror, m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For which mirrors and images are the mirror equation and magnification formula valid?
cards.back: With the proper use of sign convention, these are, in fact, valid for all the cases of reflection by a spherical mirror (concave or convex) whether the image formed is real or virtual.
cards.quote: With the proper use of sign convention, these are, in fact, valid for all the cases of reflection by a spherical mirror (concave or convex) whether the image formed is real or virtual.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The lower half of a concave mirror is covered with opaque material. What happens to the image of an object?
cards.back: the image will be that of the whole object. However, as the area of the reflecting surface has been reduced, the intensity of the image will be low (in this case, half).
cards.quote: the image will be that of the whole object. However, as the area of the reflecting surface has been reduced, the intensity of the image will be low (in this case, half).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define refraction of light.
cards.back: The direction of propagation of an obliquely incident (0°< i < 90°) ray of light that enters the other medium, changes at the interface of the two media. This phenomenon is called refraction of light.
cards.quote: The direction of propagation of an obliquely incident (0°< i < 90°) ray of light that enters the other medium, changes at the interface of the two media. This phenomenon is called refraction of light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Snell's laws of refraction.
cards.back:
The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
cards.quote: (i) The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane. (ii) The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is constant.
cards.note: Snell's law: sin i / sin r = n21, the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a refracted ray bends towards the normal, what is the second medium said to be?
cards.back: the refracted ray bends towards the normal. In such a case medium 2 is said to be optically denser (or denser, in short) than medium 1.
cards.quote: the refracted ray bends towards the normal. In such a case medium 2 is said to be optically denser (or denser, in short) than medium 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A ray goes from a denser medium into a rarer medium. How does it bend?
cards.back: refracted ray bends away from the normal. This is the case when incident ray in a denser medium refracts into a rarer medium.
cards.quote: refracted ray bends away from the normal. This is the case when incident ray in a denser medium refracts into a rarer medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Optical density vs mass density.
cards.back: Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media).
cards.quote: Optical density should not be confused with mass density, which is mass per unit volume. It is possible that mass density of an optically denser medium may be less than that of an optically rarer medium (optical density is the ratio of the speed of light in two media).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Turpentine and water: compare their mass density and their optical density.
cards.back: Mass density of turpentine is less than that of water but its optical density is higher.
cards.quote: Mass density of turpentine is less than that of water but its optical density is higher.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A ray passes through a rectangular glass slab. Is the emergent ray deviated or shifted?
cards.back: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray—there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray.
cards.quote: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray—there is no deviation, but it does suffer lateral displacement/shift with respect to the incident ray.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is internal reflection?
cards.back: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at the interface, it is partly reflected back into the same medium and partly refracted to the second medium. This reflection is called the internal reflection.
cards.quote: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at the interface, it is partly reflected back into the same medium and partly refracted to the second medium. This reflection is called the internal reflection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, ____ of light takes place.
cards.back: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, no transmission of light takes place.
cards.quote: In total internal reflection, on the other hand, no transmission of light takes place.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is total internal reflection used in prisms?
cards.back: Prisms designed to bend light by 90° or by 180° make use of total internal reflection [Fig. 9.13(a) and (b)]. Such a prism is also used to invert images without changing their size [Fig. 9.13(c)].
cards.quote: Prisms designed to bend light by 90° or by 180° make use of total internal reflection [Fig. 9.13(a) and (b)]. Such a prism is also used to invert images without changing their size [Fig. 9.13(c)].

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an optical fibre made of, and how do the refractive indices of its parts compare?
cards.back: Each fibre consists of a core and cladding. The refractive index of the material of the core is higher than that of the cladding.
cards.quote: Each fibre consists of a core and cladding. The refractive index of the material of the core is higher than that of the cladding.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a light signal travel along an optical fibre?
cards.back: When a signal in the form of light is directed at one end of the fibre at a suitable angle, it undergoes repeated total internal reflections along the length of the fibre and finally comes out at the other end (Fig. 9.14).
cards.quote: When a signal in the form of light is directed at one end of the fibre at a suitable angle, it undergoes repeated total internal reflections along the length of the fibre and finally comes out at the other end (Fig. 9.14).

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is ____ in the intensity of the light signal.
cards.back: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is no appreciable loss in the intensity of the light signal.
cards.quote: Since light undergoes total internal reflection at each stage, there is no appreciable loss in the intensity of the light signal.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can an optical fibre act as an optical pipe even when it is bent?
cards.back: Optical fibres are fabricated such that light reflected at one side of inner surface strikes the other at an angle larger than the critical angle. Even if the fibre is bent, light can easily travel along its length. Thus, an optical fibre can be used to act as an optical pipe.
cards.quote: Optical fibres are fabricated such that light reflected at one side of inner surface strikes the other at an angle larger than the critical angle. Even if the fibre is bent, light can easily travel along its length. Thus, an optical fibre can be used to act as an optical pipe.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Give a medical use of optical fibres as a 'light pipe'.
cards.back: For example, these are used as a ‘light pipe’ to facilitate visual examination of internal organs like esophagus, stomach and intestines.
cards.quote: For example, these are used as a ‘light pipe’ to facilitate visual examination of internal organs like esophagus, stomach and intestines.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the main requirement in fabricating optical fibres?
cards.back: The main requirement in fabricating optical fibres is that there should be very little absorption of light as it travels for long distances inside them.
cards.quote: The main requirement in fabricating optical fibres is that there should be very little absorption of light as it travels for long distances inside them.

source.section: Total internal reflection in nature and its technological applications

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Optical fibres: what coats the glass fibre, and what happens to light even if the fibre is bent?
cards.back: Optical fibres consist of glass fibres coated with a thin layer of material of lower refractive index. Light incident at an angle at one end comes out at the other, after multiple internal reflections, even if the fibre is bent.
cards.quote: Optical fibres consist of glass fibres coated with a thin layer of material of lower refractive index. Light incident at an angle at one end comes out at the other, after multiple internal reflections, even if the fibre is bent.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a thin lens?
cards.back: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical.
cards.quote: A thin lens is a transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces; at least one of which should be spherical.

source.section: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the focus and the focal length of a lens.
cards.back: The point where image of an object placed at infinity is formed is called the focus F, of the lens and the distance f gives its focal length.
cards.quote: The point where image of an object placed at infinity is formed is called the focus F, of the lens and the distance f gives its focal length.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How many foci does a lens have?
cards.back: A lens has two foci, F and F′, on either side of it (Fig. 9.17).
cards.quote: A lens has two foci, F and F′, on either side of it (Fig. 9.17).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the lens maker's formula useful for?
cards.back: It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature.
cards.quote: It is useful to design lenses of desired focal length using surfaces of suitable radii of curvature.
cards.note: Lens maker's formula: 1/f = [(n2 - n1)/n1] x (1/R1 - 1/R2); n2 = lens material, n1 = surrounding medium.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the focal length f of a converging lens and of a diverging lens.
cards.back: f is positive for a converging lens; f is negative for a diverging lens.
cards.quote: f is positive for a converging lens; f is negative for a diverging lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For which lenses and images is the thin lens formula valid?
cards.back: Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula. Though we derived it for a real image formed by a convex lens, the formula is valid for both convex as well as concave lenses and for both real and virtual images.
cards.quote: Equation (9.23) is the familiar thin lens formula. Though we derived it for a real image formed by a convex lens, the formula is valid for both convex as well as concave lenses and for both real and virtual images.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where are the two foci of a double convex or concave lens, and what are they called?
cards.back: the two foci, F and F′, of a double convex or concave lens are equidistant from the optical centre. The focus on the side of the (original) source of light is called the first focal point, whereas the other is called the second focal point.
cards.quote: the two foci, F and F′, of a double convex or concave lens are equidistant from the optical centre. The focus on the side of the (original) source of light is called the first focal point, whereas the other is called the second focal point.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Rays used to locate an image formed by a lens.
cards.back:
A ray emanating from the object parallel to the principal axis of the lens after refraction passes through the second principal focus F′ (in a convex lens) or appears to diverge (in a concave lens) from the first principal focus F.
A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.
A ray of light passing through the first principal focus of a convex lens [Fig. 9.17(a)] emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction.
A ray of light incident on a concave lens appearing to meet the principal axis at second focus point emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction [Fig. 9.17(b)].
cards.quote: (i) A ray emanating from the object parallel to the principal axis of the lens after refraction passes through the second principal focus F′ (in a convex lens) or appears to diverge (in a concave lens) from the first principal focus F. (ii) A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction. (iii) (a) A ray of light passing through the first principal focus of a convex lens [Fig. 9.17(a)] emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction. (b) A ray of light incident on a concave lens appearing to meet the principal axis at second focus point emerges parallel to the principal axis after refraction [Fig. 9.17(b)].

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Lens ray diagram: what happens to a ray passing through the optical centre?
cards.back: A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.
cards.quote: A ray of light, passing through the optical centre of the lens, emerges without any deviation after refraction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the magnification (m) produced by a lens.
cards.back: Magnification (m) produced by a lens is defined, like that for a mirror, as the ratio of the size of the image to that of the object.
cards.quote: Magnification (m) produced by a lens is defined, like that for a mirror, as the ratio of the size of the image to that of the object.
cards.note: For a lens, m = h'/h = v/u.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the magnification m for an erect (virtual) image and for an inverted (real) image formed by a lens.
cards.back: When we apply the sign convention, we see that, for erect (and virtual) image formed by a convex or concave lens, m is positive, while for an inverted (and real) image, m is negative.
cards.quote: When we apply the sign convention, we see that, for erect (and virtual) image formed by a convex or concave lens, m is positive, while for an inverted (and real) image, m is negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A glass lens of refractive index 1.47 disappears in a liquid. What is the refractive index of the liquid?
cards.back: The refractive index of the liquid must be equal to 1.47 in order to make the lens disappear.
cards.quote: The refractive index of the liquid must be equal to 1.47 in order to make the lens disappear.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does the power of a lens measure?
cards.back: Power of a lens is a measure of the convergence or divergence, which a lens introduces in the light falling on it.
cards.quote: Power of a lens is a measure of the convergence or divergence, which a lens introduces in the light falling on it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the power P of a lens.
cards.back: The power P of a lens is defined as the tangent of the angle by which it converges or diverges a beam of light parallel to the principal axis falling at unit distance from the optical centre (Fig. 9.18).
cards.quote: The power P of a lens is defined as the tangent of the angle by which it converges or diverges a beam of light parallel to the principal axis falling at unit distance from the optical centre (Fig. 9.18).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: power P of a lens in terms of its focal length f.
cards.back: The power of a lens P = 1/f.
cards.quote: The power of a lens P = 1/f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the SI unit of the power of a lens?
cards.back: The SI unit for power of a lens is dioptre (D)
cards.quote: The SI unit for power of a lens is dioptre (D)

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is ____.
cards.back: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is one dioptre.
cards.quote: The power of a lens of focal length of 1 metre is one dioptre.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the power of a converging lens and of a diverging lens.
cards.back: Power of a lens is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens.
cards.quote: Power of a lens is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What lens does a power of +2.5 D mean, and what lens does -4.0 D mean?
cards.back: Thus, when an optician prescribes a corrective lens of power + 2.5 D, the required lens is a convex lens of focal length + 40 cm. A lens of power of – 4.0 D means a concave lens of focal length – 25 cm.
cards.quote: Thus, when an optician prescribes a corrective lens of power + 2.5 D, the required lens is a convex lens of focal length + 40 cm. A lens of power of – 4.0 D means a concave lens of focal length – 25 cm.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Lenses in contact: how are the individual powers added, convex and concave lenses together?
cards.back: Note that the sum in Eq. (9.32) is an algebraic sum of individual powers, so some of the terms on the right side may be positive (for convex lenses) and some negative (for concave lenses).
cards.quote: Note that the sum in Eq. (9.32) is an algebraic sum of individual powers, so some of the terms on the right side may be positive (for convex lenses) and some negative (for concave lenses).

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.note: For thin lenses in contact the net power is the sum of the individual powers, and the net 1/f is the sum of the individual 1/f values.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What do combinations of lenses help to obtain, and what do they enhance?
cards.back: Combination of lenses helps to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired magnification. It also enhances sharpness of the image.
cards.quote: Combination of lenses helps to obtain diverging or converging lenses of desired magnification. It also enhances sharpness of the image.

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where is a combination of lenses commonly used?
cards.back: Such a system of combination of lenses is commonly used in designing lenses for cameras, microscopes, telescopes and other optical instruments.
cards.quote: Such a system of combination of lenses is commonly used in designing lenses for cameras, microscopes, telescopes and other optical instruments.

source.section: Combination of thin lenses in contact

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the angle of deviation for a ray passing through a prism (incident ray PQ, emergent ray RS).
cards.back: The angle between the emergent ray RS and the direction of the incident ray PQ is called the angle of deviation
cards.quote: The angle between the emergent ray RS and the direction of the incident ray PQ is called the angle of deviation

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define dispersion of light.
cards.back: Dispersion is the splitting of light into its constituent colour.
cards.quote: Dispersion is the splitting of light into its constituent colour.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do thick lenses give coloured images?
cards.back: Thick lenses give coloured images due to dispersion.
cards.quote: Thick lenses give coloured images due to dispersion.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a simple magnifier or microscope?
cards.back: A simple magnifier or microscope is a converging lens of small focal length (Fig. 9.23).
cards.quote: A simple magnifier or microscope is a converging lens of small focal length (Fig. 9.23).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a converging lens used as a simple microscope?
cards.back: In order to use such a lens as a microscope, the lens is held near the object, one focal length away or less, and the eye is positioned close to the lens on the other side.
cards.quote: In order to use such a lens as a microscope, the lens is held near the object, one focal length away or less, and the eye is positioned close to the lens on the other side.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What image does a simple microscope aim to give?
cards.back: The idea is to get an erect, magnified and virtual image of the object at a distance so that it can be viewed comfortably, i.e., at 25 cm or more.
cards.quote: The idea is to get an erect, magnified and virtual image of the object at a distance so that it can be viewed comfortably, i.e., at 25 cm or more.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Simple microscope: where is the image if the object is at a distance f?
cards.back: If the object is at a distance f, the image is at infinity.
cards.quote: If the object is at a distance f, the image is at infinity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power m of a simple microscope.
cards.back: Magnifying power m of a simple microscope is given by m = 1 + (D/f), where D = 25 cm is the least distance of distinct vision and f is the focal length of the convex lens.
cards.quote: Magnifying power m of a simple microscope is given by m = 1 + (D/f), where D = 25 cm is the least distance of distinct vision and f is the focal length of the convex lens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Formula: magnifying power of a simple microscope when the image is at infinity.
cards.back: If the image is at infinity, m = D/f.
cards.quote: If the image is at infinity, m = D/f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a compound microscope?
cards.back: For much larger magnifications, one uses two lenses, one compounding the effect of the other. This is known as a compound microscope.
cards.quote: For much larger magnifications, one uses two lenses, one compounding the effect of the other. This is known as a compound microscope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Compound microscope: what do the objective and the eyepiece each do?
cards.back: The lens nearest the object, called the objective, forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object. This serves as the object for the second lens, the eyepiece, which functions essentially like a simple microscope or magnifier, produces the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.
cards.quote: The lens nearest the object, called the objective, forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object. This serves as the object for the second lens, the eyepiece, which functions essentially like a simple microscope or magnifier, produces the final image, which is enlarged and virtual.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Clearly, the final image is ____ with respect to the original object.
cards.back: Clearly, the final image is inverted with respect to the original object.
cards.quote: Clearly, the final image is inverted with respect to the original object.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: For large magnification, what should be true of the focal lengths of a compound microscope's objective and eyepiece?
cards.back: Clearly, to achieve a large magnification of a small object (hence the name microscope), the objective and eyepiece should have small focal lengths.
cards.quote: Clearly, to achieve a large magnification of a small object (hence the name microscope), the objective and eyepiece should have small focal lengths.

cards.subject: physics
