cards.front: Why are multicomponent lenses used in modern microscopes?
cards.back: In modern microscopes, multicomponent lenses are used for both the objective and the eyepiece to improve image quality by minimising various optical aberrations (defects) in lenses.
cards.quote: In modern microscopes, multicomponent lenses are used for both the objective and the eyepiece to improve image quality by minimising various optical aberrations (defects) in lenses.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the telescope used for?
cards.back: The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects (Fig. 9.25).
cards.quote: The telescope is used to provide angular magnification of distant objects (Fig. 9.25).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Telescope: how does the objective compare with the eyepiece?
cards.back: It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece.
cards.quote: It also has an objective and an eyepiece. But here, the objective has a large focal length and a much larger aperture than the eyepiece.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Refracting telescope: how is the final image formed?
cards.back: Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.
cards.quote: Light from a distant object enters the objective and a real image is formed in the tube at its second focal point. The eyepiece magnifies this image producing a final inverted image.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How do terrestrial telescopes make the final image erect?
cards.back: Terrestrial telescopes have, in addition, a pair of inverting lenses to make the final image erect.
cards.quote: Terrestrial telescopes have, in addition, a pair of inverting lenses to make the final image erect.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the main considerations with an astronomical telescope?
cards.back: The main considerations with an astronomical telescope are its light gathering power and its resolution or resolving power.
cards.quote: The main considerations with an astronomical telescope are its light gathering power and its resolution or resolving power.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: On what does the resolving power of a telescope depend?
cards.back: The resolving power, or the ability to observe two objects distinctly, which are in very nearly the same direction, also depends on the diameter of the objective.
cards.quote: The resolving power, or the ability to observe two objects distinctly, which are in very nearly the same direction, also depends on the diameter of the objective.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the desirable aim in making optical telescopes?
cards.back: So, the desirable aim in optical telescopes is to make them with objective of large diameter.
cards.quote: So, the desirable aim in optical telescopes is to make them with objective of large diameter.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why are very large lens objectives hard to use?
cards.back: Such big lenses tend to be very heavy and therefore, difficult to make and support by their edges.
cards.quote: Such big lenses tend to be very heavy and therefore, difficult to make and support by their edges.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a reflecting telescope, and why does it have no chromatic aberration?
cards.back: For these reasons, modern telescopes use a concave mirror rather than a lens for the objective. Telescopes with mirror objectives are called reflecting telescopes. There is no chromatic aberration in a mirror.
cards.quote: For these reasons, modern telescopes use a concave mirror rather than a lens for the objective. Telescopes with mirror objectives are called reflecting telescopes. There is no chromatic aberration in a mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is mechanical support less of a problem for a mirror objective?
cards.back: Mechanical support is much less of a problem since a mirror weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality, and can be supported over its entire back surface, not just over its rim.
cards.quote: Mechanical support is much less of a problem since a mirror weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality, and can be supported over its entire back surface, not just over its rim.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a Cassegrain telescope, and what is its advantage?
cards.back: One such arrangement using a convex secondary mirror to focus the incident light, which now passes through a hole in the objective primary mirror, is shown in Fig. 9.26. This is known as a Cassegrain telescope, after its inventor. It has the advantages of a large focal length in a short telescope.
cards.quote: One such arrangement using a convex secondary mirror to focus the incident light, which now passes through a hole in the objective primary mirror, is shown in Fig. 9.26. This is known as a Cassegrain telescope, after its inventor. It has the advantages of a large focal length in a short telescope.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Where is the largest telescope in India, and what kind is it?
cards.back: The largest telescope in India is in Kavalur, Tamil Nadu. It is a 2.34 m diameter reflecting telescope (Cassegrain).
cards.quote: The largest telescope in India is in Kavalur, Tamil Nadu. It is a 2.34 m diameter reflecting telescope (Cassegrain).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State the Cartesian sign convention.
cards.back:
Distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are positive; those measured in the opposite direction are negative.
All distances are measured from the pole/optic centre of the mirror/lens on the principal axis.
The heights measured upwards above x-axis and normal to the principal axis of the mirror/ lens are taken as positive.
The heights measured downwards are taken as negative.
cards.quote: Distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are positive; those measured in the opposite direction are negative. All distances are measured from the pole/optic centre of the mirror/lens on the principal axis. The heights measured upwards above x-axis and normal to the principal axis of the mirror/ lens are taken as positive. The heights measured downwards are taken as negative.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sign of the focal length of a concave mirror and of a convex mirror.
cards.back: f is negative for concave mirror; f is positive for a convex mirror.
cards.quote: f is negative for concave mirror; f is positive for a convex mirror.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for ____ and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.
cards.back: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for all surfaces and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.
cards.quote: The laws of reflection and refraction are true for all surfaces and pairs of media at the point of the incidence.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why do you not see your image in the page of a book?
cards.back: In principle, all rays from a given point should reach the same image point. This is why you do not see your image by an irregular reflecting object, say the page of a book.
cards.quote: In principle, all rays from a given point should reach the same image point. This is why you do not see your image by an irregular reflecting object, say the page of a book.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of metals?
cards.back: Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).
cards.quote: Metals: They possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity).

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of semiconductors?
cards.back: Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.
cards.quote: Semiconductors: They have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does NCERT describe the resistivity of insulators?
cards.back: Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).
cards.quote: Insulators: They have high resistivity (or low conductivity).

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of semiconductors (elemental and compound).
cards.back:
Elemental semiconductors: Si and Ge
Compound semiconductors
Inorganic: CdS, GaAs, CdSe, InP, etc.
Organic: anthracene, doped pthalocyanines, etc.
Organic polymers: polypyrrole, polyaniline, polythiophene, etc.
cards.quote: (i) Elemental semiconductors: Si and Ge (ii) Compound semiconductors: Examples are: Inorganic: CdS, GaAs, CdSe, InP, etc. Organic: anthracene, doped pthalocyanines, etc. Organic polymers: polypyrrole, polyaniline, polythiophene, etc.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors ____ and compound inorganic semiconductors.
cards.back: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors Si or Ge and compound inorganic semiconductors.
cards.quote: Most of the currently available semiconductor devices are based on elemental semiconductors Si or Ge and compound inorganic semiconductors.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the ____ in which it revolves.
cards.back: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the orbit in which it revolves.
cards.quote: According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of any of its electrons is decided by the orbit in which it revolves.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are energy bands?
cards.back: These different energy levels with continuous energy variation form what are called energy bands.
cards.quote: These different energy levels with continuous energy variation form what are called energy bands.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the valence band.
cards.back: The energy band which includes the energy levels of the valence electrons is called the valence band.
cards.quote: The energy band which includes the energy levels of the valence electrons is called the valence band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define the conduction band.
cards.back: The energy band above the valence band is called the conduction band.
cards.quote: The energy band above the valence band is called the conduction band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the ____.
cards.back: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the valence band.
cards.quote: With no external energy, all the valence electrons will reside in the valence band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the energy band gap (energy gap)?
cards.back: The gap between the top of the valence band and bottom of the conduction band is called the energy band gap.
cards.quote: The gap between the top of the valence band and bottom of the conduction band is called the energy band gap.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a metal where the bands overlap, what happens to the electrons of the valence band?
cards.back: When there is overlap electrons from valence band can easily move into the conduction band. This situation makes a large number of electrons available for electrical conduction.
cards.quote: When there is overlap electrons from valence band can easily move into the conduction band. This situation makes a large number of electrons available for electrical conduction.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the resistance of materials whose valence band is partially empty (metals)?
cards.back: Therefore, the resistance of such materials is low or the conductivity is high.
cards.quote: Therefore, the resistance of such materials is low or the conductivity is high.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the valence electrons if there is a gap between the valence and conduction bands?
cards.back: If there is some gap between the conduction band and the valence band, electrons in the valence band all remain bound and no free electrons are available in the conduction band. This makes the material an insulator.
cards.quote: If there is some gap between the conduction band and the valence band, electrons in the valence band all remain bound and no free electrons are available in the conduction band. This makes the material an insulator.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There are ____ in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.
cards.back: There are no electrons in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.
cards.quote: There are no electrons in the conduction band, and therefore no electrical conduction is possible.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an insulator, why can electrons not be excited to the conduction band?
cards.back: Note that the energy gap is so large that electrons cannot be excited from the valence band to the conduction band by thermal excitation. This is the case of insulators.
cards.quote: Note that the energy gap is so large that electrons cannot be excited from the valence band to the conduction band by thermal excitation. This is the case of insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why can some electrons of a semiconductor conduct at room temperature?
cards.back: Because of the small band gap, at room temperature some electrons from valence band can acquire enough energy to cross the energy gap and enter the conduction band.
cards.quote: Because of the small band gap, at room temperature some electrons from valence band can acquire enough energy to cross the energy gap and enter the conduction band.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of semiconductors compare with that of insulators?
cards.back: Hence, the resistance of semiconductors is not as high as that of the insulators.
cards.quote: Hence, the resistance of semiconductors is not as high as that of the insulators.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are the energy gaps of C (diamond), Si and Ge?
cards.back: For C (diamond), Si and Ge, the energy gaps are 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV and 0.7 eV, respectively.
cards.quote: For C (diamond), Si and Ge, the energy gaps are 5.4 eV, 1.1 eV and 0.7 eV, respectively.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Sn is a group IV element, so why is it a metal?
cards.back: Sn also is a group IV element but it is a metal because the energy gap in its case is 0 eV.
cards.quote: Sn also is a group IV element but it is a metal because the energy gap in its case is 0 eV.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the ____ between their conduction and valence bands.
cards.back: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the energy gap between their conduction and valence bands.
cards.quote: The difference in the resistivity of C, Si and Ge depends upon the energy gap between their conduction and valence bands.

source.section: Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In a Si or Ge crystal, how does each atom share electrons with its four nearest neighbours?
cards.back: In its crystalline structure, every Si or Ge atom tends to share one of its four valence electrons with each of its four nearest neighbour atoms, and also to take share of one electron from each such neighbour.
cards.quote: In its crystalline structure, every Si or Ge atom tends to share one of its four valence electrons with each of its four nearest neighbour atoms, and also to take share of one electron from each such neighbour.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a covalent bond (valence bond) in Si or Ge?
cards.back: These shared electron pairs are referred to as forming a covalent bond or simply a valence bond.
cards.quote: These shared electron pairs are referred to as forming a covalent bond or simply a valence bond.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
cards.back: This vacancy with the effective positive electronic charge is called a hole. The hole behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge.
cards.quote: This vacancy with the effective positive electronic charge is called a hole. The hole behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are intrinsic semiconductors?
cards.back: Pure semiconductors are called "intrinsic semiconductors". The presence of charge carriers (electrons and holes) is an "intrinsic" property of the material and these are obtained as a result of thermal excitation.
cards.quote: Pure semiconductors are called "intrinsic semiconductors". The presence of charge carriers (electrons and holes) is an "intrinsic" property of the material and these are obtained as a result of thermal excitation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is recombination of charge carriers, and what holds at equilibrium?
cards.back: It may be noted that apart from the process of generation of conduction electrons and holes, a simultaneous process of recombination occurs in which the electrons recombine with the holes. At equilibrium, the rate of generation is equal to the rate of recombination of charge carriers.
cards.quote: It may be noted that apart from the process of generation of conduction electrons and holes, a simultaneous process of recombination occurs in which the electrons recombine with the holes. At equilibrium, the rate of generation is equal to the rate of recombination of charge carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an ____ at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).
cards.back: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an insulator at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).
cards.quote: An intrinsic semiconductor will behave like an insulator at T = 0 K as shown in Fig. 14.6(a).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: ____ and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.
cards.back: Lattice structure and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.
cards.quote: Lattice structure and the atomic structure of constituent elements decide whether a particular material will be insulator, metal or semiconductor.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is ____.
cards.back: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is very low.
cards.quote: The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on its temperature, but at room temperature its conductivity is very low.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Example 14.1: in which orbits do the 4 bonding electrons of C, Si and Ge lie?
cards.back: The 4 bonding electrons of C, Si or Ge lie, respectively, in the second, third and fourth orbit.
cards.quote: The 4 bonding electrons of C, Si or Ge lie, respectively, in the second, third and fourth orbit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are extrinsic (impurity) semiconductors?
cards.back: When a small amount, say, a few parts per million (ppm), of a suitable impurity is added to the pure semiconductor, the conductivity of the semiconductor is increased manifold. Such materials are known as extrinsic semiconductors or impurity semiconductors.
cards.quote: When a small amount, say, a few parts per million (ppm), of a suitable impurity is added to the pure semiconductor, the conductivity of the semiconductor is increased manifold. Such materials are known as extrinsic semiconductors or impurity semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is doping, and what are the impurity atoms called?
cards.back: The deliberate addition of a desirable impurity is called doping and the impurity atoms are called dopants.
cards.quote: The deliberate addition of a desirable impurity is called doping and the impurity atoms are called dopants.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the necessary condition on the size of a dopant atom?
cards.back: A necessary condition to attain this is that the sizes of the dopant and the semiconductor atoms should be nearly the same.
cards.quote: A necessary condition to attain this is that the sizes of the dopant and the semiconductor atoms should be nearly the same.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of dopants used in doping tetravalent Si or Ge.
cards.back:
Pentavalent (valency 5); like Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Phosphorous (P), etc.
Trivalent (valency 3); like Indium (In), Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), etc.
cards.quote: There are two types of dopants used in doping the tetravalent Si or Ge: (i) Pentavalent (valency 5); like Arsenic (As), Antimony (Sb), Phosphorous (P), etc. (ii) Trivalent (valency 3); like Indium (In), Boron (B), Aluminium (Al), etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the dopant for tetravalent Si or Ge chosen from the nearby fifth or third group?
cards.back: Si or Ge belongs to the fourth group in the Periodic table and, therefore, we choose the dopant element from nearby fifth or third group, expecting and taking care that the size of the dopant atom is nearly the same as that of Si or Ge.
cards.quote: Si or Ge belongs to the fourth group in the Periodic table and, therefore, we choose the dopant element from nearby fifth or third group, expecting and taking care that the size of the dopant atom is nearly the same as that of Si or Ge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In n-type doping, what happens to the fifth electron of a +5 valency atom in the Si lattice?
cards.back: When an atom of +5 valency element occupies the position of an atom in the crystal lattice of Si, four of its electrons bond with the four silicon neighbours while the fifth remains very weakly bound to its parent atom.
cards.quote: When an atom of +5 valency element occupies the position of an atom in the crystal lattice of Si, four of its electrons bond with the four silicon neighbours while the fifth remains very weakly bound to its parent atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What energy frees the extra electron of a donor atom in germanium and in silicon?
cards.back: For example, the energy required is ~ 0.01 eV for germanium, and 0.05 eV for silicon, to separate this electron from its atom.
cards.quote: For example, the energy required is ~ 0.01 eV for germanium, and 0.05 eV for silicon, to separate this electron from its atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a donor impurity?
cards.back: Thus, the pentavalent dopant is donating one extra electron for conduction and hence is known as donor impurity.
cards.quote: Thus, the pentavalent dopant is donating one extra electron for conduction and hence is known as donor impurity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the number of electrons from donor atoms depend on the doping level and temperature?
cards.back: The number of electrons made available for conduction by dopant atoms depends strongly upon the doping level and is independent of any increase in ambient temperature.
cards.quote: The number of electrons made available for conduction by dopant atoms depends strongly upon the doping level and is independent of any increase in ambient temperature.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In an n-type semiconductor, why does the number of holes get reduced further?
cards.back: But the rate of recombination of holes would increase due to the increase in the number of electrons. As a result, the number of holes would get reduced further.
cards.quote: But the rate of recombination of holes would increase due to the increase in the number of electrons. As a result, the number of holes would get reduced further.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is an n-type semiconductor? Name its majority and minority carriers.
cards.back: Hence in an extrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent impurity, electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. These semiconductors are, therefore, known as n-type semiconductors.
cards.quote: Hence in an extrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent impurity, electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. These semiconductors are, therefore, known as n-type semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a p-type semiconductor obtained?
cards.back: This is obtained when Si or Ge is doped with a trivalent impurity like Al, B, In, etc.
cards.quote: This is obtained when Si or Ge is doped with a trivalent impurity like Al, B, In, etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In p-type doping, why does the bond with the fourth Si neighbour have a vacancy?
cards.back: The dopant has one valence electron less than Si or Ge and, therefore, this atom can form covalent bonds with neighbouring three Si atoms but does not have any electron to offer to the fourth Si atom. So the bond between the fourth neighbour and the trivalent atom has a vacancy or hole as shown in Fig. 14.8.
cards.quote: The dopant has one valence electron less than Si or Ge and, therefore, this atom can form covalent bonds with neighbouring three Si atoms but does not have any electron to offer to the fourth Si atom. So the bond between the fourth neighbour and the trivalent atom has a vacancy or hole as shown in Fig. 14.8.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively ____ when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.
cards.back: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively negatively charged when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.
cards.quote: Note that the trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively negatively charged when it shares fourth electron with neighbouring Si atom.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a p-type semiconductor? Name its majority and minority carriers.
cards.back: Thus, for such a material, the holes are the majority carriers and electrons are minority carriers. Therefore, extrinsic semiconductors doped with trivalent impurity are called p-type semiconductors.
cards.quote: Thus, for such a material, the holes are the majority carriers and electrons are minority carriers. Therefore, extrinsic semiconductors doped with trivalent impurity are called p-type semiconductors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does an extrinsic semiconductor crystal stay overall charge neutral?
cards.back: Note that the crystal maintains an overall charge neutrality as the charge of additional charge carriers is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores in the lattice.
cards.quote: Note that the crystal maintains an overall charge neutrality as the charge of additional charge carriers is just equal and opposite to that of the ionised cores in the lattice.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does a dopant reduce the concentration of minority carriers?
cards.back: Hence, the dopant, by adding a large number of current carriers of one type, which become the majority carriers, indirectly helps to reduce the intrinsic concentration of minority carriers.
cards.quote: Hence, the dopant, by adding a large number of current carriers of one type, which become the majority carriers, indirectly helps to reduce the intrinsic concentration of minority carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Types of extrinsic semiconductors.
cards.back:
n-type
p-type
cards.quote: Such semiconductors are known as extrinsic semiconductors. These are of two types (n-type and p-type).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: n-type vs p-type Si or Ge: the dopant used.
cards.back: n-type semiconducting Si or Ge is obtained by doping with pentavalent atoms (donors) like As, Sb, P, etc., while p-type Si or Ge can be obtained by doping with trivalent atom (acceptors) like B, Al, In etc.
cards.quote: n-type semiconducting Si or Ge is obtained by doping with pentavalent atoms (donors) like As, Sb, P, etc., while p-type Si or Ge can be obtained by doping with trivalent atom (acceptors) like B, Al, In etc.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Semiconductors are elemental (Si, Ge) as well as ____ (GaAs, CdS, etc.).
cards.back: Semiconductors are elemental (Si, Ge) as well as compound (GaAs, CdS, etc.).
cards.quote: Semiconductors are elemental (Si, Ge) as well as compound (GaAs, CdS, etc.).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Compare the energies of the valence and conduction bands and how filled each is.
cards.back: Valence band energies are low as compared to conduction band energies. All energy levels in the valence band are filled while energy levels in the conduction band may be fully empty or partially filled.
cards.quote: Valence band energies are low as compared to conduction band energies. All energy levels in the valence band are filled while energy levels in the conduction band may be fully empty or partially filled.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The electrons in the ____ are free to move in a solid and are responsible for the conductivity.
cards.back: The electrons in the conduction band are free to move in a solid and are responsible for the conductivity.
cards.quote: The electrons in the conduction band are free to move in a solid and are responsible for the conductivity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction: ____.
cards.back: Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction: diffusion and drift.
cards.quote: Two important processes occur during the formation of a p-n junction: diffusion and drift.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: During p-n junction formation, how do holes and electrons diffuse, and what does this give rise to?
cards.back: holes diffuse from p-side to n-side (p → n) and electrons diffuse from n-side to p-side (n → p). This motion of charge carries gives rise to diffusion current across the junction.
cards.quote: holes diffuse from p-side to n-side (p → n) and electrons diffuse from n-side to p-side (n → p). This motion of charge carries gives rise to diffusion current across the junction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When an electron diffuses from the n-side to the p-side, what does it leave behind?
cards.back: When an electron diffuses from n → p, it leaves behind an ionised donor on n-side. This ionised donor (positive charge) is immobile as it is bonded to the surrounding atoms.
cards.quote: When an electron diffuses from n → p, it leaves behind an ionised donor on n-side. This ionised donor (positive charge) is immobile as it is bonded to the surrounding atoms.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When a hole diffuses from the p-side to the n-side, what does it leave behind?
cards.back: Similarly, when a hole diffuses from p → n due to the concentration gradient, it leaves behind an ionised acceptor (negative charge) which is immobile.
cards.quote: Similarly, when a hole diffuses from p → n due to the concentration gradient, it leaves behind an ionised acceptor (negative charge) which is immobile.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the depletion region of a p-n junction?
cards.back: This space-charge region on either side of the junction together is known as depletion region as the electrons and holes taking part in the initial movement across the junction depleted the region of its free charges
cards.quote: This space-charge region on either side of the junction together is known as depletion region as the electrons and holes taking part in the initial movement across the junction depleted the region of its free charges

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the order of the thickness of the depletion region?
cards.back: The thickness of depletion region is of the order of one-tenth of a micrometre.
cards.quote: The thickness of depletion region is of the order of one-tenth of a micrometre.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What electric field develops across the junction after diffusion begins?
cards.back: Due to the positive space-charge region on n-side of the junction and negative space charge region on p-side of the junction, an electric field directed from positive charge towards negative charge develops.
cards.quote: Due to the positive space-charge region on n-side of the junction and negative space charge region on p-side of the junction, an electric field directed from positive charge towards negative charge develops.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is drift in a p-n junction?
cards.back: The motion of charge carriers due to the electric field is called drift.
cards.quote: The motion of charge carriers due to the electric field is called drift.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the drift current compare in direction with the diffusion current?
cards.back: Thus a drift current, which is opposite in direction to the diffusion current (Fig. 14.10) starts.
cards.quote: Thus a drift current, which is opposite in direction to the diffusion current (Fig. 14.10) starts.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is a p-n junction formed, and what is the net current at equilibrium?
cards.back: This process continues until the diffusion current equals the drift current. Thus a p-n junction is formed. In a p-n junction under equilibrium there is no net current.
cards.quote: This process continues until the diffusion current equals the drift current. Thus a p-n junction is formed. In a p-n junction under equilibrium there is no net current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the barrier potential of a p-n junction?
cards.back: Since this potential tends to prevent the movement of electron from the n region into the p region, it is often called a barrier potential.
cards.quote: Since this potential tends to prevent the movement of electron from the n region into the p region, it is often called a barrier potential.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Can a p-n junction be made by physically joining a slab of p-type to a slab of n-type semiconductor?
cards.back: No! Any slab, howsoever flat, will have roughness much larger than the inter-atomic crystal spacing (~2 to 3 Å) and hence continuous contact at the atomic level will not be possible. The junction will behave as a discontinuity for the flowing charge carriers.
cards.quote: No! Any slab, howsoever flat, will have roughness much larger than the inter-atomic crystal spacing (~2 to 3 Å) and hence continuous contact at the atomic level will not be possible. The junction will behave as a discontinuity for the flowing charge carriers.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the depletion layer, and what is it responsible for?
cards.back: p-n junction is the "key" to all semiconductor devices. When such a junction is made, a "depletion layer" is formed consisting of immobile ion-cores devoid of their electrons or holes. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier.
cards.quote: p-n junction is the "key" to all semiconductor devices. When such a junction is made, a "depletion layer" is formed consisting of immobile ion-cores devoid of their electrons or holes. This is responsible for a junction potential barrier.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a semiconductor diode?
cards.back: A semiconductor diode [Fig. 14.12(a)] is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for the application of an external voltage. It is a two terminal device.
cards.quote: A semiconductor diode [Fig. 14.12(a)] is basically a p-n junction with metallic contacts provided at the ends for the application of an external voltage. It is a two terminal device.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is a p-n junction diode said to be forward biased?
cards.back: When an external voltage V is applied across a semiconductor diode such that p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and n-side to the negative terminal [Fig. 14.13(a)], it is said to be forward biased.
cards.quote: When an external voltage V is applied across a semiconductor diode such that p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery and n-side to the negative terminal [Fig. 14.13(a)], it is said to be forward biased.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The applied voltage mostly drops across the ____ and the voltage drop across the p-side and n-side of the junction is negligible.
cards.back: The applied voltage mostly drops across the depletion region and the voltage drop across the p-side and n-side of the junction is negligible.
cards.quote: The applied voltage mostly drops across the depletion region and the voltage drop across the p-side and n-side of the junction is negligible.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why does the applied voltage mostly drop across the depletion region?
cards.back: This is because the resistance of the depletion region – a region where there are no charges – is very high compared to the resistance of n-side and p-side.
cards.quote: This is because the resistance of the depletion region – a region where there are no charges – is very high compared to the resistance of n-side and p-side.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Under forward bias, what happens to the current if the applied voltage is increased significantly?
cards.back: If we increase the applied voltage significantly, the barrier height will be reduced and more number of carriers will have the required energy. Thus the current increases.
cards.quote: If we increase the applied voltage significantly, the barrier height will be reduced and more number of carriers will have the required energy. Thus the current increases.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is minority carrier injection?
cards.back: Due to the applied voltage, electrons from n-side cross the depletion region and reach p-side (where they are minority carries). Similarly, holes from p-side cross the junction and reach the n-side (where they are minority carries). This process under forward bias is known as minority carrier injection.
cards.quote: Due to the applied voltage, electrons from n-side cross the depletion region and reach p-side (where they are minority carries). Similarly, holes from p-side cross the junction and reach the n-side (where they are minority carries). This process under forward bias is known as minority carrier injection.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What makes up the total diode forward current?
cards.back: The total diode forward current is sum of hole diffusion current and conventional current due to electron diffusion. The magnitude of this current is usually in mA.
cards.quote: The total diode forward current is sum of hole diffusion current and conventional current due to electron diffusion. The magnitude of this current is usually in mA.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When is a p-n junction diode said to be reverse biased?
cards.back: When an external voltage (V) is applied across the diode such that n-side is positive and p-side is negative, it is said to be reverse biased [Fig.14.15(a)].
cards.quote: When an external voltage (V) is applied across the diode such that n-side is positive and p-side is negative, it is said to be reverse biased [Fig.14.15(a)].

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Under reverse bias, what happens to the barrier height and the depletion region?
cards.back: As a result, the barrier height increases and the depletion region widens due to the change in the electric field.
cards.quote: As a result, the barrier height increases and the depletion region widens due to the change in the electric field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Forward bias vs reverse bias: the effect on the barrier.
cards.back: In forward bias (n-side is connected to negative terminal of the battery and p-side is connected to the positive), the barrier is decreased while the barrier increases in reverse bias.
cards.quote: In forward bias (n-side is connected to negative terminal of the battery and p-side is connected to the positive), the barrier is decreased while the barrier increases in reverse bias.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Under reverse bias, what happens to minority carriers that come close to the junction?
cards.back: The electric field direction of the junction is such that if electrons on p-side or holes on n-side in their random motion come close to the junction, they will be swept to its majority zone. This drift of carriers gives rise to current.
cards.quote: The electric field direction of the junction is such that if electrons on p-side or holes on n-side in their random motion come close to the junction, they will be swept to its majority zone. This drift of carriers gives rise to current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the reverse-bias current quite low?
cards.back: This is quite low because it is due to the motion of carriers from their minority side to their majority side across the junction.
cards.quote: This is quite low because it is due to the motion of carriers from their minority side to their majority side across the junction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What limits the reverse current of a diode?
cards.back: The current is not limited by the magnitude of the applied voltage but is limited due to the concentration of the minority carrier on either side of the junction.
cards.quote: The current is not limited by the magnitude of the applied voltage but is limited due to the concentration of the minority carrier on either side of the junction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens if the current through a diode exceeds the rated value?
cards.back: If the reverse current is not limited by an external circuit below the rated value (specified by the manufacturer) the p-n junction will get destroyed. Once it exceeds the rated value, the diode gets destroyed due to overheating. This can happen even for the diode under forward bias, if the forward current exceeds the rated value.
cards.quote: If the reverse current is not limited by an external circuit below the rated value (specified by the manufacturer) the p-n junction will get destroyed. Once it exceeds the rated value, the diode gets destroyed due to overheating. This can happen even for the diode under forward bias, if the forward current exceeds the rated value.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the diode current vary in the forward V-I characteristic before the threshold voltage?
cards.back: the current first increases very slowly, almost negligibly, till the voltage across the diode crosses a certain value.
cards.quote: the current first increases very slowly, almost negligibly, till the voltage across the diode crosses a certain value.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the threshold (cut-in) voltage of a diode? Give the values for Ge and Si.
cards.back: After the characteristic voltage, the diode current increases significantly (exponentially), even for a very small increase in the diode bias voltage. This voltage is called the threshold voltage or cut-in voltage (~0.2V for germanium diode and ~0.7 V for silicon diode).
cards.quote: After the characteristic voltage, the diode current increases significantly (exponentially), even for a very small increase in the diode bias voltage. This voltage is called the threshold voltage or cut-in voltage (~0.2V for germanium diode and ~0.7 V for silicon diode).

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the small, almost constant current of a diode in reverse bias called?
cards.back: almost remains constant with change in bias. It is called reverse saturation current.
cards.quote: almost remains constant with change in bias. It is called reverse saturation current.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to the diode current at very high reverse bias (break down voltage)?
cards.back: However, for special cases, at very high reverse bias (break down voltage), the current suddenly increases.
cards.quote: However, for special cases, at very high reverse bias (break down voltage), the current suddenly increases.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How does the resistance of a diode in forward bias compare with that in reverse bias, and what is this property used for?
cards.back: The forward bias resistance is low as compared to the reverse bias resistance. This property is used for rectification of ac voltages as discussed in the next section.
cards.quote: The forward bias resistance is low as compared to the reverse bias resistance. This property is used for rectification of ac voltages as discussed in the next section.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a rectifier?
cards.back: This property is used to rectify alternating voltages and the circuit used for this purpose is called a rectifier.
cards.quote: This property is used to rectify alternating voltages and the circuit used for this purpose is called a rectifier.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If an alternating voltage is applied across a diode, in which part of the cycle does current flow?
cards.back: So if an alternating voltage is applied across a diode the current flows only in that part of the cycle when the diode is forward biased.
cards.quote: So if an alternating voltage is applied across a diode the current flows only in that part of the cycle when the diode is forward biased.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a half-wave rectifier?
cards.back: If an alternating voltage is applied across a diode in series with a load, a pulsating voltage will appear across the load only during the half cycles of the ac input during which the diode is forward biased. Such rectifier circuit, as shown in Fig. 14.18, is called a half-wave rectifier.
cards.quote: If an alternating voltage is applied across a diode in series with a load, a pulsating voltage will appear across the load only during the half cycles of the ac input during which the diode is forward biased. Such rectifier circuit, as shown in Fig. 14.18, is called a half-wave rectifier.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the half-wave rectifier, when does the diode conduct and when does it not?
cards.back: When the voltage at A is positive, the diode is forward biased and it conducts. When A is negative, the diode is reverse-biased and it does not conduct.
cards.quote: When the voltage at A is positive, the diode is forward biased and it conducts. When A is negative, the diode is reverse-biased and it does not conduct.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is a full-wave rectifier?
cards.back: The circuit using two diodes, shown in Fig. 14.19(a), gives output rectified voltage corresponding to both the positive as well as negative half of the ac cycle. Hence, it is known as full-wave rectifier.
cards.quote: The circuit using two diodes, shown in Fig. 14.19(a), gives output rectified voltage corresponding to both the positive as well as negative half of the ac cycle. Hence, it is known as full-wave rectifier.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How are the two diodes of the full-wave rectifier connected to the transformer?
cards.back: Here the p-side of the two diodes are connected to the ends of the secondary of the transformer. The n-side of the diodes are connected together and the output is taken between this common point of diodes and the midpoint of the secondary of the transformer.
cards.quote: Here the p-side of the two diodes are connected to the ends of the secondary of the transformer. The n-side of the diodes are connected together and the output is taken between this common point of diodes and the midpoint of the secondary of the transformer.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Why is the transformer of a full-wave rectifier called a centre-tap transformer?
cards.back: So for a full-wave rectifier the secondary of the transformer is provided with a centre tapping and so it is called centre-tap transformer.
cards.quote: So for a full-wave rectifier the secondary of the transformer is provided with a centre tapping and so it is called centre-tap transformer.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Is there another full-wave rectifier circuit that does not need a centre-tap transformer?
cards.back: (Note that there is another circuit of full wave rectifier which does not need a centre-tap transformer but needs four diodes.)
cards.quote: (Note that there is another circuit of full wave rectifier which does not need a centre-tap transformer but needs four diodes.)

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the full-wave rectifier, how much of the cycle does each diode rectify?
cards.back: Each diode rectifies only for half the cycle, but the two do so for alternate cycles.
cards.quote: Each diode rectifies only for half the cycle, but the two do so for alternate cycles.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Full-wave vs half-wave rectifier: which is more efficient?
cards.back: Obviously, this is a more efficient circuit for getting rectified voltage or current than the half-wave rectifier.
cards.quote: Obviously, this is a more efficient circuit for getting rectified voltage or current than the half-wave rectifier.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the shape of the rectified voltage, and is its value steady?
cards.back: The rectified voltage is in the form of pulses of the shape of half sinusoids. Though it is unidirectional it does not have a steady value.
cards.quote: The rectified voltage is in the form of pulses of the shape of half sinusoids. Though it is unidirectional it does not have a steady value.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: How is a steady dc output obtained from the pulsating rectified voltage?
cards.back: To get steady dc output from the pulsating voltage normally a capacitor is connected across the output terminals
cards.quote: To get steady dc output from the pulsating voltage normally a capacitor is connected across the output terminals

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What are filters in a rectifier circuit?
cards.back: Since these additional circuits appear to filter out the ac ripple and give a pure dc voltage, so they are called filters.
cards.quote: Since these additional circuits appear to filter out the ac ripple and give a pure dc voltage, so they are called filters.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: If there is no external load, it remains charged to the ____ of the rectified output.
cards.back: If there is no external load, it remains charged to the peak voltage of the rectified output.
cards.quote: If there is no external load, it remains charged to the peak voltage of the rectified output.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is the output of a capacitor input filter close to, and where is this filter widely used?
cards.back: So capacitor input filters use large capacitors. The output voltage obtained by using capacitor input filter is nearer to the peak voltage of the rectified voltage. This type of filter is most widely used in power supplies.
cards.quote: So capacitor input filters use large capacitors. The output voltage obtained by using capacitor input filter is nearer to the peak voltage of the rectified voltage. This type of filter is most widely used in power supplies.

source.section: Application of Junction Diode as a Rectifier

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Summary: what can diodes be used for, and how is a dc voltage obtained?
cards.back: Diodes can be used for rectifying an ac voltage (restricting the ac voltage to one direction). With the help of a capacitor or a suitable filter, a dc voltage can be obtained.
cards.quote: Diodes can be used for rectifying an ac voltage (restricting the ac voltage to one direction). With the help of a capacitor or a suitable filter, a dc voltage can be obtained.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who gave the corpuscular model of light in 1637, and what did he derive with it?
cards.back: In 1637 Descartes gave the corpuscular model of light and derived Snell's law.
cards.quote: In 1637 Descartes gave the corpuscular model of light and derived Snell's law.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who put forward the wave theory of light in 1678?
cards.back: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens put forward the wave theory of light
cards.quote: In 1678, the Dutch physicist Christiaan Huygens put forward the wave theory of light

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Which scientist carried out the experiment in 1850 showing that the speed of light in water is less than in air?
cards.back: It was much later confirmed by experiments where it was shown that the speed of light in water is less than the speed in air confirming the prediction of the wave model; Foucault carried out this experiment in 1850.
cards.quote: It was much later confirmed by experiments where it was shown that the speed of light in water is less than the speed in air confirming the prediction of the wave model; Foucault carried out this experiment in 1850.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What experiment of 1801 firmly established that light is a wave phenomenon?
cards.back: when Thomas Young performed his famous interference experiment in 1801
cards.quote: However, when Thomas Young performed his famous interference experiment in 1801, it was firmly established that light is indeed a wave phenomenon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is geometrical optics?
cards.back: the branch of optics in which one completely neglects the finiteness of the wavelength is called geometrical optics and a ray is defined as the path of energy propagation in the limit of wavelength tending to zero.
cards.quote: Indeed, the branch of optics in which one completely neglects the finiteness of the wavelength is called geometrical optics and a ray is defined as the path of energy propagation in the limit of wavelength tending to zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Define a wavefront.
cards.back: a wavefront is defined as a surface of constant phase.
cards.quote: Such a locus of points, which oscillate in phase is called a wavefront; thus a wavefront is defined as a surface of constant phase.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: At a large distance from the source, a small portion of the sphere can be considered as a plane and we have what is known as a ____
cards.back: At a large distance from the source, a small portion of the sphere can be considered as a plane and we have what is known as a plane wave
cards.quote: At a large distance from the source, a small portion of the sphere can be considered as a plane and we have what is known as a plane wave

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Huygens argued that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the ____ direction and zero in the backward direction
cards.back: Huygens argued that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction
cards.quote: Huygens argued that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Who was Christiaan Huygens (1629 - 1695)?
cards.back: Dutch physicist, astronomer, mathematician and the founder of the wave theory of light.
cards.quote: Dutch physicist, astronomer, mathematician and the founder of the wave theory of light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What happens to a plane wavefront passing through a thin prism?
cards.back: Clearly, since the speed of light waves is less in glass, the lower portion of the incoming wavefront (which travels through the greatest thickness of glass) will get delayed resulting in a tilt in the emerging wavefront
cards.quote: Clearly, since the speed of light waves is less in glass, the lower portion of the incoming wavefront (which travels through the greatest thickness of glass) will get delayed resulting in a tilt in the emerging wavefront

source.section: Reflection of a Plane Wave by a Plane Surface

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What shape does the wavefront take after a plane wave passes through a thin convex lens?
cards.back: The emerging wavefront has a depression at the centre and therefore the wavefront becomes spherical and converges to the point F which is known as the focus.
cards.quote: The emerging wavefront has a depression at the centre and therefore the wavefront becomes spherical and converges to the point F which is known as the focus.

source.section: Reflection of a Plane Wave by a Plane Surface

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What does a plane wave become on reflection from a concave mirror?
cards.back: a spherical wave converging to the focal point F.
cards.quote: a plane wave is incident on a concave mirror and on reflection we have a spherical wave converging to the focal point F.

source.section: Reflection of a Plane Wave by a Plane Surface

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When monochromatic light is reflected or refracted at a surface, how does the frequency of the scattered light compare with the incident light?
cards.back: Thus, the frequency of scattered light equals the frequency of incident light.
cards.quote: Thus, the frequency of scattered light equals the frequency of incident light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Does the reduction in speed of light in a denser medium imply a reduction in the energy carried by the wave?
cards.back: No. Energy carried by a wave depends on the amplitude of the wave, not on the speed of wave propagation.
cards.quote: No. Energy carried by a wave depends on the amplitude of the wave, not on the speed of wave propagation.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When are two sources said to be coherent?
cards.back: at a particular point, the phase difference between the displacements produced by each of the waves does not change with time; when this happens the two sources are said to be coherent.
cards.quote: at a particular point, the phase difference between the displacements produced by each of the waves does not change with time; when this happens the two sources are said to be coherent.

source.section: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What is destructive interference?
cards.back: The two displacements are now out of phase and the two displacements will cancel out to give zero intensity. This is referred to as destructive interference.
cards.quote: The two displacements are now out of phase and the two displacements will cancel out to give zero intensity. This is referred to as destructive interference.

source.section: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When are two sources said to be incoherent, and what happens to the intensities?
cards.back: When the phase difference between the two vibrating sources changes rapidly with time, we say that the two sources are incoherent and when this happens the intensities just add up.
cards.quote: When the phase difference between the two vibrating sources changes rapidly with time, we say that the two sources are incoherent and when this happens the intensities just add up.

source.section: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What everyday case shows incoherent sources whose intensities just add up?
cards.back: when two separate light sources illuminate a wall.
cards.quote: This is indeed what happens when two separate light sources illuminate a wall.

source.section: Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What did Thomas Young (1773 - 1829) recognise about interference phenomena?
cards.back: recognised that interference phenomena provide proof of the wave properties of light.
cards.quote: He revived the wave theory of light and recognised that interference phenomena provide proof of the wave properties of light.

source.section: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In Young's experiment, constructive interference at a point of the screen results in what?
cards.back: a bright region
cards.quote: We will have constructive interference resulting in a bright region

source.section: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In Young's experiment, destructive interference at a point of the screen results in what?
cards.back: a dark region
cards.quote: we will have destructive interference resulting in a dark region

source.section: Interference of Light Waves and Young's Experiment

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Young's double slit of separation d gives ____ interference fringes.
cards.back: Young's double slit of separation d gives equally spaced interference fringes.
cards.quote: Young's double slit of separation d gives equally spaced interference fringes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What phenomenon causes alternate dark and bright regions close to the geometrical shadow of an opaque object?
cards.back: If we look clearly at the shadow cast by an opaque object, close to the region of geometrical shadow, there are alternate dark and bright regions just like in interference. This happens due to the phenomenon of diffraction.
cards.quote: If we look clearly at the shadow cast by an opaque object, close to the region of geometrical shadow, there are alternate dark and bright regions just like in interference. This happens due to the phenomenon of diffraction.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What causes the colours you see when a CD is viewed?
cards.back: is due to diffraction effects.
cards.quote: Indeed the colours that you see when a CD is viewed is due to diffraction effects.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: What pattern is seen when the double slit in Young's experiment is replaced by a single narrow slit lit by a monochromatic source?
cards.back: a broad pattern with a central bright region is seen. On both sides, there are alternate dark and bright regions, the intensity becoming weaker away from the centre
cards.quote: When the double slit in Young's experiment is replaced by a single narrow slit (illuminated by a monochromatic source), a broad pattern with a central bright region is seen. On both sides, there are alternate dark and bright regions, the intensity becoming weaker away from the centre

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In the single-slit analysis, how are the different parts of the wavefront at the slit treated?
cards.back: We are treating different parts of the wavefront at the slit as secondary sources. Because the incoming wavefront is parallel to the plane of the slit, these sources are in phase.
cards.quote: We are treating different parts of the wavefront at the slit as secondary sources. Because the incoming wavefront is parallel to the plane of the slit, these sources are in phase.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: A single slit of width a gives a diffraction pattern with a central ____.
cards.back: A single slit of width a gives a diffraction pattern with a central maximum.
cards.quote: A single slit of width a gives a diffraction pattern with a central maximum.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: By usage, when is a result called interference and when diffraction?
cards.back: when there are only a few sources, say two interfering sources, then the result is usually called interference, but if there is a large number of them, it seems that the word diffraction is more often used.
cards.quote: when there are only a few sources, say two interfering sources, then the result is usually called interference, but if there is a large number of them, it seems that the word diffraction is more often used.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: There is no gain or loss of energy, which is consistent with the principle of ____.
cards.back: There is no gain or loss of energy, which is consistent with the principle of conservation of energy.
cards.quote: There is no gain or loss of energy, which is consistent with the principle of conservation of energy.

source.section: Seeing the Single Slit Diffraction Pattern

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: Huygens' construction tells us that the new wavefront is the ____ envelope of the secondary waves.
cards.back: Huygens' construction tells us that the new wavefront is the forward envelope of the secondary waves.
cards.quote: Huygens' construction tells us that the new wavefront is the forward envelope of the secondary waves.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: State Huygens' principle.
cards.back: Huygens' principle tells us that each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary waves, which add up to give the wavefront at a later time.
cards.quote: Huygens' principle tells us that each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary waves, which add up to give the wavefront at a later time.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: The limit of the ability of microscopes and telescopes to distinguish very close objects is set by the ____ of light.
cards.back: The limit of the ability of microscopes and telescopes to distinguish very close objects is set by the wavelength of light.
cards.quote: The limit of the ability of microscopes and telescopes to distinguish very close objects is set by the wavelength of light.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: In which direction does the energy of a wave travel with respect to the wavefront?
cards.back: in a direction perpendicular to the wavefront.
cards.quote: in a direction perpendicular to the wavefront.

cards.subject: physics
cards.front: When the speed of light is independent of direction, the secondary waves are ____.
cards.back: When the speed of light is independent of direction, the secondary waves are spherical.
cards.quote: When the speed of light is independent of direction, the secondary waves are spherical.
